topic:mt_AzTrT5ySCx:name: AI in Daily Life
topic:mt_AzTrT5ySCx:description: Spotting AI in daily life: face unlock on a phone, video recommendations, spelling auto-correct, automatic doors that detect people; technology that seems to 'know' things
topic:mt_AzTrT5ySCx:assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} point out several things they use every day — like auto-correct or face unlock — and explain that these are examples of AI?

topic:mt_XbGfVhfiUz:name: Computers in Everyday Life
topic:mt_XbGfVhfiUz:description: Identifying computers in everyday life — not just laptops but phones, tablets, smart speakers, traffic lights, washing machines; what makes something a computer

topic:mt_XbGfVhfiUz:evidence:0: Point out at least five everyday objects that contain computers
topic:mt_XbGfVhfiUz:evidence:1: Explain what all computers have in common (they follow instructions and process information)

topic:mt_jvJ35MmCvK:name: Real-World Robots

topic:mt_WRRv1ABECC:name: Smart Versus Not-Smart Devices
topic:mt_WRRv1ABECC:description: Sorting objects into 'smart' (can sense and respond) and 'not smart' (just sits there); a toaster vs a smart speaker; introduction to the idea that some machines can sense and respond to the world
topic:mt_WRRv1ABECC:assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain the difference between a normal light switch and one that turns on automatically when you walk into a room?
topic:mt_WRRv1ABECC:evidence:0: Sort a set of objects into 'smart' (responds to input) and 'not smart' (does the same thing every time)

topic:mt_WRRv1ABECC:evidence:2: Give an example of a machine that senses something and responds (automatic door, motion-sensor light)
topic:mt__p5n8z5soJ:name: Step-by-Step Instructions

topic:mt_u6SYiVx7FX:name: Voice Assistants and How They Work
topic:mt_u6SYiVx7FX:description: What happens when you talk to Alexa, Siri, or Google Assistant; they listen, try to understand, look up answers; sometimes they get it wrong; they are tools, not alive

topic:mt_u6SYiVx7FX:evidence:0: Describe the steps that happen when you ask a voice assistant a question (it listens, processes words, finds an answer, speaks back)
topic:mt_u6SYiVx7FX:evidence:1: Give an example of a time a voice assistant might get something wrong
topic:mt_u6SYiVx7FX:evidence:2: Explain that a voice assistant is a computer program, not a person — it doesn't understand or feel
topic:mt_fT4G0QloX5:name: AI in Computer Games
topic:mt_fT4G0QloX5:description: How computer game characters 'decide' what to do; simple rule-based AI vs learning AI; NPCs, difficulty adjustment; AI as the opponent in chess or board games

topic:mt_fT4G0QloX5:evidence:0: Explain how a computer opponent in a game decides its moves

topic:mt_fT4G0QloX5:evidence:2: Give an example of AI making a game more fun (adjusting difficulty, generating levels)
topic:mt_bPFToj0OhZ:name: AI Mistakes and Limitations

topic:mt_bPFToj0OhZ:evidence:2: Describe why AI is not magic — it follows mathematical rules applied to data
topic:mt_kH1DzOPsXG:name: Data and Information for Computers
topic:mt_kH1DzOPsXG:description: What data is: information that computers use — numbers, words, pictures, sounds; everything a computer knows comes from data that people give it

topic:mt_kH1DzOPsXG:evidence:1: Give at least three examples of data they create every day (photos, messages, search queries)
topic:mt_kH1DzOPsXG:evidence:2: Explain that a computer only knows what it has been given — it has no knowledge of its own
topic:mt_oajUvqAiBJ:name: Humans Versus Machines
topic:mt_oajUvqAiBJ:description: Comparing human and machine capabilities: creativity, empathy, common sense vs speed, memory, repetition; the Turing Test (simplified); what makes humans unique

topic:mt_K6qtan847r:name: Machine Learning Basics
topic:mt_K6qtan847r:description: How machine learning works at a conceptual level: show the computer many examples, it finds patterns, then it makes predictions about new things; hands-on experience with Teachable Machine or similar tool

topic:mt_ofOGCQ7FWj:name: Patterns and Classification

topic:mt_EedcpioR0v:name: Recommendation Systems and Filter Bubbles

topic:mt_cVp_nop-5L:name: AI and Fairness in Decisions

topic:mt_cVp_nop-5L:evidence:2: Suggest who should be responsible if an AI system makes an unfair decision

topic:mt__AWSThGJ0d:name: AI and the Future of Work
topic:mt__AWSThGJ0d:description: How AI is changing the world of work: some jobs disappear, new ones are created, many change; jobs AI can't do (yet); what skills matter in an AI world

topic:mt_HopZomN12L:name: AI Data Collection and Privacy

topic:mt_HopZomN12L:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that apps and websites collect information about what they do online, and could they explain why that matters?

topic:mt_scBgiMKhG_:name: Reading for Meaning

topic:mt_aFvsj35QzC:name: Main Topic of Informational Texts

topic:mt_fL1Xz8ostr:name: Expressive and Sensory Language

topic:mt_ZhUuT__i2H:name: Non-Fiction Text Features

topic:mt_zlSoIKPyId:name: Retelling Stories with Structure

topic:mt_v33BwiyRnd:name: Story Lessons and Morals

topic:mt_aVZJhPbc_1:name: Text Features & Presentation

topic:mt_4IxR66uGLc:name: Poems, Drama & Prose
topic:mt_4IxR66uGLc:description: Explain major differences between poems, drama, and prose, identifying structural elements unique to each form: verse, rhythm, and meter in poetry; cast of characters, dialogue, and stage directions in drama; chapters and paragraphs in prose
topic:mt_4IxR66uGLc:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at a poem, a play, and a chapter from a novel and explain how each is laid out differently — for example, that a play has stage directions and a poem has verses?
topic:mt_4IxR66uGLc:evidence:0: Compare a poem, a play script, and a prose passage on a similar theme, identifying the structural features unique to each form (e.g. stanzas vs scenes vs chapters)
topic:mt_4IxR66uGLc:evidence:1: Identify and explain the function of structural elements in drama: cast list, stage directions (in italics or brackets), dialogue format, and scene divisions
topic:mt_4IxR66uGLc:evidence:2: Describe how structural elements of poetry such as verse, rhythm, meter, and line breaks affect how a poem is read aloud and how meaning is conveyed
topic:mt_0MfpLj0Uhb:name: Recommending Books
topic:mt_0MfpLj0Uhb:description: Recommend books to peers, giving reasons for choices based on knowledge of a wide range of genres, authors, and themes, and making comparisons within and across books
topic:mt_0MfpLj0Uhb:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} recommends a book to a friend, can they explain clearly why they think that person would enjoy it — mentioning the genre, characters, and themes rather than just saying "it's good"?
topic:mt_0MfpLj0Uhb:evidence:0: Recommend a book to a peer by explaining its genre, theme, and what makes it engaging, comparing it to other books the peer has enjoyed
topic:mt_0MfpLj0Uhb:evidence:1: Justify a book recommendation by referring to specific features such as the author's style, the plot structure, or how a theme is developed
topic:mt_0MfpLj0Uhb:evidence:2: Maintain a reading log or book review collection that captures key responses to books read and serves as a reference for future recommendations
topic:mt_oVwNnjYPUY:name: Structure of information texts
topic:mt_oVwNnjYPUY:description: Describe the overall structure of an informational text (chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) and explain how the author's chosen structure helps convey information and ideas
topic:mt_oVwNnjYPUY:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a non-fiction text, can they identify how it's organised — for example, "this one is structured as a problem and solution" or "this one goes through events in time order" — and explain why that structure works?
topic:mt_oVwNnjYPUY:evidence:0: Identify which organisational structure an informational text uses (chronological order, compare/contrast, cause/effect, or problem/solution) and cite textual features that signal it
topic:mt_oVwNnjYPUY:evidence:1: Explain how signal words (first, then, finally for chronology; however, similarly for comparison; because, as a result for cause/effect; the solution was for problem/solution) reveal text structure
topic:mt_oVwNnjYPUY:evidence:2: Compare two informational texts on the same topic that use different structures and explain how each structure affects the way information is presented to the reader
topic:mt_t06dHX2ZYw:name: Text & Media Connections
topic:mt_t06dHX2ZYw:description: Make connections between the text of a story or drama and a visual or oral presentation of the text, identifying where each version reflects specific descriptions and directions from the text
topic:mt_t06dHX2ZYw:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has read a book and then seen a film version, can they compare the two — pointing out moments where the film showed something differently from how the book described it?
topic:mt_t06dHX2ZYw:evidence:0: Compare a passage from a book with a film or audio adaptation, identifying specific moments where the visual or oral version matches or departs from the written text
topic:mt_t06dHX2ZYw:evidence:1: Explain how a film, illustration, or dramatic performance interprets a scene from a story, citing specific textual descriptions the adaptation reflects
topic:mt_t06dHX2ZYw:evidence:2: Identify details in the written text (descriptions of setting, character appearance, dialogue) that a visual or oral presentation brings to life, and note any differences
topic:mt_tX0R4-4WXy:name: Themes Across Cultures and Traditions
topic:mt_tX0R4-4WXy:description: Compare and contrast the treatment of similar themes, topics, and story patterns (e.g., good vs evil, quest narratives, trickster tales) in stories, myths, and traditional literature from different cultures
topic:mt_tX0R4-4WXy:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has read two quest stories from different cultures — like a Greek myth and a West African folktale — can they compare how each treats the hero's journey and what values each story prizes?
topic:mt_tX0R4-4WXy:evidence:0: Compare how two myths or folk tales from different cultures treat a similar theme (e.g., creation, heroism, the importance of honesty) and explain both similarities and differences
topic:mt_tX0R4-4WXy:evidence:1: Identify recurring story patterns across cultures such as the trickster figure, the quest, or the transformation, providing specific examples from texts read
topic:mt_tX0R4-4WXy:evidence:2: Explain how cultural context shapes the way a universal theme is expressed differently in stories from various traditions
topic:mt_sUVOS2jH3J:name: Comparing Books
topic:mt_sUVOS2jH3J:description: Make comparisons within and across books, identifying similarities and differences in themes, characters, settings, and authorial choices across multiple texts
topic:mt_sUVOS2jH3J:assessmentPrompt: After reading a few books by the same author or in the same genre, can {{name}} compare them — discussing what themes, styles, or character types the author tends to use?
topic:mt_sUVOS2jH3J:evidence:0: Compare how two authors develop similar themes using different narrative techniques
topic:mt_sUVOS2jH3J:evidence:1: Identify similarities and differences between characters across books by the same author
topic:mt_sUVOS2jH3J:evidence:2: Analyse how settings function differently in two texts from the same genre
topic:mt_WRlJ0-hAOG:name: Comparing Characters, Settings and Events
topic:mt_WRlJ0-hAOG:description: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details about how characters interact, settings influence action, or events connect
topic:mt_WRlJ0-hAOG:assessmentPrompt: After reading a novel with several main characters, can {{name}} compare two of them in detail — explaining how their personalities, experiences, and relationships are both similar and different?
topic:mt_WRlJ0-hAOG:evidence:0: Create a Venn diagram comparing two characters' traits using textual evidence
topic:mt_WRlJ0-hAOG:evidence:1: Explain how a change in setting affects the mood and characters' actions in a story
topic:mt_WRlJ0-hAOG:evidence:2: Analyse how two events in a narrative are connected through cause and effect
topic:mt_-1okUh0Jdv:name: Comparing Structure in Information Texts
topic:mt_-1okUh0Jdv:description: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more informational texts, identifying patterns such as chronology, comparison, cause/effect, or problem/solution
topic:mt_-1okUh0Jdv:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads two non-fiction texts about the same topic that are organised differently — one in time order and one comparing two sides — can they describe those structural differences and explain how each one shapes the reader's experience?
topic:mt_-1okUh0Jdv:evidence:0: Identify the organisational structure of two texts on the same topic
topic:mt_-1okUh0Jdv:evidence:1: Explain how one text uses cause/effect while another uses problem/solution to present information
topic:mt_-1okUh0Jdv:evidence:2: Analyse why an author chose a particular structure for their informational text
topic:mt_LCJNRaRXtW:name: Different viewpoints in texts
topic:mt_LCJNRaRXtW:description: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described, recognising the difference between limited and omniscient narration and how perspective shapes storytelling
topic:mt_LCJNRaRXtW:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a story told by an all-knowing narrator feels different from one told by a single character who only knows their own side — and give an example of how that changes what the reader knows?
topic:mt_LCJNRaRXtW:evidence:0: Identify whether a story uses first-person or third-person narration and explain the effect
topic:mt_LCJNRaRXtW:evidence:1: Explain how events would be described differently if told from another character's perspective
topic:mt_LCJNRaRXtW:evidence:2: Analyse how the narrator's knowledge or bias affects what information the reader receives
topic:mt_iv-BJS9W60:name: Explaining Relationships in Texts
topic:mt_iv-BJS9W60:description: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in historical, scientific, or technical texts based on specific information
topic:mt_iv-BJS9W60:assessmentPrompt: After reading a history or science text about how two events or discoveries were connected, can {{name}} explain that relationship clearly — describing how one thing led to or influenced the other?
topic:mt_iv-BJS9W60:evidence:0: Explain the cause-and-effect relationship between events in a historical text
topic:mt_iv-BJS9W60:evidence:1: Describe how a scientific process involves sequential steps that depend on each other
topic:mt_iv-BJS9W60:evidence:2: Identify how key individuals in a text influenced events or other people
topic:mt_V6456X6pJE:name: Fact vs opinion
topic:mt_V6456X6pJE:description: Distinguish between statements of fact and statements of opinion in texts, recognising how authors blend factual information with subjective viewpoints
topic:mt_V6456X6pJE:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a newspaper article or non-fiction text, can they point out which parts are facts and which parts are the author's opinions — and explain how they can tell the difference?
topic:mt_V6456X6pJE:evidence:0: Identify and label statements as fact or opinion in a newspaper article
topic:mt_V6456X6pJE:evidence:1: Explain why a statement is a fact by citing verifiable evidence or why it is an opinion
topic:mt_V6456X6pJE:evidence:2: Recognise persuasive techniques that present opinions as if they were facts
topic:mt_jO0gHMk7Ti:name: How Authors Treat Similar Themes
topic:mt_jO0gHMk7Ti:description: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre on their approaches to similar themes and topics, identifying how different authors treat common ideas
topic:mt_jO0gHMk7Ti:assessmentPrompt: After reading two adventure stories in the same genre, can {{name}} compare how each author handled similar elements — like the hero's challenge or the resolution — and say which approach they preferred and why?
topic:mt_jO0gHMk7Ti:evidence:0: Compare how two mystery stories create suspense using different techniques
topic:mt_jO0gHMk7Ti:evidence:1: Identify common themes in adventure stories and explain how each author develops them differently
topic:mt_jO0gHMk7Ti:evidence:2: Analyse how two authors from the same genre approach the theme of friendship or courage
topic:mt_furAIwoO9t:name: How Language Choices Affect the Reader
topic:mt_furAIwoO9t:description: Evaluate how authors use language including figurative language, considering the impact of word choices, imagery, and literary devices on the reader
topic:mt_furAIwoO9t:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a descriptive passage with figurative language — like "the sun was a burning eye" — can they explain what image or feeling the author was creating and whether it was effective?
topic:mt_furAIwoO9t:evidence:0: Explain how a specific metaphor or simile affects the reader's understanding or emotions
topic:mt_furAIwoO9t:evidence:1: Evaluate an author's choice of descriptive language and its impact on atmosphere
topic:mt_furAIwoO9t:evidence:2: Compare how different authors use figurative language to achieve similar effects
topic:mt_PetJM-AYz9:name: How Parts Build a Whole Text
topic:mt_PetJM-AYz9:description: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to provide the overall structure of a story, drama, or poem, analysing how each part contributes to the whole
topic:mt_PetJM-AYz9:assessmentPrompt: After finishing a novel, can {{name}} explain how each chapter contributed to the whole — like how an early chapter introduced a tension that wasn't resolved until much later?
topic:mt_PetJM-AYz9:evidence:0: Map the structure of a novel showing how each chapter advances plot or character development
topic:mt_PetJM-AYz9:evidence:1: Explain how individual stanzas in a poem build toward a central theme or message
topic:mt_PetJM-AYz9:evidence:2: Analyse how scenes in a play work together to develop conflict and resolution
topic:mt_IX37F4rNed:name: Justifying Views About Texts
topic:mt_IX37F4rNed:description: Provide reasoned justifications for views about texts, supporting interpretations and opinions with evidence and logical arguments
topic:mt_IX37F4rNed:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} shares an opinion about a book — like "I think the villain had a point" — can they back it up with specific quotes or events from the text, rather than just saying how they feel?
topic:mt_IX37F4rNed:evidence:0: State an opinion about a character's motivations and support it with three pieces of textual evidence
topic:mt_IX37F4rNed:evidence:1: Construct a reasoned argument about an author's message using quotes from the text
topic:mt_IX37F4rNed:evidence:2: Respond to an alternative interpretation by providing counter-evidence from the text
topic:mt_xsk3iuNVVI:name: Multimedia elements in texts
topic:mt_xsk3iuNVVI:description: Analyse how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text such as graphic novels, multimedia presentations, or illustrated editions of fiction and poetry
topic:mt_xsk3iuNVVI:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a graphic novel or illustrated book, can they explain how the pictures and layout — not just the words — help tell the story or create a particular mood?
topic:mt_xsk3iuNVVI:evidence:0: Explain how illustrations in a graphic novel convey emotion or advance the story
topic:mt_xsk3iuNVVI:evidence:1: Analyse how visual elements such as colour and layout affect the tone of a multimedia text
topic:mt_xsk3iuNVVI:evidence:2: Compare how the same scene is portrayed in text versus in visual or audio format
topic:mt_5FREdVoS8s:name: Multiple Accounts of Events
topic:mt_5FREdVoS8s:description: Analyse multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent
topic:mt_5FREdVoS8s:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads two different accounts of the same event — like two news articles covering the same story — can they explain what each account emphasises, what each leaves out, and why the perspectives differ?
topic:mt_5FREdVoS8s:evidence:0: Compare two news articles about the same event and identify differences in perspective
topic:mt_5FREdVoS8s:evidence:1: Explain how the author's background or purpose affects their account of an event
topic:mt_5FREdVoS8s:evidence:2: Identify which facts are consistent across accounts and which details differ based on viewpoint
topic:mt_ak_ZgoMKRQ:name: Quoting Accurately from Texts
topic:mt_ak_ZgoMKRQ:description: Quote accurately from literary and informational texts when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences, using quotation marks and citations correctly
topic:mt_ak_ZgoMKRQ:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about a book or article for school, do they quote from the text directly — putting the exact words in speech marks — to support their points?
topic:mt_ak_ZgoMKRQ:evidence:0: Select and copy exact words from a text to support an inference about character motivation
topic:mt_ak_ZgoMKRQ:evidence:1: Use quotation marks correctly when incorporating textual evidence into written responses
topic:mt_ak_ZgoMKRQ:evidence:2: Introduce quotes with signal phrases such as 'The author states' or 'According to the text'
topic:mt_XnRhhEqJLJ:name: Summarising Non-Fiction Main Ideas
topic:mt_XnRhhEqJLJ:description: Determine two or more main ideas of an informational text and explain how they are supported by key details, then summarise the text without personal opinions
topic:mt_XnRhhEqJLJ:assessmentPrompt: After reading a long non-fiction article, can {{name}} identify two or three main ideas it covers and write a brief summary that captures all of them — without adding their own opinions?

topic:mt_XnRhhEqJLJ:evidence:1: List key details that support each main idea in a multi-paragraph text
topic:mt_XnRhhEqJLJ:evidence:2: Write an objective summary capturing the main ideas without adding personal opinions
topic:mt_S3XMQOYt_D:name: Supporting ideas with evidence
topic:mt_S3XMQOYt_D:description: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which specific points
topic:mt_S3XMQOYt_D:assessmentPrompt: After reading a persuasive text, can {{name}} map out which reasons the author uses to support which specific points — showing that they understand the structure of the argument, not just the conclusion?
topic:mt_S3XMQOYt_D:evidence:0: Match each of an author's main points with the evidence used to support it
topic:mt_S3XMQOYt_D:evidence:1: Evaluate whether the evidence provided adequately supports the author's argument
topic:mt_S3XMQOYt_D:evidence:2: Identify points in a text that lack sufficient evidence or reasoning
topic:mt_kJ4xXKL_nO:name: Synthesising across multiple texts

topic:mt_kJ4xXKL_nO:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a school report using several sources, do they bring together information from all of them into their own words — rather than just quoting or copying from one source at a time?
topic:mt_kJ4xXKL_nO:evidence:0: Combine information from three sources into a coherent paragraph using own words

topic:mt_JVVKT-_AD9:name: Using Multiple Sources
topic:mt_JVVKT-_AD9:description: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or solve a problem efficiently
topic:mt_JVVKT-_AD9:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} needs to answer a research question for school, can they search across several books or websites to find the relevant information quickly — rather than reading every source from start to finish?
topic:mt_JVVKT-_AD9:evidence:0: Use search features, indexes, and headings to locate specific information across sources
topic:mt_JVVKT-_AD9:evidence:1: Synthesise information from two or more sources to answer a research question
topic:mt_JVVKT-_AD9:evidence:2: Evaluate which source provides the most relevant information for a given question
topic:mt_II6iw4BmJI:name: Analysing Text Structure
topic:mt_II6iw4BmJI:description: Analyse how a text's structure — including its overall organisation, use of chapters, stanzas, scenes, paragraphs, or sections — contributes to its meaning, style, and development of ideas
topic:mt_II6iw4BmJI:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} analyses a poem or novel, can they explain how the author's structural choices — like starting in the middle of the action, or ending with a repeated image — shape the overall meaning of the text?
topic:mt_II6iw4BmJI:evidence:0: Explain how a non-chronological structure (e.g., flashback, frame narrative) creates suspense or surprise
topic:mt_II6iw4BmJI:evidence:1: Analyse the role of a specific paragraph in developing and refining a key concept in a non-fiction text
topic:mt_II6iw4BmJI:evidence:2: Compare how two texts use different structures (e.g., epistolary vs. linear narrative) and the effect of each
topic:mt_1GF5MeNZPA:name: Critical comparison across texts

topic:mt_1GF5MeNZPA:assessmentPrompt: After reading texts from very different times or cultures, can {{name}} compare them thoughtfully — noting not just surface similarities but deeper differences in values, style, and what the author assumed about their reader?
topic:mt_1GF5MeNZPA:evidence:0: Compare how two novels treat a shared theme (e.g., growing up) using specific evidence from both
topic:mt_1GF5MeNZPA:evidence:1: Analyse how a modern retelling draws on and transforms elements from a traditional story or myth
topic:mt_1GF5MeNZPA:evidence:2: Compare conflicting accounts of the same event in two non-fiction texts and evaluate which is more convincing

topic:mt_gMSFymQlrW:description: Evaluate arguments and claims in non-fiction texts — assess whether reasoning is sound, evidence is relevant and sufficient, distinguish between fact and opinion, and recognise bias, propaganda, and rhetorical techniques
topic:mt_gMSFymQlrW:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a persuasive piece — like an editorial or a speech — can they identify the rhetorical techniques being used, evaluate whether the argument is logically sound, and explain what might be biased or misleading?
topic:mt_gMSFymQlrW:evidence:0: Identify the main claim in an argument text and evaluate whether the evidence presented is sufficient
topic:mt_gMSFymQlrW:evidence:1: Spot logical fallacies or irrelevant evidence introduced to distract from weak reasoning
topic:mt_gMSFymQlrW:evidence:2: Compare two opposing arguments on the same issue and evaluate which is more convincing, with reasons
topic:mt_DVSHx3YMkN:name: Figurative Language and Literary Devices
topic:mt_DVSHx3YMkN:description: Determine the meaning of figurative and connotative language in context, analyse the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, and identify literary devices such as metaphor, simile, personification, allusion, and irony
topic:mt_DVSHx3YMkN:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a passage containing a metaphor, irony, or allusion, can they explain what the author really meant — going beyond the literal words to describe the effect that device creates for the reader?
topic:mt_DVSHx3YMkN:evidence:0: Identify a metaphor or simile in a passage and explain its effect on the reader
topic:mt_DVSHx3YMkN:evidence:1: Explain how an author's word choice creates a particular tone (e.g., menacing, humorous, melancholic)
topic:mt_DVSHx3YMkN:evidence:2: Recognise an allusion to a myth, the Bible, or another text and explain what it adds to the meaning
topic:mt_x2sWtfTeYT:name: Narrative Perspective and Unreliable Narrators
topic:mt_x2sWtfTeYT:description: Analyse point of view and narrative perspective — including first person, third person limited and omniscient, and unreliable narrator — and how the author's or narrator's perspective shapes the reader's understanding and creates effects such as suspense, irony, or humour

topic:mt_x2sWtfTeYT:evidence:0: Identify the narrative perspective of a text and explain how it limits or expands the reader's knowledge
topic:mt_x2sWtfTeYT:evidence:1: Explain how dramatic irony arises when the reader knows something a character does not
topic:mt_x2sWtfTeYT:evidence:2: Compare how the same event might be told differently from two characters' perspectives
topic:mt_Hqz5y_tWz2:name: Plot Structure and Character Development
topic:mt_Hqz5y_tWz2:description: Analyse how plot structure unfolds through episodes or key events, and how characters develop, respond to challenges, and change over the course of a narrative — including the relationship between character, setting, and plot
topic:mt_Hqz5y_tWz2:assessmentPrompt: After reading a novel, can {{name}} explain how the main character changed from the beginning to the end — pointing to specific events that caused that change and how the setting shaped who they became?
topic:mt_Hqz5y_tWz2:evidence:0: Trace how a character's attitude changes across a story and identify the turning points
topic:mt_Hqz5y_tWz2:evidence:1: Explain how a specific incident in a drama propels the action or provokes a decision
topic:mt_Hqz5y_tWz2:evidence:2: Analyse how the setting influences a character's behaviour or the mood of a scene
topic:mt_aClzPBiS9k:name: Poetic forms and conventions
topic:mt_aClzPBiS9k:description: Recognise and understand poetic conventions — including form (sonnet, ballad, free verse), metre, rhyme scheme, stanza structure, imagery, and sound devices (alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia) — and analyse how poets use them for effect
topic:mt_aClzPBiS9k:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a poem, can they identify its form — like a sonnet or a ballad — and explain how the poet's use of rhyme, rhythm, and imagery contributes to the poem's meaning or emotional impact?
topic:mt_aClzPBiS9k:evidence:0: Identify the form of a poem (e.g., sonnet, haiku, ballad) and explain its key structural features
topic:mt_aClzPBiS9k:evidence:1: Analyse how a poet uses rhythm or sound devices to reinforce meaning or mood
topic:mt_aClzPBiS9k:evidence:2: Explain how enjambment or a caesura affects the pace and emphasis of a line
topic:mt_jIcgbCmziD:name: Purpose, audience, and context
topic:mt_jIcgbCmziD:description: Identify the purpose, audience, and context of a text and use this knowledge to support comprehension — recognising how writing aimed at different audiences (academic, popular, persuasive) uses different conventions, register, and tone
topic:mt_jIcgbCmziD:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads something written for a very different audience — like a scientific journal article versus a children's book on the same topic — can they explain how the purpose and audience shaped the language, tone, and structure?
topic:mt_jIcgbCmziD:evidence:0: Identify the intended audience and purpose of a text and explain how the language choices reflect this
topic:mt_jIcgbCmziD:evidence:1: Compare a newspaper article and a scientific report on the same topic, noting differences in register and structure
topic:mt_jIcgbCmziD:evidence:2: Explain how knowing the historical or social context of a text deepens understanding
topic:mt_wGxq92Na5g:name: Tracing Theme Across a Text

topic:mt_wGxq92Na5g:assessmentPrompt: After reading a novel or long poem, can {{name}} explain what it was really about at its deepest level — the central idea or theme — and trace how that idea developed through key moments in the text?
topic:mt_wGxq92Na5g:evidence:0: Identify a theme in a novel and explain how specific events develop it across the plot
topic:mt_wGxq92Na5g:evidence:1: Distinguish between the topic of a text (what it is about) and the theme (what it is saying)
topic:mt_wGxq92Na5g:evidence:2: Write a concise, objective summary of a chapter or article without inserting personal opinion
topic:mt_tIi6L1n7kF:name: Understanding drama and performance
topic:mt_tIi6L1n7kF:description: Understand how dramatists communicate meaning through performance — including staging, direction, set design, lighting, and actors' choices — and how different productions can interpret the same script differently
topic:mt_tIi6L1n7kF:assessmentPrompt: After watching a stage or film production of a play they've read, can {{name}} discuss how specific choices — like the lighting, the actor's tone, or the set design — interpreted the script, and whether they agreed with those choices?
topic:mt_tIi6L1n7kF:evidence:0: Explain how a director's staging choices (e.g., set, lighting, blocking) affect the audience's understanding
topic:mt_tIi6L1n7kF:evidence:1: Compare two productions or adaptations of the same play and evaluate different interpretive choices
topic:mt_tIi6L1n7kF:evidence:2: Analyse how a filmed or live production stays faithful to or departs from the original script
topic:mt_dmFnJzxKwz:name: Using and Evaluating Textual Evidence
topic:mt_dmFnJzxKwz:description: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of what a text says explicitly and what can be inferred, distinguishing between strong and weak evidence and explaining how the evidence supports a point
topic:mt_dmFnJzxKwz:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} makes a point about a text in class or in writing, do they back it up with a specific quote or reference — and can they explain whether that evidence strongly supports their point or only weakly?
topic:mt_dmFnJzxKwz:evidence:0: Identify a relevant quotation to support an inference about a character's feelings
topic:mt_dmFnJzxKwz:evidence:1: Explain why one piece of evidence is stronger than another for supporting a claim

topic:mt_9k1qcpvVi_:name: Wide Independent Reading Across Genres
topic:mt_9k1qcpvVi_:description: Read widely and independently across fiction and non-fiction — including whole novels, short stories, plays, poetry, and non-fiction from different genres, periods, and cultures — building stamina, breadth, and personal taste as a reader
topic:mt_9k1qcpvVi_:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} read for pleasure across a wide range of books — fiction, non-fiction, poetry, plays — and can they talk enthusiastically about authors, genres, or themes they've discovered on their own?
topic:mt_9k1qcpvVi_:evidence:0: Choose books independently that offer appropriate challenge and genuine interest
topic:mt_9k1qcpvVi_:evidence:1: Read at least two Shakespeare plays and a range of pre-1914 and contemporary literature during KS3
topic:mt_9k1qcpvVi_:evidence:2: Maintain a personal reading record and articulate preferences with reasons
topic:mt_f8n4txtLej:name: Asking Questions
topic:mt_f8n4txtLej:description: Ask relevant questions to extend understanding; ask and answer questions to seek help, get information, or clarify something not understood
topic:mt_f8n4txtLej:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} doesn't understand something — like instructions for a game or an explanation from a teacher — do they ask a question to find out more rather than just guessing?
topic:mt_f8n4txtLej:evidence:0: Ask a question when something is unclear or more information is needed
topic:mt_f8n4txtLej:evidence:1: Answer questions with relevant and specific information
topic:mt_f8n4txtLej:evidence:2: Request clarification politely (e.g. 'Can you explain that again?')
topic:mt_4A7FYmvVhA:name: Describing Aloud
topic:mt_4A7FYmvVhA:description: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events with detail; speak audibly and express thoughts, feelings, and ideas clearly; give well-structured descriptions and explanations
topic:mt_4A7FYmvVhA:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you about something that happened — like a trip or a film — in enough detail that you could really picture it, speaking clearly so you can follow along?
topic:mt_4A7FYmvVhA:evidence:0: Describe a familiar person or place using several details
topic:mt_4A7FYmvVhA:evidence:1: Speak clearly and loudly enough for the whole group to hear
topic:mt_4A7FYmvVhA:evidence:2: Organise ideas logically when sharing information or telling about an event
topic:mt_n6GhzDPllD:name: Exploring Ideas Through Talk
topic:mt_n6GhzDPllD:description: Use spoken language to develop understanding through speculating, hypothesising, imagining, and exploring ideas; use strategies to build vocabulary through talk
topic:mt_n6GhzDPllD:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is trying to figure something out — like why something happened in a story or how something works — do they talk through their ideas out loud and explore possibilities before settling on an answer?
topic:mt_n6GhzDPllD:evidence:0: Wonder aloud about possibilities (e.g. 'What if...' or 'I think it might be because...')
topic:mt_n6GhzDPllD:evidence:1: Try out new vocabulary in conversation after hearing it in a story or lesson
topic:mt_n6GhzDPllD:evidence:2: Explore ideas through talk before committing them to writing
topic:mt_S0hzjAeLSK:name: Expressing & Justifying Opinions
topic:mt_S0hzjAeLSK:description: Articulate and justify answers, arguments, and opinions; participate in discussions, presentations, performances, role play, and debates
topic:mt_S0hzjAeLSK:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} disagrees with something or has an opinion, can they say why they think that and back it up with a reason rather than just saying "because I just do"?
topic:mt_S0hzjAeLSK:evidence:0: State an opinion and give a reason (e.g. 'I think ... because ...')
topic:mt_S0hzjAeLSK:evidence:1: Participate in a class presentation or performance with confidence
topic:mt_S0hzjAeLSK:evidence:2: Explain thinking when answering a question rather than just giving a one-word answer
topic:mt_wwdRhPyz6s:name: Group discussions
topic:mt_wwdRhPyz6s:description: Participate actively in collaborative conversations staying on topic; continue a conversation through multiple exchanges; maintain attention in discussions
topic:mt_wwdRhPyz6s:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is chatting with a friend or taking part in a group activity, can they keep a conversation going back and forth — listening, responding, and building on what the other person said?
topic:mt_wwdRhPyz6s:evidence:0: Stay on topic during a conversation for multiple turns
topic:mt_wwdRhPyz6s:evidence:1: Build on what another speaker has said (e.g. 'I agree because...')
topic:mt_wwdRhPyz6s:evidence:2: Maintain focus and contribute meaningfully in group discussions
topic:mt_mB7DVai-Uf:name: Listening and responding
topic:mt_mB7DVai-Uf:description: Listen and respond appropriately to adults and peers; follow agreed-upon rules for discussion such as listening to others and taking turns speaking
topic:mt_mB7DVai-Uf:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is in a group conversation at school or at the dinner table, do they listen while others are talking and wait for their turn before speaking?
topic:mt_mB7DVai-Uf:evidence:0: Demonstrate attentive listening by making eye contact and responding relevantly
topic:mt_mB7DVai-Uf:evidence:1: Follow classroom discussion rules (e.g. raise hand, wait for turn)
topic:mt_mB7DVai-Uf:evidence:2: Show understanding of what was said by paraphrasing or responding appropriately
topic:mt_ZBMcX2oRor:name: Reciting Poetry
topic:mt_ZBMcX2oRor:description: Learn poems by heart and recite with appropriate intonation, adding visual displays to descriptions when appropriate, and producing complete sentences in spoken presentations
topic:mt_ZBMcX2oRor:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} memorise a short poem and recite it with expression — changing their voice to match the mood of the words?
topic:mt_ZBMcX2oRor:evidence:0: Recite a poem from memory with expression and clear enunciation
topic:mt_ZBMcX2oRor:evidence:1: Add a drawing or visual display to support an oral description or presentation
topic:mt_ZBMcX2oRor:evidence:2: Present information to the class using complete sentences and audible voice
topic:mt_sXRHr7tfS5:name: Engaging Listeners and Valuing Viewpoints
topic:mt_sXRHr7tfS5:description: Gain, maintain and monitor the interest of listeners when speaking; consider and evaluate different viewpoints, attending to and building on others' contributions; begin to select appropriate language for different situations
topic:mt_sXRHr7tfS5:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is talking in a group, do they notice if people are losing interest and adjust how they're speaking — or pick up on what others have said and add to it thoughtfully?
topic:mt_sXRHr7tfS5:evidence:0: Use strategies to engage listeners during a presentation (e.g., make eye contact, vary tone and pace, ask the audience a question)
topic:mt_sXRHr7tfS5:evidence:1: Listen to a peer's viewpoint and respond by agreeing, disagreeing, or extending their idea with a reason (e.g., 'I agree with Priya because… but I also think…')
topic:mt_sXRHr7tfS5:evidence:2: Choose more formal language for a class presentation and more informal language for a group discussion, explaining the difference
topic:mt_yrMniCJu_S:name: Preparing for and Explaining in Discussions
topic:mt_yrMniCJu_S:description: Come to discussions prepared, draw on preparation and known information, and explain ideas in light of the discussion
topic:mt_yrMniCJu_S:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows they're going to discuss a topic in class, do they think about it beforehand and come ready with ideas or facts to share?
topic:mt_yrMniCJu_S:evidence:0: Read assigned material and prepare three discussion points or questions before a group conversation
topic:mt_yrMniCJu_S:evidence:1: During discussion, refer explicitly to the text or preparation notes to support a point
topic:mt_yrMniCJu_S:evidence:2: After a group exchange, explain how one's own thinking changed or was confirmed by others' contributions
topic:mt_ds2TOtP8I1:name: Reporting & Recounting
topic:mt_ds2TOtP8I1:description: Report on a topic or recount an experience with organised facts and descriptive details, speaking clearly at an understandable pace
topic:mt_ds2TOtP8I1:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give a short talk about a topic they've researched — presenting the key facts in a logical order and speaking clearly enough for others to follow?
topic:mt_ds2TOtP8I1:evidence:0: Deliver a one-minute oral report on a chosen topic, including at least three organised facts
topic:mt_ds2TOtP8I1:evidence:1: Recount a personal experience using descriptive details and a clear beginning, middle, and end
topic:mt_ds2TOtP8I1:evidence:2: Self-assess a recorded presentation for pace, clarity, and inclusion of relevant details
topic:mt_iodbOOmEQs:name: Identifying Reasons Behind a Speaker's Points
topic:mt_iodbOOmEQs:description: Identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points, evaluating whether the reasoning is logical and the evidence is relevant
topic:mt_iodbOOmEQs:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} listens to someone making an argument or giving reasons for something, can they tell you whether the reasons given actually support what the person is claiming?
topic:mt_iodbOOmEQs:evidence:0: Listen to a speaker's argument or presentation and list the specific reasons and evidence provided to support each main point
topic:mt_iodbOOmEQs:evidence:1: Evaluate whether the reasons a speaker gives are logical and whether the evidence cited is relevant to the claim being made
topic:mt_iodbOOmEQs:evidence:2: Ask follow-up questions that probe the strength of a speaker's reasoning, e.g. 'What evidence supports that claim?' or 'Are there other explanations?'
topic:mt_-DuXzMVVXQ:name: Paraphrasing What You Hear
topic:mt_-DuXzMVVXQ:description: Paraphrase portions of a text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats, capturing the key ideas accurately in one's own words
topic:mt_-DuXzMVVXQ:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} listens to a short talk or watches a video clip about a topic, can they explain the main points back to you in their own words?
topic:mt_-DuXzMVVXQ:evidence:0: Listen to a passage read aloud and restate the main idea and key details in own words without looking at the original text
topic:mt_-DuXzMVVXQ:evidence:1: Paraphrase information from a short video, podcast, or presentation, identifying the central message and supporting details
topic:mt_-DuXzMVVXQ:evidence:2: Distinguish between paraphrasing (restating in own words) and copying, demonstrating the ability to capture meaning without repeating exact wording
topic:mt_bkvB7QYKwg:name: Adapting Speech to Context
topic:mt_bkvB7QYKwg:description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, using formal English when appropriate to task and situation while adjusting tone, vocabulary, and style for different audiences
topic:mt_bkvB7QYKwg:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} naturally speak differently depending on who they're talking to — for example, more formally with a teacher than with a friend at the playground?
topic:mt_bkvB7QYKwg:evidence:0: Present the same information formally to a panel and informally to peers
topic:mt_bkvB7QYKwg:evidence:1: Adjust vocabulary and sentence structure when speaking to different audiences
topic:mt_bkvB7QYKwg:evidence:2: Identify contexts that require formal English and those where informal speech is appropriate
topic:mt_LNYTNpJOGT:name: Building on Others in Discussions
topic:mt_LNYTNpJOGT:description: Pose and respond to specific questions in discussions, making comments that contribute to the discussion and elaborate on the remarks of others
topic:mt_LNYTNpJOGT:assessmentPrompt: In a class discussion, does {{name}} ask questions that move the conversation forward and add comments that build on what others have said rather than just repeating the same ideas?
topic:mt_LNYTNpJOGT:evidence:0: Ask follow-up questions that build on another speaker's comment
topic:mt_LNYTNpJOGT:evidence:1: Respond to a classmate's idea by adding supporting evidence or a related example
topic:mt_LNYTNpJOGT:evidence:2: Redirect a discussion by posing a question that connects to the main topic
topic:mt_Cc-QHVo747:name: Drawing Conclusions from Discussion
topic:mt_Cc-QHVo747:description: Review the key ideas expressed in discussions and draw conclusions in light of information and knowledge gained from the discussion
topic:mt_Cc-QHVo747:assessmentPrompt: After a group discussion, can {{name}} pull together the main points that were made and explain what conclusion the group reached?
topic:mt_Cc-QHVo747:evidence:0: Summarise the main points made by different speakers in a group discussion
topic:mt_Cc-QHVo747:evidence:1: Draw a conclusion that synthesises multiple viewpoints expressed in the discussion
topic:mt_Cc-QHVo747:evidence:2: Explain how the discussion changed or confirmed initial understanding of a topic
topic:mt_on7FHCDmi-:name: Evaluating a Speaker's Argument
topic:mt_on7FHCDmi-:description: Summarise the points a speaker makes and explain how each claim is supported by reasons and evidence, evaluating the logic and relevance of the support
topic:mt_on7FHCDmi-:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} listens to a speaker making a case for something, can they explain back to you both what the speaker claimed and the reasons and evidence they gave to back it up?
topic:mt_on7FHCDmi-:evidence:0: Identify the main claim in a spoken presentation and the evidence used to support it
topic:mt_on7FHCDmi-:evidence:1: Evaluate whether a speaker's reasons logically support their main argument
topic:mt_on7FHCDmi-:evidence:2: Explain which pieces of evidence most effectively support a speaker's points
topic:mt_VtqvUORa8K:name: Multimedia Presentations
topic:mt_VtqvUORa8K:description: Include multimedia components and visual displays in presentations when appropriate to enhance the development of main ideas or themes
topic:mt_VtqvUORa8K:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} gives a presentation at school, do they think about including things like diagrams, slides, or pictures to help make their points clearer for the audience?
topic:mt_VtqvUORa8K:evidence:0: Select graphics, images, or sound that support and clarify main ideas in a presentation
topic:mt_VtqvUORa8K:evidence:1: Create slides or visual aids that enhance rather than distract from the spoken content
topic:mt_VtqvUORa8K:evidence:2: Integrate multimedia elements smoothly into an oral presentation
topic:mt_A4YUbzUFan:name: Summarising Spoken and Media Presentations
topic:mt_A4YUbzUFan:description: Summarise a written text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats including visually, quantitatively, and orally
topic:mt_A4YUbzUFan:assessmentPrompt: After listening to a talk or watching an informational video, can {{name}} give you a spoken summary of what the main message was in their own words?
topic:mt_A4YUbzUFan:evidence:0: Summarise the main points of a video or audio presentation in own words
topic:mt_A4YUbzUFan:evidence:1: Identify key information from a graph, chart, or infographic and explain it orally
topic:mt_A4YUbzUFan:evidence:2: Listen to a passage read aloud and provide an accurate summary of the content
topic:mt_ylFTYS80d1:name: Performing Scripts & Poetry
topic:mt_ylFTYS80d1:description: Improvise, rehearse, and perform play scripts and poetry — using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness, and action to generate language, explore meaning, and add impact to performance
topic:mt_ylFTYS80d1:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} performs in a play or reads aloud from a script, do they use their voice — volume, pace, and expression — to bring the character or poem to life?
topic:mt_ylFTYS80d1:evidence:0: Perform a scene from a play using appropriate intonation, volume, and pauses to convey character and mood
topic:mt_ylFTYS80d1:evidence:1: Use improvisation to explore how a character might respond in a new situation
topic:mt_ylFTYS80d1:evidence:2: Rehearse and perform a poem aloud, using pace and emphasis to bring out the meaning
topic:mt_z07UNAIsNc:name: Speaking Formally and Giving Presentations
topic:mt_z07UNAIsNc:description: Use Standard English confidently in formal and informal spoken contexts — give short speeches and presentations expressing own ideas clearly, keeping to the point, and adapting register and vocabulary to the audience
topic:mt_z07UNAIsNc:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give a short prepared speech or presentation in Standard English — staying on point and adjusting their vocabulary to suit the audience?
topic:mt_z07UNAIsNc:evidence:0: Deliver a 2-3 minute presentation on a topic with a clear opening, organised points, and a conclusion
topic:mt_z07UNAIsNc:evidence:1: Adapt language between formal and informal registers depending on the context and audience
topic:mt_z07UNAIsNc:evidence:2: Maintain eye contact, appropriate pace, and clear articulation when speaking to a group
topic:mt_Yrjn8jAt1c:name: Formal Debates
topic:mt_Yrjn8jAt1c:description: Participate in formal debates and structured discussions — presenting a position with supporting evidence, responding to others’ points, summarising and building on what has been said, and following rules of discussion
topic:mt_Yrjn8jAt1c:assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} taken part in a school debate where they had to argue a position with evidence, respond to the other side's points, and keep to the rules of formal discussion?
topic:mt_Yrjn8jAt1c:evidence:0: Present an argument in a debate with a clear claim supported by evidence
topic:mt_Yrjn8jAt1c:evidence:1: Respond to an opposing point by summarising it fairly before offering a counterargument
topic:mt_Yrjn8jAt1c:evidence:2: Build on a previous speaker’s idea by extending, questioning, or challenging it constructively
topic:mt_EqXlZfB4jp:name: Phonics Vocabulary
topic:mt_EqXlZfB4jp:description: Know and use the vocabulary of phonics and word structure — phoneme, grapheme, GPC (grapheme-phoneme correspondence), blend, segment, digraph, CVC, vowel, consonant, syllable, root word, suffix, prefix, and homophone — and understand that these words describe the building blocks that phonics instruction is built on
topic:mt_EqXlZfB4jp:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}}'s teacher asks them to 'segment a word into phonemes' or spot a 'digraph', do they understand what those words mean and can they do the task without looking confused?
topic:mt_EqXlZfB4jp:evidence:0: Say the sounds for common graphemes (e.g. 'sh', 'ch', 'th', 'ee', 'igh') and use 'phoneme' and 'grapheme' correctly when explaining
topic:mt_EqXlZfB4jp:evidence:1: Blend sounds together to read an unfamiliar word and explain what they are doing using the word 'blend'
topic:mt_EqXlZfB4jp:evidence:2: Segment a word into its individual sounds for spelling and use the term 'segment' to describe the process
topic:mt_BhYJZUsErp:name: Segmenting words into sounds
topic:mt_BhYJZUsErp:description: Segment spoken words into phonemes and spell CVC and simple phonetically regular words by writing a letter or letters for each sound
topic:mt_BhYJZUsErp:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} listen to a simple word like "cat" or "ship" and write down the letters for each sound they hear?
topic:mt_BhYJZUsErp:evidence:1: Segment words into individual sounds before choosing letters to write
topic:mt_BhYJZUsErp:evidence:2: Spell simple words phonetically drawing on sound-letter knowledge
topic:mt_AhfyJoTQtY:name: Spelling from Dictation
topic:mt_AhfyJoTQtY:description: Write simple sentences from memory when dictated by the teacher, applying taught GPCs, spelling rules, and common exception words
topic:mt_AhfyJoTQtY:assessmentPrompt: If you read a sentence out loud to {{name}} and ask them to write it down, can they spell the words correctly and put the letters in the right order?
topic:mt_AhfyJoTQtY:evidence:0: Write a dictated sentence using phonically plausible spellings
topic:mt_AhfyJoTQtY:evidence:1: Include correct spelling of taught exception words in dictation
topic:mt_AhfyJoTQtY:evidence:2: Apply sentence punctuation in dictated writing
topic:mt_QdMMLRYWhn:name: Spelling Verb Endings
topic:mt_QdMMLRYWhn:description: Spell words with common suffixes (-s/-es for plurals and third person verbs, -ing, -ed, -er, -est) where no change to the root word is needed
topic:mt_QdMMLRYWhn:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about more than one dog or talks about something that is happening now, do they add the right ending — like "dogs" or "jumping" — without making spelling mistakes?
topic:mt_QdMMLRYWhn:evidence:0: Add -s or -es correctly to make plurals (e.g. 'cats', 'boxes')
topic:mt_zBUcAPDRPM:name: The Prefix un-
topic:mt_zBUcAPDRPM:description: Spell words using the prefix un- to change meaning; understand that un- creates opposites or reverses actions
topic:mt_zBUcAPDRPM:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that adding "un-" to the front of a word like "happy" or "lock" flips its meaning, and can they spell those words correctly?
topic:mt_zBUcAPDRPM:evidence:0: Spell words with un- prefix correctly (e.g. 'unhappy', 'unfair', 'undo')
topic:mt_zBUcAPDRPM:evidence:1: Explain how un- changes the meaning of a word
topic:mt_zBUcAPDRPM:evidence:2: Create new words by adding un- to known words
topic:mt_Jq0MjURrRC:name: Tricky words
topic:mt_Jq0MjURrRC:description: Spell common exception words from memory that do not follow regular phonic patterns, including the days of the week
topic:mt_Jq0MjURrRC:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} spell tricky everyday words like "said," "were," "come," and the days of the week from memory without needing to sound them out?
topic:mt_Jq0MjURrRC:evidence:1: Write all seven days of the week correctly
topic:mt_Jq0MjURrRC:evidence:2: Recall and write exception words in dictated sentences
topic:mt_p_jxNLdus4:name: Alternative Spellings for Sounds
topic:mt_p_jxNLdus4:description: Spell words using alternative grapheme choices for known phonemes, learning new spellings for sounds already encountered (e.g., /ɔ:/ as 'a' before ll, /ʌ/ as 'o', words ending -tion), including distinguishing common homophones
topic:mt_p_jxNLdus4:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes and comes across a word where the same sound can be spelled different ways — like "see" and "sea" — do they know which spelling to use?
topic:mt_p_jxNLdus4:evidence:0: Spell 'ball', 'call', 'walk' using alternative grapheme /ɔ:/ as 'a' before ll
topic:mt_Z3G_97fnha:name: Apostrophes for possession
topic:mt_Z3G_97fnha:description: Use the possessive apostrophe with singular nouns to show ownership (e.g., the girl's book, the dog's bone)
topic:mt_Z3G_97fnha:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes something belonging to one person or thing — like "the dog's lead" or "the girl's bag" — do they put the apostrophe in the right place?
topic:mt_Z3G_97fnha:evidence:0: Write 'the cat's tail' to show the tail belongs to the cat
topic:mt_Z3G_97fnha:evidence:1: Distinguish plural -s ('the cats ran') from possessive 's ('the cat's bed') in writing
topic:mt_Z3G_97fnha:evidence:2: Add a possessive apostrophe to a singular noun in a dictated sentence
topic:mt_IntmJBg4VQ:name: Spelling Contracted Forms
topic:mt_IntmJBg4VQ:description: Spell contracted forms correctly by placing the apostrophe where letters are omitted (can't, didn't, I'll, it's, etc.)
topic:mt_IntmJBg4VQ:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a short form like "can't" or "didn't," do they put the apostrophe in the right place to show where letters are missing?
topic:mt_IntmJBg4VQ:evidence:0: Write 'can't' for 'cannot', 'didn't' for 'did not' with apostrophe correctly placed
topic:mt_IntmJBg4VQ:evidence:1: Distinguish 'it's' (it is) from 'its' (possessive) in a sentence
topic:mt_IntmJBg4VQ:evidence:2: Expand a contraction back to its full form and explain which letters are missing
topic:mt_FYK8m6eHQm:name: Suffixes
topic:mt_FYK8m6eHQm:description: Apply suffix spelling rules that require changes to the root word: dropping final -e before vowel suffixes, changing -y to -i, doubling final consonants in short-vowel words; use suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful, -less, -ly
topic:mt_FYK8m6eHQm:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} adds an ending like "-ing" or "-ed" to a word, do they know when to drop a silent "e," double the last letter, or change a "y" to an "i" — for example, "running," "baked," or "happily"?
topic:mt_FYK8m6eHQm:evidence:0: Spell 'hoping' (drop e), 'cried' (y to i), 'running' (double consonant) applying the correct rule
topic:mt_FYK8m6eHQm:evidence:2: Identify which suffix rule to apply to a given root word and explain why
topic:mt_HdI1y5KsBl:name: Apostrophes for possession (age 7+)
topic:mt_HdI1y5KsBl:description: Use the possessive apostrophe accurately with both regular and irregular plural nouns (e.g., the girls' bags, the children's toys), distinguishing singular from plural possession
topic:mt_HdI1y5KsBl:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about something belonging to a group — like "the children's coats" or "the teachers' cars" — do they put the apostrophe in the right place?
topic:mt_HdI1y5KsBl:evidence:0: Place the apostrophe correctly in plural possessives: 'the dogs' kennel' vs 'the dog's kennel'
topic:mt_HdI1y5KsBl:evidence:1: Write possessive forms of irregular plurals correctly (e.g. 'children's', 'women's', 'mice's')
topic:mt_HdI1y5KsBl:evidence:2: Distinguish singular possession (the boy's hat) from plural possession (the boys' hats) in dictated sentences
topic:mt_37QCuGOxFe:name: Homophones
topic:mt_37QCuGOxFe:description: Distinguish and correctly spell common homophones and near-homophones encountered at Y3-4 level (e.g., accept/except, affect/effect, brake/break, grate/great), including using the /eɪ/ sound spelt ei, eigh, or ey
topic:mt_37QCuGOxFe:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes, do they use the right spelling for words that sound the same but mean different things — like "brake" (on a bike) and "break" (snap something)?
topic:mt_37QCuGOxFe:evidence:0: Spell pairs of homophones correctly in context (e.g., 'there/their/they're', 'brake/break', 'grate/great')
topic:mt_37QCuGOxFe:evidence:1: Choose the correct homophone to complete a sentence (e.g., 'The dog wagged its/it's tail')
topic:mt_37QCuGOxFe:evidence:2: Spell words with the /eɪ/ sound as ei, eigh, or ey (e.g., vein, eight, they, neighbour)
topic:mt_T6nrrf2K43:name: Prefixes (age 7+)
topic:mt_T6nrrf2K43:description: Spell words with a range of prefixes (dis-, mis-, un-, re-, pre-, anti-, auto-, super-) understanding how each prefix modifies the root word's meaning without changing its spelling
topic:mt_T6nrrf2K43:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a word starting with "dis-," "mis-," or "pre-," can they work out what the word means and spell it correctly by thinking about the prefix?
topic:mt_T6nrrf2K43:evidence:0: Spell words with prefixes dis-, mis-, re- correctly without altering the root (e.g., disappoint, misspell, return)
topic:mt_T6nrrf2K43:evidence:1: Add prefixes un-, pre-, anti-, auto-, super- to root words and use the new word in a sentence (e.g., unhappy, preview, autograph)
topic:mt_T6nrrf2K43:evidence:2: Explain how a prefix changes the meaning of a root word (e.g., 'dis-' means 'not' or 'opposite of')
topic:mt_O2dS6gvClw:name: Spelling Word Lists (age 7+)
topic:mt_O2dS6gvClw:description: Spell words from the statutory word list for Years 3 and 4, including commonly misspelt words that do not follow regular patterns
topic:mt_O2dS6gvClw:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} spell the tricky words on their school's Year 3 and 4 word list — like "enough," "believe," or "separate" — from memory when writing?
topic:mt_O2dS6gvClw:evidence:0: Spell at least 20 words from the Y3-4 statutory list correctly (e.g., accident, believe, different, favourite, imagine)
topic:mt_O2dS6gvClw:evidence:1: Identify tricky parts of statutory words and use a strategy to remember them (e.g., 'separate' has 'a rat' in the middle)

topic:mt_U_HQXCnAaG:name: Advanced Spelling Conventions
topic:mt_U_HQXCnAaG:description: Spell words using assorted Y5-6 conventions: doubling after -fer when the stress remains (referring but reference), using hyphens to join prefixes to root words (co-ordinate, re-enter), the /iː/ sound spelt ei after c (receive, ceiling), and the letter string ough representing different sounds (though, through, thought, thorough, plough)
topic:mt_U_HQXCnAaG:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} correctly spell tricky words like "receive," "though," or "co-ordinate," including knowing when to use a hyphen or the "-ei" pattern after "c"?

topic:mt_U_HQXCnAaG:evidence:1: Use hyphens correctly when a prefix ends with the same letter the root begins with (re-enter, co-own) or to avoid ambiguity (re-cover vs recover)
topic:mt_U_HQXCnAaG:evidence:2: Read and spell words containing ough by recognising its multiple pronunciations: /oʊ/ (though), /uː/ (through), /ɔː/ (thought), /ʌf/ (rough), /aʊ/ (plough)

topic:mt_u3OuIXqmAo:evidence:2: Identify and correct homophone errors in extended writing, including to/too/two, there/their/they're, whose/who's, and its/it's
