topic:mt_mydcMoa8gN:name: Emotional Intelligence
topic:mt_mydcMoa8gN:description: Introduce Goleman's emotional intelligence model (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills); develop vocabulary for complex emotional states (ambivalence, ennui, schadenfreude, awe, nostalgia, cognitive dissonance); understand the evidence linking emotional intelligence to wellbeing, relationship quality, and long-term life outcomes; reflect on personal emotional growth over the secondary school years; explore the relationship between emotional literacy and mental health, and know when to seek professional support
topic:mt_mydcMoa8gN:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe a real situation where being aware of their own emotions — knowing what they were feeling and why — helped them handle a difficult moment better than if they had just reacted automatically?
topic:mt_lAvS72LOUO:name: Everyday Kindness and Care
topic:mt_lAvS72LOUO:description: Show kindness and care towards others in simple everyday ways — comforting a friend who is upset, helping someone who has dropped their things, sharing without being asked, and saying kind words
topic:mt_lAvS72LOUO:assessmentPrompt: If a younger child at school falls over in the playground, does {{name}} go over to help or comfort them without being told to by an adult?
topic:mt_lAvS72LOUO:evidence:0: Spontaneously offer comfort to someone who is visibly upset
topic:mt_lAvS72LOUO:evidence:1: Help another person with a practical task without being asked
topic:mt_lAvS72LOUO:evidence:2: Use kind words to encourage or cheer up someone who is struggling
topic:mt_wzUzVEBqJb:name: Other People's Feelings and Thoughts
topic:mt_wzUzVEBqJb:description: Understand that other people have their own feelings and thoughts, and that these might be different from your own — a foundational awareness that not everyone sees or feels things the same way
topic:mt_wzUzVEBqJb:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} loves dogs but their friend is scared of dogs, can {{name}} understand that their friend's fear is real even though they don't feel it themselves?
topic:mt_wzUzVEBqJb:evidence:0: State that other people can feel differently about the same thing
topic:mt_wzUzVEBqJb:evidence:1: Give an example of a time someone felt differently from them about the same situation
topic:mt_wzUzVEBqJb:evidence:2: Accept another child's feeling as valid even when it differs from their own
topic:mt_OJVkWvIaM_:name: Similarities & Differences
topic:mt_OJVkWvIaM_:description: Notice and appreciate ways that people are similar to and different from each other — including appearance, family structures, languages spoken, foods eaten, and celebrations observed — and understand that differences make communities interesting
topic:mt_OJVkWvIaM_:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} talk positively about how families in their class are different — some have two mums, some speak another language at home, some celebrate different holidays — and see this as interesting rather than strange?
topic:mt_OJVkWvIaM_:evidence:0: Name several ways people in their class or community are different from each other
topic:mt_OJVkWvIaM_:evidence:1: Describe at least one thing they have learned from someone who is different from them
topic:mt_OJVkWvIaM_:evidence:2: Express a positive attitude about differences rather than judging them
topic:mt_wRlf0g2MbB:name: Vocabulary: understanding others
topic:mt_wRlf0g2MbB:description: Know and use the key vocabulary for understanding others — empathy, perspective, kind, fair, community, similar, different, and care — and understand that these words describe real habits of thinking and feeling
topic:mt_wRlf0g2MbB:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} sees someone who seems sad or left out, can they describe what that person might be feeling using words like 'empathy' or 'perspective' — showing they're thinking about the other person, not just themselves?
topic:mt_wRlf0g2MbB:evidence:0: Use the word 'empathy' correctly and distinguish it from 'sympathy' — e.g. 'Empathy means I try to feel what they feel'
topic:mt_wRlf0g2MbB:evidence:1: Explain what 'perspective' and 'point of view' mean and demonstrate by describing how two people might see the same event differently
topic:mt_wRlf0g2MbB:evidence:2: Use words like 'community', 'belonging', and 'inclusion' accurately when talking about their school or neighbourhood
topic:mt_S7UTAhptLi:name: Different Lives and Experiences
topic:mt_S7UTAhptLi:description: Understand that people's lives and experiences can be very different from their own — that some children face challenges like disability, poverty, family difficulties, or being new to a country — and develop compassion rather than judgement
topic:mt_S7UTAhptLi:assessmentPrompt: If a new child joins {{name}}'s class who doesn't speak much English or whose family situation is very different, does {{name}} show understanding and try to include them rather than avoiding them?
topic:mt_S7UTAhptLi:evidence:0: Describe at least two ways another child's life experience might differ significantly from their own
topic:mt_S7UTAhptLi:evidence:1: Explain why it's important not to judge someone based on their circumstances
topic:mt_S7UTAhptLi:evidence:2: Suggest a kind action they could take to help someone facing a difficult situation
topic:mt_mDp-1vlL3R:name: Fairness, Equality and Equity
topic:mt_mDp-1vlL3R:description: Understand what fairness means and why it matters — recognising that fair doesn't always mean equal (everyone getting the same) but can mean equitable (everyone getting what they need), and applying this understanding in group situations
topic:mt_mDp-1vlL3R:assessmentPrompt: If a child with a broken arm gets extra time to finish a task at school, can {{name}} explain why that's fair even though other children don't get extra time?
topic:mt_mDp-1vlL3R:evidence:0: Explain the difference between treating everyone the same and treating everyone fairly
topic:mt_mDp-1vlL3R:evidence:1: Give an example of a situation where equal treatment wouldn't be fair
topic:mt_mDp-1vlL3R:evidence:2: Apply fairness thinking when sharing resources or making group decisions
topic:mt_9NQEiYLQA3:name: Seeing Someone Else's Point of View
topic:mt_9NQEiYLQA3:description: Practise perspective-taking by imagining how someone else might feel in a given situation — using prompts like 'How would you feel if that happened to you?' and applying this when reading stories or during real interactions
topic:mt_9NQEiYLQA3:assessmentPrompt: When reading a story together, can {{name}} pause and explain how a character might be feeling and why — putting themselves in the character's shoes?
topic:mt_9NQEiYLQA3:evidence:0: Describe how a character in a story feels and give reasons based on the plot
topic:mt_9NQEiYLQA3:evidence:1: Predict how another child would feel in a described scenario
topic:mt_9NQEiYLQA3:evidence:2: Use perspective-taking during a real disagreement to understand the other person's view
topic:mt_a6AYrbb7x4:name: Vocabulary: social awareness
topic:mt_a6AYrbb7x4:description: Know and use the vocabulary of social awareness — including stereotype, prejudice, discrimination, equality, equity, bias, compassion, and fairness — and understand what distinguishes these closely related concepts
topic:mt_a6AYrbb7x4:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a classmate say something that groups all people of a certain background together, can they explain why that's a stereotype and how it differs from a fact about an individual person?
topic:mt_a6AYrbb7x4:evidence:0: Explain what 'stereotype' and 'prejudice' mean and give an example of each from everyday life
topic:mt_a6AYrbb7x4:evidence:1: Use words like 'equality', 'equity', and 'bias' correctly when discussing a scenario — e.g. 'That's not equity because not everyone got what they needed'
topic:mt_a6AYrbb7x4:evidence:2: Identify an example of discrimination in a story or news article and explain why it is unfair using the correct vocabulary
topic:mt_HFN1pGASpZ:name: Prejudice and Discrimination
topic:mt_HFN1pGASpZ:description: Understand the impact of prejudice and discrimination on individuals and communities — that treating people unfairly because of their identity causes real harm — and recognise their own responsibility to stand against it
topic:mt_HFN1pGASpZ:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees someone at school being excluded or teased because of their race, religion, or disability, can they explain why that's wrong and describe what they could do about it?
topic:mt_HFN1pGASpZ:evidence:0: Define prejudice and discrimination in their own words with examples
topic:mt_HFN1pGASpZ:evidence:1: Describe the emotional and social impact of discrimination on the person experiencing it
topic:mt_HFN1pGASpZ:evidence:2: Identify at least one action they can personally take to challenge unfair treatment
topic:mt_cOknxrYhwL:name: Questioning Your Own Biases
topic:mt_cOknxrYhwL:description: Reflect on their own assumptions and biases — recognising that everyone carries unconscious assumptions about others, and that actively questioning these assumptions is an ongoing practice that leads to greater fairness and empathy
topic:mt_cOknxrYhwL:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} catch themselves making an assumption about someone — like assuming a quiet child is unfriendly — and then question whether that assumption is fair?
topic:mt_cOknxrYhwL:evidence:0: Describe a time they made an assumption about someone that turned out to be wrong
topic:mt_cOknxrYhwL:evidence:1: Explain what unconscious bias means in simple terms
topic:mt_cOknxrYhwL:evidence:2: Describe a strategy for checking their own assumptions, such as asking questions before judging
topic:mt_2oswCNuapH:name: Stereotypes and Individual Differences
topic:mt_2oswCNuapH:description: Recognise stereotypes — oversimplified beliefs about groups of people based on gender, race, age, or other characteristics — and understand that stereotypes are unfair because they ignore individual differences
topic:mt_2oswCNuapH:assessmentPrompt: If someone says 'boys don't cry' or 'girls aren't good at maths', can {{name}} explain why those statements are unfair stereotypes that don't apply to everyone?
topic:mt_2oswCNuapH:evidence:0: Define what a stereotype is in their own words
topic:mt_2oswCNuapH:evidence:1: Identify a common stereotype and explain why it is inaccurate
topic:mt_2oswCNuapH:evidence:2: Challenge a stereotype they encounter by giving a counter-example
topic:mt_DkzsZdyaL2:name: The world contains many cultures, traditions
topic:mt_DkzsZdyaL2:description: Understand that the world contains many cultures, traditions, and belief systems, and that learning about others' perspectives enriches our own understanding — developing genuine curiosity about and respect for cultural diversity
topic:mt_DkzsZdyaL2:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} show genuine interest when learning about how families from different cultures celebrate, eat, or worship — asking questions respectfully rather than dismissing things that are unfamiliar?
topic:mt_DkzsZdyaL2:evidence:0: Describe a cultural practice different from their own and explain what they find interesting about it
topic:mt_DkzsZdyaL2:evidence:1: Ask respectful questions to learn about someone else's traditions or beliefs
topic:mt_DkzsZdyaL2:evidence:2: Explain why understanding different cultures makes communities stronger
topic:mt_oqvJJKCJXw:name: Systemic Inequality and Allyship
topic:mt_oqvJJKCJXw:description: Move beyond 'treating everyone the same' to understand that structural advantages and disadvantages exist regardless of individual effort or intention; explore concrete examples of systemic inequality (educational attainment gaps, gender pay gap, representation in leadership); distinguish between individual prejudice and structural discrimination; understand intersectionality — how multiple aspects of identity interact; develop informed compassion rooted in evidence rather than pity; explore what being a genuine ally means in practice
topic:mt_oqvJJKCJXw:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the difference between treating everyone 'the same' and actually making things fair — and give a real example of a structural barrier that means two people starting in different positions face unequal opportunities even if they try equally hard?
topic:mt_VA126P6Wp5:name: Sympathy Versus Empathy
topic:mt_VA126P6Wp5:description: Distinguish sympathy ('I feel sorry for you') from empathy ('I understand what you're experiencing'); develop active listening skills: reflecting, paraphrasing, asking open questions, resisting the urge to problem-solve too quickly; understand empathic curiosity as genuine interest in another person's inner world; practise being present for someone in distress without trying to fix or minimise their experience; understand vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue, and how empathetic people can protect their own wellbeing while staying present for others
topic:mt_VA126P6Wp5:assessmentPrompt: When a friend is going through something really difficult, can {{name}} describe what makes a listener genuinely helpful — and explain the difference between empathy and sympathy, using an example of something that sounds supportive but actually isn't?
topic:mt_5XLhiqmocP:name: Global Citizenship
topic:mt_5XLhiqmocP:description: Understand what it means to be a citizen in an interconnected world where decisions in one place affect people elsewhere; explore global issues (climate justice, forced migration, global health, poverty) through an empathy lens, distinguishing facts from value judgements; engage with the ethical tension between obligations to those close to us and obligations to distant strangers; introduce evidence-based giving and effective altruism as one framework for thinking about global responsibility; develop a personal, reasoned stance on global citizenship that acknowledges complexity
topic:mt_5XLhiqmocP:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads about a crisis happening in another country, can they describe how they think about their own responsibility — and name one practical thing young people can genuinely do about large-scale problems rather than just feeling helpless?
topic:mt_PdYlsA33jB:name: Asking for Help
topic:mt_PdYlsA33jB:description: Ask for help when they need it — from a friend, teacher, or family member — and understand that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness
topic:mt_PdYlsA33jB:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is stuck on something at school or feeling worried about something, will they ask a teacher or friend for help rather than struggling in silence?
topic:mt_PdYlsA33jB:evidence:0: Approach an appropriate person and ask for help clearly
topic:mt_PdYlsA33jB:evidence:1: Identify who to go to for different kinds of help (academic, emotional, practical)
topic:mt_PdYlsA33jB:evidence:2: Explain why asking for help is sensible rather than something to be embarrassed about
topic:mt_YbX3LD0Eca:name: Listening to Others
topic:mt_YbX3LD0Eca:description: Listen to others when they are speaking — looking at the speaker, waiting until they finish, and showing they have heard by responding to what was said rather than just talking about their own ideas
topic:mt_YbX3LD0Eca:assessmentPrompt: When a friend is telling {{name}} about their weekend, does {{name}} actually listen and ask questions about it — rather than immediately jumping in to talk about their own weekend?
topic:mt_YbX3LD0Eca:evidence:0: Face the speaker and maintain attention while someone else is talking
topic:mt_YbX3LD0Eca:evidence:1: Wait until the other person has finished before responding
topic:mt_YbX3LD0Eca:evidence:2: Respond to what was actually said rather than changing the subject to their own idea
topic:mt_HBcvu0UxYe:name: Makes someone a good friend
topic:mt_HBcvu0UxYe:description: Understand what makes someone a good friend — being kind, honest, reliable, and including others — and recognise behaviours that are not friendly, such as being bossy, leaving people out, or saying mean things
topic:mt_HBcvu0UxYe:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe what makes a good friend and recognise when someone — including themselves — isn't being a good friend?
topic:mt_HBcvu0UxYe:evidence:0: List at least four qualities of a good friend
topic:mt_HBcvu0UxYe:evidence:1: Identify unfriendly behaviour in a story or real situation
topic:mt_HBcvu0UxYe:evidence:2: Reflect on a time they were a good friend and explain what they did
topic:mt_FwI7q7DSIx:name: Taking Turns and Sharing
topic:mt_FwI7q7DSIx:description: Take turns, share materials, and play cooperatively with others — understanding that group activities work better when everyone gets a fair go and that waiting for your turn is part of being a good friend
topic:mt_FwI7q7DSIx:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is playing a board game with friends or siblings, can they wait for their turn and share the pieces without grabbing or getting upset?
topic:mt_FwI7q7DSIx:evidence:0: Take turns in a game or group activity without needing adult reminders
topic:mt_FwI7q7DSIx:evidence:1: Share materials willingly during a shared task or playtime
topic:mt_FwI7q7DSIx:evidence:2: Explain why taking turns makes games and group work more fun for everyone
topic:mt_NS5t-Jzlh8:name: Vocabulary: working with others
topic:mt_NS5t-Jzlh8:description: Know and use the vocabulary of working with others — cooperate, share, take turns, team, listen, agree, disagree respectfully, and include — and understand that these words describe habits that friendships and group work depend on
topic:mt_NS5t-Jzlh8:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is working on something with a friend or sibling, can they use words like 'cooperate' or 'take turns' to describe what they're doing — and actually practise those things?
topic:mt_NS5t-Jzlh8:evidence:0: Use 'cooperate' and 'compromise' correctly — e.g. 'We cooperated by taking turns choosing the game'
topic:mt_NS5t-Jzlh8:evidence:1: Explain what 'active listening' means and demonstrate it: facing the speaker, not interrupting, responding to what was said
topic:mt_NS5t-Jzlh8:evidence:2: Use 'share', 'take turns', and 'include' to describe how they work with others in a group activity
topic:mt_Ag9NSWJu-X:name: Communication Vocabulary
topic:mt_Ag9NSWJu-X:description: Know and use the vocabulary of healthy communication and conflict — assertive, passive, aggressive, compromise, conflict, resolution, mediate, bystander, upstander, and peer pressure — and understand the difference between these contrasting approaches
topic:mt_Ag9NSWJu-X:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} and a friend have a disagreement, can they describe it using words like 'conflict' or 'compromise' — and explain how assertive communication is different from aggressive or passive behaviour?
topic:mt_Ag9NSWJu-X:evidence:0: Use 'assertive' correctly and distinguish it from 'aggressive' — e.g. 'Being assertive means saying what I need calmly'
topic:mt_Ag9NSWJu-X:evidence:1: Explain what 'conflict resolution' means and describe one strategy such as using 'I feel...' statements
topic:mt_Ag9NSWJu-X:evidence:2: Use words like 'negotiate', 'boundary', and 'respect' accurately in a discussion about friendships
topic:mt_X7Tu94-a2m:name: Friendships change over time
topic:mt_X7Tu94-a2m:description: Understand that friendships change over time — that it's normal for friends to drift apart or for new friendships to form — and develop strategies for making new friends and handling friendship changes without feeling like something is wrong with them
topic:mt_X7Tu94-a2m:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s best friend starts spending more time with someone else, can they handle it without falling apart — understanding that friendships shift and they can make new friends too?
topic:mt_X7Tu94-a2m:evidence:0: Explain that friendships changing is normal and doesn't mean something is wrong
topic:mt_X7Tu94-a2m:evidence:1: Describe a strategy for making new friends, such as joining a club or inviting someone to play
topic:mt_X7Tu94-a2m:evidence:2: Talk about a friendship that changed and how they handled it
topic:mt_iWGnyUyN2j:name: Resolving Disagreements with Friends
topic:mt_iWGnyUyN2j:description: Resolve simple disagreements with peers by talking it through — explaining how they feel, listening to the other person's side, and finding a compromise or solution that both can accept
topic:mt_iWGnyUyN2j:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} and a friend disagree about which game to play at break time, can they talk it through and find a compromise — rather than one person always getting their way or the argument escalating?
topic:mt_iWGnyUyN2j:evidence:0: Explain their own point of view calmly during a disagreement
topic:mt_iWGnyUyN2j:evidence:1: Listen to the other person's perspective without interrupting
topic:mt_iWGnyUyN2j:evidence:2: Suggest a compromise or solution that addresses both sides
topic:mt_w4nSIDhIgC:name: Roles in a Group
topic:mt_w4nSIDhIgC:description: Understand different roles people play in groups — leader, supporter, mediator, idea-generator — and recognise that effective groups need a mix of roles, not everyone trying to be the leader
topic:mt_w4nSIDhIgC:assessmentPrompt: In a group project, can {{name}} recognise that they don't always have to be in charge — and that sometimes the group works better when they support someone else's idea rather than pushing their own?
topic:mt_w4nSIDhIgC:evidence:0: Name at least three different roles people can play in a group
topic:mt_w4nSIDhIgC:evidence:1: Identify their own preferred role and describe its strengths
topic:mt_w4nSIDhIgC:evidence:2: Explain why groups work better when different people take different roles
topic:mt_QxsoqVUt6u:name: Working Well in a Group
topic:mt_QxsoqVUt6u:description: Work effectively as part of a small group — contributing their own ideas, listening to others' ideas, taking on a fair share of the work, and supporting the group to reach a shared goal
topic:mt_QxsoqVUt6u:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} has to do a group project at school, do they pull their weight — sharing ideas and doing their part — rather than sitting back or trying to take over?
topic:mt_QxsoqVUt6u:evidence:0: Contribute at least one idea during a group discussion
topic:mt_QxsoqVUt6u:evidence:1: Listen to and build on another group member's idea
topic:mt_QxsoqVUt6u:evidence:2: Complete their assigned part of a group task on time
topic:mt_rqLMfiw61L:name: Assertive Communication
topic:mt_rqLMfiw61L:description: Use assertive communication — expressing needs, opinions, and boundaries clearly and respectfully without being aggressive (pushy/demanding) or passive (giving in/staying silent) — including saying no when something doesn't feel right
topic:mt_rqLMfiw61L:assessmentPrompt: If friends want {{name}} to do something they're uncomfortable with — like excluding another child or breaking a rule — can {{name}} say 'I don't want to do that' firmly but politely?
topic:mt_rqLMfiw61L:evidence:0: Explain the difference between assertive, aggressive, and passive responses
topic:mt_rqLMfiw61L:evidence:1: Role-play saying no in a peer pressure scenario
topic:mt_rqLMfiw61L:evidence:2: Express a personal boundary clearly and respectfully in a real situation
topic:mt_33zncDHC3N:name: Giving and Receiving Feedback
topic:mt_33zncDHC3N:description: Give and receive constructive feedback — telling someone what they did well and what could be improved in a way that is helpful rather than hurtful, and receiving feedback about their own work without becoming defensive
topic:mt_33zncDHC3N:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reviews a classmate's story and finds mistakes, can they give feedback that's helpful — like 'I loved this part, and this bit could be clearer' — rather than just saying 'it's wrong'?
topic:mt_33zncDHC3N:evidence:0: Give feedback that includes both a specific positive point and a constructive suggestion
topic:mt_33zncDHC3N:evidence:1: Receive feedback about their own work without getting upset or dismissive
topic:mt_33zncDHC3N:evidence:2: Explain why constructive feedback helps people improve
topic:mt_AbnwmKD8oe:name: Helping Others Resolve Conflicts
topic:mt_AbnwmKD8oe:description: Mediate conflicts between others — helping two friends who are arguing by listening to both sides, helping them see each other's perspective, and guiding them toward a fair resolution
topic:mt_AbnwmKD8oe:assessmentPrompt: If two of {{name}}'s friends are arguing and both come to {{name}} for support, can {{name}} help them talk it out fairly rather than just taking one side?
topic:mt_AbnwmKD8oe:evidence:0: Listen to both sides of a conflict without taking sides initially
topic:mt_AbnwmKD8oe:evidence:1: Help each person articulate their perspective to the other
topic:mt_AbnwmKD8oe:evidence:2: Suggest a fair resolution or compromise that both parties can accept
topic:mt_z98J_Zg2L3:name: Self-Reflection in Relationships
topic:mt_z98J_Zg2L3:description: Reflect on their own role and behaviour in relationships — recognising patterns in how they interact with others, understanding what they contribute to friendships, and identifying areas where they could improve as a friend or team member
topic:mt_z98J_Zg2L3:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} honestly reflect on their friendships and say something like 'I think I sometimes take over in group work and I'm trying to listen more' — showing awareness of their own social patterns?
topic:mt_z98J_Zg2L3:evidence:0: Identify a pattern in their own social behaviour, such as always wanting to lead or avoiding confrontation
topic:mt_z98J_Zg2L3:evidence:1: Describe what they do well in relationships and one area they'd like to improve
topic:mt_z98J_Zg2L3:evidence:2: Set a specific social goal, such as 'I will ask others for their ideas before sharing mine'
topic:mt_nqM2OW0Qlm:name: Social Cues and Group Dynamics
topic:mt_nqM2OW0Qlm:description: Understand subtext, indirect communication, and social cues in adolescent peer groups; analyse the psychology of in-group and out-group dynamics and why belonging can come at the cost of exclusion; understand gossip as a social bonding and status mechanism, and its costs; develop strategies for navigating social hierarchies without compromising values; distinguish between assertiveness and aggression in peer settings; understand how to respond to exclusion — whether experiencing it or witnessing it
topic:mt_nqM2OW0Qlm:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} senses tension or unspoken 'undercurrents' in a group of friends, can they describe what social cues they pick up on and explain the difference between being assertive and being aggressive when they choose to address it?
topic:mt_NCrbQe0LdB:name: Honest Conversations and Conflict Repair
topic:mt_NCrbQe0LdB:description: Understand how to have honest, direct conversations that address problems without attacking the person; apply the principles of non-violent communication (observation, feeling, need, request); understand the repair process after significant conflicts: taking responsibility without defensiveness, offering a genuine apology (without blame-shifting), and rebuilding trust through consistent behaviour over time; distinguish between a real apology and a face-saving 'sorry'; understand how friendships survive and deepen through navigated conflict rather than avoidance
topic:mt_NCrbQe0LdB:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} falls out seriously with a friend, can they describe what makes an apology actually repair a relationship — and what the difference is between a genuine apology and just saying sorry to end the awkwardness?
topic:mt_8StiXnYq1u:name: Leadership Styles and Influence
topic:mt_8StiXnYq1u:description: Distinguish different leadership styles (directive, democratic, servant, transformational) and understand when each is appropriate; understand that influence in a group comes with responsibility, and explore the difference between leading through inspiration versus coercion; practise inclusive leadership: actively creating space for quieter voices and diverse perspectives; understand the ethics of influence and the boundary between persuasion and manipulation; explore concepts of consent and coercion in peer relationships; reflect on what kind of influence they want to have in their communities
topic:mt_8StiXnYq1u:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were leading a group project where one person was dominating all the decisions, can they describe two different leadership approaches they could take and explain why the most authoritative person in a group isn't always the best leader?
topic:mt_UHQfb-n-w3:name: Actions and Their Consequences
topic:mt_UHQfb-n-w3:description: Understand that actions have consequences — that what you choose to do affects both yourself and other people — and begin to think about what might happen before they act
topic:mt_UHQfb-n-w3:assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} does something — like taking a toy from a sibling or running in the corridor — can they stop and think about what might happen as a result?
topic:mt_UHQfb-n-w3:evidence:0: Describe what happened as a consequence of a specific action they took
topic:mt_UHQfb-n-w3:evidence:1: Predict what might happen if they choose a particular action before doing it
topic:mt_UHQfb-n-w3:evidence:2: Explain that actions can have good or bad consequences for themselves and others
topic:mt_q3vRl4dddK:name: Everyday Safety Awareness
topic:mt_q3vRl4dddK:description: Keep themselves safe in everyday situations — knowing basic safety rules about roads, strangers, water, and the internet — and understanding who their trusted adults are and when to tell them something
topic:mt_q3vRl4dddK:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know their basic safety rules — like not going off with someone they don't know, looking both ways before crossing, and telling you if something online makes them uncomfortable?
topic:mt_q3vRl4dddK:evidence:0: State at least three basic safety rules and explain why each matters
topic:mt_q3vRl4dddK:evidence:1: Name their trusted adults and describe when they should tell them something
topic:mt_q3vRl4dddK:evidence:2: Demonstrate safe behaviour in a familiar everyday situation without being reminded
topic:mt_Wc6cOTQ1bA:name: Right and Wrong Choices
topic:mt_Wc6cOTQ1bA:description: Know the difference between right and wrong in familiar everyday situations — understanding basic rules about honesty, not hurting others, respecting others' property, and being fair — and choose to do the right thing even when it's harder
topic:mt_Wc6cOTQ1bA:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} accidentally breaks something at a friend's house, do they tell the truth about it rather than hiding it or blaming someone else?
topic:mt_Wc6cOTQ1bA:evidence:0: Identify the right and wrong choice in a simple moral scenario
topic:mt_Wc6cOTQ1bA:evidence:1: Choose to be honest even when lying would avoid trouble
topic:mt_Wc6cOTQ1bA:evidence:2: Explain why rules about not hurting others and being honest matter
topic:mt_rkrG2w7WXI:name: Rules and agreements exist
topic:mt_rkrG2w7WXI:description: Understand why rules and agreements exist — that they help keep people safe, make things fair, and help groups work well together — and follow agreed rules willingly rather than only when being watched
topic:mt_rkrG2w7WXI:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} follow the class rules or family agreements even when no adult is watching — not because they're scared of punishment but because they understand why the rules matter?
topic:mt_rkrG2w7WXI:evidence:0: Explain the reason behind at least two rules at home or school
topic:mt_rkrG2w7WXI:evidence:1: Follow a rule consistently without needing to be reminded or monitored
topic:mt_rkrG2w7WXI:evidence:2: Describe what would happen if nobody followed the rules in a specific context
topic:mt_uTKgmWqSoI:name: Vocabulary: making decisions and keeping safe
topic:mt_uTKgmWqSoI:description: Know and use the vocabulary of making decisions and keeping safe — choice, consequence, rule, safe, fair, honest, trusted adult, and right and wrong — and understand that naming these ideas clearly helps make better choices
topic:mt_uTKgmWqSoI:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} faces a situation where they need to make a choice — like whether to tell the truth about something that went wrong — can they talk through what might happen using words like 'consequence' and 'fair'?
topic:mt_uTKgmWqSoI:evidence:0: Explain what 'consequence' means and give an example of a positive and a negative consequence of a choice
topic:mt_uTKgmWqSoI:evidence:1: Use 'responsible' and 'safe' correctly when talking about everyday decisions — e.g. 'The responsible choice is to tell an adult'
topic:mt_uTKgmWqSoI:evidence:2: Define 'rule' and 'fairness' and explain why rules exist using their own examples from school or home
topic:mt_zIzJGkaj0Q:name: Basic digital citizenship
topic:mt_zIzJGkaj0Q:description: Understand basic digital citizenship — being kind online, protecting personal information, recognising that people behind screens are real people with real feelings, and knowing what to do if something online makes them uncomfortable
topic:mt_zIzJGkaj0Q:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is chatting with friends online or playing multiplayer games, do they treat people kindly and know not to share personal details like their address or school name?
topic:mt_zIzJGkaj0Q:evidence:0: State at least three rules for staying safe and being kind online
topic:mt_zIzJGkaj0Q:evidence:1: Explain why hurtful messages online are just as harmful as saying them in person
topic:mt_zIzJGkaj0Q:evidence:2: Describe what they should do if someone online makes them feel uncomfortable or asks for personal information
topic:mt_yCmYV9ruQu:name: Bystanders and Upstanders
topic:mt_yCmYV9ruQu:description: Understand the bystander role — that when someone witnesses unkind or unfair behaviour, they have a choice: they can be a passive bystander (doing nothing), join in, or be an upstander (speaking up or getting help) — and develop the confidence to be an upstander
topic:mt_yCmYV9ruQu:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a group of children being mean to someone at school, do they have the courage to say something, walk away with the person being targeted, or tell a teacher — rather than just watching?
topic:mt_yCmYV9ruQu:evidence:0: Explain the difference between a bystander and an upstander
topic:mt_yCmYV9ruQu:evidence:1: Describe at least two safe actions an upstander can take
topic:mt_yCmYV9ruQu:evidence:2: Give an example of a time they or someone they know stood up for someone else
topic:mt_RhntJz7p_6:name: Stop, Think, Then Choose
topic:mt_RhntJz7p_6:description: Use a simple decision-making process when faced with a choice — stopping to think, identifying the options, considering the consequences of each option, and then choosing — rather than acting impulsively
topic:mt_RhntJz7p_6:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} faces a tricky choice — like whether to tell the teacher that a friend cheated — can they think through their options and the consequences rather than just reacting?
topic:mt_RhntJz7p_6:evidence:0: Describe at least two options when facing a decision
topic:mt_RhntJz7p_6:evidence:1: Predict a likely consequence for each option
topic:mt_RhntJz7p_6:evidence:2: Explain which option they chose and why, showing they considered the consequences
topic:mt_I9iSzpGRn5:name: Understanding Bullying
topic:mt_I9iSzpGRn5:description: Understand what bullying is — repeated behaviour intended to hurt someone, including physical, verbal, social (exclusion, spreading rumours), and cyberbullying — and know that it is always wrong and what to do if they experience or witness it
topic:mt_I9iSzpGRn5:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand the difference between a one-off argument and bullying, and do they know what to do if they see someone being bullied — rather than just ignoring it?
topic:mt_I9iSzpGRn5:evidence:0: Define bullying and distinguish it from a one-off conflict
topic:mt_I9iSzpGRn5:evidence:1: Name at least three forms of bullying including cyberbullying
topic:mt_I9iSzpGRn5:evidence:2: Describe the steps they should take if they experience or witness bullying
topic:mt_h-z88yf9Pn:name: Vocabulary: ethics and citizenship
topic:mt_h-z88yf9Pn:description: Know and use the vocabulary of ethics and citizenship — bullying, cyberbullying, bystander, upstander, peer pressure, digital citizenship, rights, responsibility, and ethical — and understand the distinctions between these closely related terms
topic:mt_h-z88yf9Pn:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw someone being treated unkindly online and you asked them about it, could they explain the difference between being a bystander and an upstander — and what 'digital citizenship' means?
topic:mt_h-z88yf9Pn:evidence:0: Explain what 'ethics' means in their own words and give an example of an ethical dilemma
topic:mt_h-z88yf9Pn:evidence:1: Use 'citizen', 'rights', and 'responsibilities' correctly — e.g. 'A citizen has the right to vote and the responsibility to follow laws'
topic:mt_h-z88yf9Pn:evidence:2: Define 'consent' and 'integrity' and explain why they matter in relationships and online behaviour
topic:mt_h_shhH-6DC:name: Community Rights and Responsibilities
topic:mt_h_shhH-6DC:description: Understand their rights and responsibilities as a member of a community — that everyone has a right to be treated with respect and to feel safe, and that with rights come responsibilities to treat others the same way
topic:mt_h_shhH-6DC:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that they have a right to feel safe at school AND a responsibility to help make school safe for others — understanding that rights and responsibilities go together?
topic:mt_h_shhH-6DC:evidence:0: Name at least three rights that every child has (e.g., safety, education, respect)
topic:mt_h_shhH-6DC:evidence:1: Describe the responsibilities that go along with those rights
topic:mt_h_shhH-6DC:evidence:2: Give an example of how exercising their own rights responsibly supports the community
topic:mt_6xj94tmpi-:name: Difficult Ethical Choices
topic:mt_6xj94tmpi-:description: Understand that ethical decisions are not always black and white — that sometimes there is no perfect answer and reasonable people can disagree — and practise weighing up competing values when making difficult choices
topic:mt_6xj94tmpi-:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friend tells them a secret but the secret involves something dangerous, can {{name}} think through the tension between loyalty to their friend and the need to keep someone safe?
topic:mt_6xj94tmpi-:evidence:0: Describe a moral dilemma where both sides have valid points
topic:mt_6xj94tmpi-:evidence:1: Explain the values in tension (e.g., loyalty vs safety, honesty vs kindness)
topic:mt_6xj94tmpi-:evidence:2: Describe how they would make a decision in such a situation and justify their reasoning
topic:mt_RNeEF1JU4J:name: Ethics in Real-World Issues
topic:mt_RNeEF1JU4J:description: Evaluate the ethical dimensions of real-world issues they encounter — such as environmental responsibility, fairness in sport, digital ethics, or social justice — considering multiple perspectives and forming a reasoned personal position
topic:mt_RNeEF1JU4J:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} discuss a real issue — like whether it's fair that some children have more than others, or whether animals should be kept in zoos — considering different viewpoints and explaining their own position thoughtfully?
topic:mt_RNeEF1JU4J:evidence:0: Identify an ethical issue and describe at least two different perspectives on it
topic:mt_RNeEF1JU4J:evidence:1: Explain which perspective they agree with most and give reasons for their position
topic:mt_RNeEF1JU4J:evidence:2: Acknowledge that the other perspective has some validity even if they disagree
topic:mt_JivEBTD_KV:name: Peer Pressure and Resisting It
topic:mt_JivEBTD_KV:description: Understand peer pressure — the influence friends and peers can have on your choices and behaviour — and develop strategies for resisting pressure to do something they know is wrong or that makes them uncomfortable
topic:mt_JivEBTD_KV:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friends dare them to do something risky or unkind — like shoplifting a sweet or posting an embarrassing photo of someone — can they resist the pressure and explain why they won't do it?
topic:mt_JivEBTD_KV:evidence:0: Define peer pressure in their own words and give a real-world example
topic:mt_JivEBTD_KV:evidence:1: Describe at least two strategies for resisting peer pressure, such as walking away or using humour
topic:mt_JivEBTD_KV:evidence:2: Explain why going along with something wrong to fit in usually makes things worse
topic:mt_JiZ3H90Xg8:name: Risk, Uncertainty, and Cognitive Bias
topic:mt_JiZ3H90Xg8:description: Distinguish between risk (decisions with known probabilities) and uncertainty (decisions with unknown outcomes); identify cognitive biases that distort risk assessment: availability heuristic (judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind), present bias (overvaluing the immediate over the future), optimism bias (underestimating personal risk), and groupthink; understand why adolescent brains are biologically calibrated toward higher risk tolerance; apply a structured decision-making framework to real choices; understand the role of personal values in decisions where facts alone cannot determine the answer
topic:mt_JiZ3H90Xg8:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why taking a risk isn't always irrational — and describe one cognitive bias that causes people to misjudge risk in their everyday decisions, such as why teenagers tend to underestimate certain dangers?
topic:mt_WtO50EZQkf:name: Online Identity and Misinformation
topic:mt_WtO50EZQkf:description: Understand the ethics of online identity and the importance of consistency between who you are online and offline; explain how recommendation algorithms and filter bubbles narrow information exposure; evaluate the psychology of misinformation: why it spreads, why smart people believe it, and how to apply source evaluation (lateral reading, checking evidence, recognising emotional manipulation); understand digital consent around sharing images or personal information; explore the ethics of AI, surveillance, and data privacy as they affect everyday life; reflect on responsible content creation and online influence
topic:mt_WtO50EZQkf:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} sees a convincing claim shared on social media, can they describe their process for deciding whether to believe or share it — and explain why even intelligent people are regularly misled online?
topic:mt_LPYPuSaxv_:name: Ethical Frameworks and Moral Reasoning
topic:mt_LPYPuSaxv_:description: Introduce the three main ethical frameworks: consequentialism (judge actions by outcomes and overall welfare), deontology (judge actions by adherence to rules and duties regardless of consequences), and virtue ethics (judge actions by the character they reflect); apply each framework to real-world moral dilemmas: climate responsibility, AI ethics, civil disobedience, wealth inequality, healthcare rationing; understand the strengths and limitations of each framework; develop the capacity for careful moral reasoning — the ability to think through ethical questions systematically rather than relying only on intuition or group opinion
topic:mt_LPYPuSaxv_:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} take a real ethical dilemma — like whether it's ever right to break a rule to help someone — and explain how a consequentialist, a deontologist, and someone focused on virtue ethics would each think about it differently, and which approach they find most persuasive?
topic:mt_69hFD2NgGe:name: Naming Your Feelings
topic:mt_69hFD2NgGe:description: Notice what you are feeling and put a name to it — being able to label an emotion is the first step to understanding and managing it
topic:mt_69hFD2NgGe:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} seems upset, excited, or frustrated, can they stop and tell you what emotion they're feeling — even if they can't fully explain why?
topic:mt_69hFD2NgGe:evidence:1: Fostering Emotional Literacy in Young Children (HeadStart.gov)
topic:mt_H4YZ1rSKP3:name: Vocabulary: self
topic:mt_H4YZ1rSKP3:description: Know and use the vocabulary of self-reflection — self-awareness, reflect, pattern, trigger, assumption, impact, perspective, and notice — and understand that having precise words for these inner experiences makes them easier to understand and talk about
topic:mt_H4YZ1rSKP3:assessmentPrompt: After a difficult moment — a falling-out with a friend or a frustrating task — can {{name}} talk about what happened using words like 'trigger' or 'reflect', showing they're thinking about their own reactions rather than just what the other person did?
topic:mt_H4YZ1rSKP3:evidence:0: Use words like 'reflect', 'pattern', and 'trigger' accurately when describing their own behaviour — e.g. 'I notice a pattern: I get frustrated when I rush'
topic:mt_H4YZ1rSKP3:evidence:1: Explain what 'self-awareness' means in their own words and give a personal example
topic:mt_H4YZ1rSKP3:evidence:2: Use the word 'perspective' correctly — e.g. 'From my perspective it felt unfair, but I can see theirs too'
topic:mt_TU3BcLOgiV:name: Feelings Versus Actions
topic:mt_TU3BcLOgiV:description: Understand that feelings and actions are separate — you can feel something strongly without having to act on it straight away
topic:mt_TU3BcLOgiV:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that feeling angry, scared, or jealous doesn't mean they have to act on it immediately — that there's a gap between the feeling and what they choose to do next?
topic:mt_TU3BcLOgiV:evidence:1: Effects of Age and Gender in Emotion Regulation (PMC 2020)
topic:mt_H8dEMH_wik:name: Patterns in Your Own Reactions
topic:mt_H8dEMH_wik:description: Notice patterns in your own reactions — 'I tend to respond like this when I'm tired, left out, or put on the spot'
topic:mt_H8dEMH_wik:assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} ever noticed a pattern in how they react — for example, that they get more upset at certain times of day, or that a particular type of situation reliably triggers a strong feeling?
topic:mt_H8dEMH_wik:evidence:0: middle childhood self-reliance in emotion regulation
topic:mt_rpug2tkYhb:name: Your Impact on Others
topic:mt_rpug2tkYhb:description: Reflect on how your behaviour lands on others — consider not just what you intended but what the actual impact was on the other person
topic:mt_rpug2tkYhb:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} think about how something they said or did might have felt to the other person — not just what they meant by it, but what the impact actually was?
topic:mt_rpug2tkYhb:evidence:0: Describe how something they said or did affected someone else — e.g. 'When I didn't include them, they looked upset'
topic:mt_rpug2tkYhb:evidence:1: Predict what might happen before acting — e.g. 'If I take the last one without asking, they'll feel it's unfair'
topic:mt_rpug2tkYhb:evidence:2: After a conflict, explain what they could have done differently and what effect that would have had
topic:mt_Mb1JUJmnbX:name: Questioning First Impressions
topic:mt_Mb1JUJmnbX:description: Notice when your first reading of a social situation might be wrong — your assumptions about why someone acted a certain way are not always facts
topic:mt_Mb1JUJmnbX:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} felt sure someone was being unfair or unkind, could they pause and consider whether there might be another explanation for what happened?
topic:mt_Mb1JUJmnbX:evidence:0: Pause before reacting to a classmate's behaviour and consider an alternative explanation — e.g. 'Maybe they bumped me by accident, not on purpose'
topic:mt_Mb1JUJmnbX:evidence:1: Describe a time they assumed the worst about someone's intention and later found out they were wrong
topic:mt_Mb1JUJmnbX:evidence:2: When told about an ambiguous social situation, suggest at least two possible reasons for the other person's behaviour instead of jumping to one conclusion
topic:mt_bkMDDstwwG:name: Personal Growth Over Time
topic:mt_bkMDDstwwG:description: Reflect on your own growth over time — the things that challenge you now are not fixed, and noticing how you have already changed builds genuine self-knowledge
topic:mt_bkMDDstwwG:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look back over the past year or two and point to something they used to find really difficult that they now handle better — and explain what changed?
topic:mt_bkMDDstwwG:evidence:0: emotion vocabulary development continues to age 11 (PMC)
topic:mt_aS-Gdh-MHx:name: Coping with Life Changes
topic:mt_aS-Gdh-MHx:description: Understand that change is a normal part of life — such as starting school, getting a new teacher, a new baby arriving, or moving house — and identify simple strategies that help them cope with changes
topic:mt_aS-Gdh-MHx:assessmentPrompt: When something changes in {{name}}'s life — like getting a new teacher at school — can they talk about how it makes them feel and think of ways to help themselves adjust?
topic:mt_aS-Gdh-MHx:evidence:0: Name at least two changes they have experienced and how they felt
topic:mt_aS-Gdh-MHx:evidence:1: Identify a person they can talk to when a change feels hard
topic:mt_aS-Gdh-MHx:evidence:2: Describe one strategy that helps them cope with change, such as keeping a familiar routine
topic:mt_UGf6jICEhs:name: Learning from Mistakes
topic:mt_UGf6jICEhs:description: Understand that making mistakes is a normal part of learning and that everyone — including adults — makes mistakes, and begin to see mistakes as opportunities to learn rather than reasons to give up
topic:mt_UGf6jICEhs:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets an answer wrong in class or messes up during a game, do they bounce back and keep trying rather than shutting down or saying 'I can't do it'?
topic:mt_UGf6jICEhs:evidence:0: Describe a time they made a mistake and what they learned from it
topic:mt_UGf6jICEhs:evidence:1: Respond to a mistake by trying again rather than giving up
topic:mt_UGf6jICEhs:evidence:2: Explain why mistakes help people learn
topic:mt_nNDX_jZ-cb:name: Patience and Delayed Gratification
topic:mt_nNDX_jZ-cb:description: Wait for things they want without becoming very distressed — practising patience and delayed gratification in everyday situations like waiting their turn, waiting for a treat, or waiting for help
topic:mt_nNDX_jZ-cb:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has to wait their turn for something they really want — like a go on the iPad or being served dinner — can they wait without a big fuss?
topic:mt_nNDX_jZ-cb:evidence:0: Wait for their turn in a game or activity without constant complaints
topic:mt_nNDX_jZ-cb:evidence:1: Describe what they do to help themselves wait, such as thinking about something else
topic:mt_nNDX_jZ-cb:evidence:2: Explain why sometimes we have to wait and that it is a skill they can practise
topic:mt_Iwg2diBSyW:name: Simple Calming Strategies
topic:mt_Iwg2diBSyW:description: Use simple calming strategies when feeling upset or overwhelmed — such as taking deep breaths, counting to ten, or going to a quiet space — and understand that these help the body and mind settle down
topic:mt_Iwg2diBSyW:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} gets really upset — say they lose a game or argue with a sibling — can they use a strategy like deep breaths to calm themselves down rather than staying in meltdown mode?
topic:mt_Iwg2diBSyW:evidence:0: Demonstrate at least two calming strategies when prompted
topic:mt_Iwg2diBSyW:evidence:1: Choose to use a calming strategy independently during a real upset
topic:mt_Iwg2diBSyW:evidence:2: Explain in simple terms why calming down helps them think better
topic:mt_SeNxOZTHCN:name: Words for Big Feelings
topic:mt_SeNxOZTHCN:description: Know and use the key words for managing big feelings — calm, strategy, cope, settle, patience, overwhelmed, and breathe — and understand that having words for these ideas is the first step to using them
topic:mt_SeNxOZTHCN:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is feeling really upset or frustrated, can they use words like 'I need to calm down' or 'I'm feeling overwhelmed' instead of just acting out?
topic:mt_SeNxOZTHCN:evidence:0: Use words like 'frustrated', 'anxious', 'overwhelmed', and 'disappointed' accurately to describe how they feel in difficult moments
topic:mt_SeNxOZTHCN:evidence:1: Explain what 'calm down' strategies are in their own words and name at least two they have tried (e.g. deep breaths, counting, walking away)
topic:mt_SeNxOZTHCN:evidence:2: Distinguish between similar feelings — e.g. explain the difference between being angry and being disappointed
topic:mt_miGrca8zaS:name: Breaking Tasks into Steps
topic:mt_miGrca8zaS:description: Break a challenging task into smaller, manageable steps rather than feeling overwhelmed by the whole thing — and celebrate progress along the way
topic:mt_miGrca8zaS:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a big school project that feels overwhelming, can they break it down into smaller steps — like 'first I'll research, then I'll write the introduction' — rather than panicking about the whole thing?
topic:mt_miGrca8zaS:evidence:0: Take a challenging task and list at least three smaller steps to complete it
topic:mt_miGrca8zaS:evidence:1: Start with the first step rather than procrastinating on the whole task
topic:mt_miGrca8zaS:evidence:2: Acknowledge progress after completing each step
topic:mt_j8Pv3s7TZR:name: Choosing the Right Coping Strategy
topic:mt_j8Pv3s7TZR:description: Understand that different situations require different coping strategies — what works for anger might not work for sadness, and what helps at school might be different from what helps at home
topic:mt_j8Pv3s7TZR:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} recognise that when they're angry they need to do something physical like walk around, but when they're worried they need to talk it through — rather than using the same approach for every difficult feeling?
topic:mt_j8Pv3s7TZR:evidence:0: Name at least two different coping strategies and explain when each one is most useful
topic:mt_j8Pv3s7TZR:evidence:1: Choose an appropriate strategy based on the specific situation and emotion
topic:mt_j8Pv3s7TZR:evidence:2: Reflect on a time a strategy didn't work and explain what they might try instead
topic:mt_pAuo9Op89t:name: Growth Mindset
topic:mt_pAuo9Op89t:description: Understand the concept of a growth mindset — that abilities and intelligence can grow with effort, practice, and good strategies — as opposed to a fixed mindset where you believe you're either good at something or you're not
topic:mt_pAuo9Op89t:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} finds something difficult like learning to ride a bike or mastering times tables, do they say 'I can't do it YET' rather than 'I'm just not good at this'?
topic:mt_pAuo9Op89t:evidence:0: Explain the difference between growth mindset and fixed mindset in their own words
topic:mt_pAuo9Op89t:evidence:1: Use 'yet' language when describing something they find difficult
topic:mt_pAuo9Op89t:evidence:2: Give an example of something they got better at through practice and effort
topic:mt_35-DhMh_Yr:name: Positive Self-Talk
topic:mt_35-DhMh_Yr:description: Use positive self-talk to manage difficult situations — replacing unhelpful thoughts like 'I'm stupid' or 'I'll never be able to do this' with encouraging ones like 'This is hard but I can keep trying' or 'I've done hard things before'
topic:mt_35-DhMh_Yr:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is struggling with homework and starts saying 'I'm rubbish at this', can they catch that thought and replace it with something more helpful like 'I just need to try a different approach'?
topic:mt_35-DhMh_Yr:evidence:0: Give an example of an unhelpful thought and rephrase it as a helpful one
topic:mt_35-DhMh_Yr:evidence:1: Use positive self-talk aloud or in writing when facing a challenge
topic:mt_35-DhMh_Yr:evidence:2: Explain how the words we say to ourselves affect how we feel and perform
topic:mt_i1kk9HDctI:name: Vocabulary: resilience and self
topic:mt_i1kk9HDctI:description: Know and use the vocabulary of resilience and self-management — including regulate, resilience, growth mindset, fixed mindset, self-talk, trigger, setback, persevere, and distress — and understand what each word means in practice
topic:mt_i1kk9HDctI:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s team loses a match or they fail a test, can they talk about what happened using words like 'resilience' or 'growth mindset' — showing they understand the difference between giving up and bouncing back?
topic:mt_i1kk9HDctI:evidence:0: Explain what 'resilience' means in their own words and give an example of a time they kept going when something was hard
topic:mt_i1kk9HDctI:evidence:1: Use 'growth mindset' correctly — e.g. 'I can't do it yet, but I can improve with practice'
topic:mt_i1kk9HDctI:evidence:2: Define 'self-regulation' and describe a strategy they use to manage frustration or setbacks
topic:mt_Jd2aWEUJ9G:name: Personal Coping Toolkit
topic:mt_Jd2aWEUJ9G:description: Reflect on which self-regulation and coping strategies work best for them personally, building a 'toolkit' of approaches they can draw on in different situations and sharing what works with others
topic:mt_Jd2aWEUJ9G:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you 'When I'm stressed about exams I go for a walk and that helps, but when I'm sad I need to talk to someone' — showing they know their own coping toolkit?
topic:mt_Jd2aWEUJ9G:evidence:0: Describe at least three personal coping strategies and when each is most effective
topic:mt_Jd2aWEUJ9G:evidence:1: Recommend a strategy to a friend based on the friend's specific situation
topic:mt_Jd2aWEUJ9G:evidence:2: Evaluate whether a strategy they tried worked well and explain their reasoning
topic:mt_cJjnPjuvCU:name: Personal Goal-Setting
topic:mt_cJjnPjuvCU:description: Set realistic personal goals, create a simple plan to achieve them, monitor their own progress, and adjust their approach when things aren't working
topic:mt_cJjnPjuvCU:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} set themselves a goal — like improving their swimming or finishing a book series — and actually work towards it step by step, adjusting their plan if needed?
topic:mt_cJjnPjuvCU:evidence:0: Write or state a specific, achievable personal goal with a timeframe
topic:mt_cJjnPjuvCU:evidence:1: Describe the steps they will take to reach the goal
topic:mt_cJjnPjuvCU:evidence:2: Review their progress and adjust their plan when something isn't working
topic:mt_Amw5ikSSQI:name: Resilience and Bouncing Back
topic:mt_Amw5ikSSQI:description: Understand resilience as the ability to recover from setbacks, adapt to difficult circumstances, and keep going — recognising that resilience is a skill that develops through experience, not a trait you either have or don't
topic:mt_Amw5ikSSQI:assessmentPrompt: After a real disappointment — like not getting a part in the school play or failing a test they studied for — can {{name}} feel upset but then pick themselves up and figure out what to do next?
topic:mt_Amw5ikSSQI:evidence:0: Define resilience in their own words and explain why it matters
topic:mt_Amw5ikSSQI:evidence:1: Describe a time they bounced back from a setback and what helped them recover
topic:mt_Amw5ikSSQI:evidence:2: Explain that resilience grows through experience and that struggling doesn't mean you're weak
topic:mt_HoJGVsMO7H:name: Time and Attention Management
topic:mt_HoJGVsMO7H:description: Manage their own time and attention effectively — prioritising tasks, minimising distractions, and maintaining focus on important work even when it's not the most exciting option
topic:mt_HoJGVsMO7H:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} has homework to finish but also wants to play a game, can they manage their time — doing the homework first or setting a timer — rather than always needing you to enforce it?
topic:mt_HoJGVsMO7H:evidence:0: Create a simple plan for completing multiple tasks in a sensible order
topic:mt_HoJGVsMO7H:evidence:1: Identify their own common distractions and describe strategies to manage them
topic:mt_HoJGVsMO7H:evidence:2: Complete a less enjoyable task before a more enjoyable one without constant reminders
topic:mt_0VOZSVjo6c:name: Good Stress and Bad Stress
topic:mt_0VOZSVjo6c:description: Distinguish between eustress (the productive, motivating kind of stress) and distress (harmful, overwhelming stress); explain the physiological stress response (fight-flight-freeze, HPA axis) and how chronic stress affects the body and mind; identify common adolescent stressors (academic pressure, social comparison, physical change, uncertainty about the future); evaluate evidence-based coping strategies (exercise, sleep, mindfulness, social support, expressive writing); recognise warning signs that stress has crossed into anxiety or depression and know where to get help
topic:mt_0VOZSVjo6c:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is under pressure from exams or social situations, can they name two or three strategies that genuinely help them manage the stress — and explain why each one actually works, not just that it 'makes them feel better'?
topic:mt_0ewYhTSHtP:name: Habits and Motivation
topic:mt_0ewYhTSHtP:description: Understand habit formation through the cue-routine-reward loop and how to design new habits intentionally; distinguish intrinsic motivation (doing something for its own value) from extrinsic motivation (rewards/punishments) and understand when each is more effective; understand procrastination as primarily an emotion regulation problem (avoiding discomfort) rather than a time management failure; apply self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness) to boost intrinsic motivation; design environments that reduce friction for desired behaviours
topic:mt_0ewYhTSHtP:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} keeps meaning to do something important but finds themselves putting it off, can they explain the real reason people procrastinate — it's not laziness — and describe one practical change they could make to their environment to make starting easier?
topic:mt__J2BO4V95l:name: Growth Through Adversity
topic:mt__J2BO4V95l:description: Understand that facing serious challenges can lead to genuine growth in three domains: new perspectives on life, improved relationships, and a strengthened sense of personal capability (post-traumatic growth); distinguish genuine growth from toxic positivity ('everything happens for a reason') and from denial; understand that resilience does not mean being unaffected by adversity but recovering and growing through it; develop a personal philosophy for handling setbacks based on meaning-making; explore how to support others going through serious difficulty without minimising their experience
topic:mt__J2BO4V95l:assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} ever come through something genuinely hard and found it changed them in a meaningful way? Can they explain what post-traumatic growth means and how it differs from just 'getting over it' or pretending something difficult was fine?
topic:mt_pwo81ls_J-:name: Animal Camouflage
topic:mt_pwo81ls_J-:description: Know that many animals use camouflage — colours and patterns that help them blend into their surroundings — to hide from predators or to sneak up on prey, like a leaf insect that looks like a leaf or an Arctic hare that turns white in winter
topic:mt_pwo81ls_J-:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} tries to spot a grasshopper in the garden, can they explain that it's hard to see because its green colour helps it hide in the grass — and give other examples of animals that use camouflage?
topic:mt_pwo81ls_J-:evidence:0: Explains that camouflage means blending in with surroundings
topic:mt_pwo81ls_J-:evidence:1: Gives at least 3 examples of camouflaged animals
topic:mt_pwo81ls_J-:evidence:2: Explains that camouflage helps animals hide from predators or sneak up on food
topic:mt_oLHXfLujmh:name: Animal Homes
topic:mt_oLHXfLujmh:description: Know that animals make or find many different kinds of homes — birds build nests, rabbits dig burrows, bees live in hives, hermit crabs use empty shells, spiders spin webs — and that these shelters protect them and their young
topic:mt_oLHXfLujmh:assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} where different animals live, can they describe several animal homes — like a bird's nest, a rabbit's burrow, or a bee's hive — and say why animals need shelter?
topic:mt_oLHXfLujmh:evidence:0: Names at least 4 different types of animal homes (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge)
topic:mt_oLHXfLujmh:evidence:1: Explains that animals need homes for shelter and to keep their babies safe
topic:mt_oLHXfLujmh:evidence:2: Matches common animals to their homes
topic:mt_goZW_hQUa4:name: Animal Record-Holders
topic:mt_goZW_hQUa4:description: Know some of the world's animal record-holders — the blue whale is the largest animal ever, the cheetah is the fastest land animal, the bee hummingbird is the smallest bird, the giraffe is the tallest — and compare their sizes to familiar objects
topic:mt_goZW_hQUa4:assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} which animal is the fastest or the biggest in the world, can they name some record-holders like the cheetah or blue whale and compare their size to something familiar, like 'a blue whale is as long as three buses'?
topic:mt_goZW_hQUa4:evidence:0: Names at least 4 animal record-holders with their record (fastest, biggest, tallest, smallest, etc.)
topic:mt_goZW_hQUa4:evidence:1: Compares an animal's size or ability to a familiar reference
topic:mt_goZW_hQUa4:evidence:2: Shows enthusiasm for superlative animal facts
topic:mt_v3Vz_Pgjjv:name: Animals Everywhere
topic:mt_v3Vz_Pgjjv:description: Know that animals live all over the world — on land, in water, and in the air — and that every continent, even icy Antarctica, is home to animals, each suited to the conditions where they live
topic:mt_v3Vz_Pgjjv:assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} pictures of a polar bear, a parrot, a camel, and a penguin, can they tell you that animals live in all sorts of different places around the world?
topic:mt_v3Vz_Pgjjv:evidence:0: Names at least 3 animals from different environments (e.g., forest, ocean, desert)
topic:mt_v3Vz_Pgjjv:evidence:1: States that animals live on land, in water, and some can fly
topic:mt_v3Vz_Pgjjv:evidence:2: Recognises that animals live on every continent
topic:mt_-vsLvsxp0L:name: How Animals Have Babies
topic:mt_-vsLvsxp0L:description: Know that different animals have their babies in different ways — some lay eggs (birds, reptiles, fish, insects), some give birth to live young (most mammals) — and that babies may look like miniature adults or look very different from their parents
topic:mt_-vsLvsxp0L:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a nest with eggs in a nature programme, can they explain that birds lay eggs and the babies hatch out, but dogs and cats have their babies born alive?
topic:mt_-vsLvsxp0L:evidence:0: Gives examples of animals that lay eggs and animals that give birth to live young
topic:mt_-vsLvsxp0L:evidence:1: Describes at least one example of a baby that looks different from its parent (e.g., tadpole/frog, caterpillar/butterfly)
topic:mt_-vsLvsxp0L:evidence:2: Shows curiosity about how different animals have their babies
topic:mt_V_wIdRZLsG:name: Nocturnal Animals
topic:mt_V_wIdRZLsG:description: Know that some animals are nocturnal — active at night and sleeping during the day — and that nocturnal animals often have special features like big eyes (owls, tarsiers), large ears (bats, fennec foxes), or sensitive whiskers to help them find food in the dark
topic:mt_V_wIdRZLsG:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears an owl hooting at bedtime, can they explain that owls are nocturnal — meaning they sleep during the day and come out at night — and that their big eyes help them see in the dark?
topic:mt_V_wIdRZLsG:evidence:1: Names at least 3 nocturnal animals (e.g., owl, bat, fox, hedgehog, moth)
topic:mt_V_wIdRZLsG:evidence:2: Describes one feature that helps a nocturnal animal (e.g., big eyes, echolocation, whiskers)
topic:mt_muxjw0fxxN:name: Wild, Farm & Pet Animals
topic:mt_muxjw0fxxN:description: Understand the difference between wild animals, farm animals, and pets — wild animals find their own food and shelter in nature; farm animals are kept by people for food, wool, or eggs; pets are animals people keep for companionship — and know that wild animals should be observed from a distance
topic:mt_muxjw0fxxN:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a fox in the garden, can they explain that it's a wild animal — different from their pet cat or a farm sheep — and that wild animals look after themselves and shouldn't be touched?
topic:mt_muxjw0fxxN:evidence:0: Sorts animals into wild, farm, and pet categories with examples
topic:mt_muxjw0fxxN:evidence:1: Explains one key difference between each category
topic:mt_muxjw0fxxN:evidence:2: Understands that wild animals should be observed, not approached
topic:mt_wHN14Unk7h:name: Animal Communication
topic:mt_wHN14Unk7h:description: Understand that animals communicate in many different ways — birds sing to attract mates and defend territory, whales call across vast ocean distances, bees dance to show other bees where food is, wolves howl to keep the pack together, and fireflies flash light signals — and that communication is essential for survival
topic:mt_wHN14Unk7h:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears birds singing in the morning, can they explain that birdsong is a way of communicating — and describe at least two other ways different animals send messages to each other?
topic:mt_wHN14Unk7h:evidence:0: Describes at least 4 different methods of animal communication (sound, dance, light, scent, body language)
topic:mt_wHN14Unk7h:evidence:1: Gives a specific animal example for each method
topic:mt_wHN14Unk7h:evidence:2: Explains that animals communicate to find mates, warn of danger, or share food locations
topic:mt_bK84sPehyP:name: Animal Migration
topic:mt_bK84sPehyP:description: Know that many animals make incredible journeys called migrations — Arctic terns fly from pole to pole, monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles across North America, wildebeest cross the Serengeti following rain, and humpback whales swim between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters — and that these journeys are linked to food, breeding, and seasons
topic:mt_bK84sPehyP:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns about the monarch butterfly's journey, can they explain what migration means and name at least two other animals that make long journeys — and say why they travel?
topic:mt_bK84sPehyP:evidence:0: Defines migration as a regular long journey animals make
topic:mt_bK84sPehyP:evidence:1: Names at least 3 migratory animals with their routes or destinations
topic:mt_bK84sPehyP:evidence:2: Explains that migration is driven by food availability, breeding, or seasonal changes
topic:mt_0zqOTjjW2k:name: Desert Animals
topic:mt_0zqOTjjW2k:description: Explore animals of the desert — camels, fennec foxes, scorpions, rattlesnakes, meerkats — and understand how desert animals survive extreme heat and lack of water through being active at night, storing water or fat, burrowing underground during the day, and having large ears to lose heat
topic:mt_0zqOTjjW2k:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads about camels in a desert, can they explain at least two ways desert animals cope with the heat and lack of water — like being active at night or having special body features?
topic:mt_0zqOTjjW2k:evidence:1: Explains at least two desert survival adaptations (nocturnal behaviour, water storage, burrowing, large ears for cooling)
topic:mt_0zqOTjjW2k:evidence:2: Knows deserts can be hot or cold but are always dry
topic:mt_D4lyx0iYyB:name: Polar Animals
topic:mt_D4lyx0iYyB:description: Explore animals of the Arctic and Antarctic — polar bears, Arctic foxes, and walruses in the north; penguins, seals, and albatrosses in the south — and understand how polar animals survive extreme cold through thick fur or blubber, huddling behaviour, and seasonal changes like white winter coats
topic:mt_D4lyx0iYyB:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a nature programme about the Arctic, can they explain how polar bears stay warm in freezing temperatures and name at least two differences between Arctic animals (north) and Antarctic animals (south)?
topic:mt_D4lyx0iYyB:evidence:0: Names at least 3 animals each from the Arctic and Antarctic
topic:mt_D4lyx0iYyB:evidence:1: Explains at least two adaptations for surviving cold (blubber, thick fur, huddling, white camouflage)
topic:mt_D4lyx0iYyB:evidence:2: Knows polar bears live only in the Arctic and penguins only in the Antarctic/Southern Hemisphere
topic:mt_Bztatrv-_v:name: Predator Hunting Strategies
topic:mt_Bztatrv-_v:description: Understand that predators have evolved hunting strategies — wolves hunt in packs, chameleons use their long tongues, spiders build webs, crocodiles ambush at water's edge — and prey animals have evolved defences — porcupine spines, skunk spray, poison dart frog toxins, zebra stripes confusing predators, playing dead
topic:mt_Bztatrv-_v:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a nature programme showing a lion hunting, can they describe at least two different ways predators catch food and two ways prey animals defend themselves?
topic:mt_Bztatrv-_v:evidence:0: Describes at least 3 predator hunting strategies with examples
topic:mt_Bztatrv-_v:evidence:1: Describes at least 3 prey defence mechanisms with examples
topic:mt_Bztatrv-_v:evidence:2: Understands the concept of an 'arms race' between predators and prey
topic:mt_DCelLx_H1A:name: Rainforest Animals
topic:mt_DCelLx_H1A:description: Explore animals of the tropical rainforest — the most species-rich habitat on Earth — learning that the forest has layers (canopy, understory, forest floor) with different animals at each level: toucans and monkeys in the canopy, jaguars and frogs on the floor, and that rainforests are found near the equator
topic:mt_DCelLx_H1A:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a documentary about rainforests, can they describe at least three animals that live there and explain that different animals live at different heights in the forest — some in the treetops and some on the ground?
topic:mt_DCelLx_H1A:evidence:0: Names at least 4 rainforest animals from different layers
topic:mt_DCelLx_H1A:evidence:1: Describes the rainforest as having layers (canopy, understory, forest floor)
topic:mt_DCelLx_H1A:evidence:2: Explains that rainforests are near the equator and are hot and wet
topic:mt_DCelLx_H1A:evidence:3: Recognises that rainforests have more species than almost any other habitat
topic:mt_YynJoQcm_M:name: Savanna & Grassland Animals
topic:mt_YynJoQcm_M:description: Explore animals of the grasslands and savanna — lions, zebras, wildebeest, elephants, cheetahs in African savanna; bison and prairie dogs in American grasslands — understanding why large herds form on open grasslands and how predators and prey interact in these wide-open spaces
topic:mt_YynJoQcm_M:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees pictures of the African savanna, can they name at least four animals that live there and explain why some animals like zebras live in large herds?
topic:mt_YynJoQcm_M:evidence:1: Explains that herding provides safety in numbers against predators
topic:mt_YynJoQcm_M:evidence:2: Describes the predator-prey relationship (e.g., lions hunt zebras)
topic:mt_YynJoQcm_M:evidence:3: Knows grasslands/savannas are wide-open habitats with few trees
topic:mt_R7LEuZjTmx:name: The World of Minibeasts
topic:mt_R7LEuZjTmx:description: Know that insects and other minibeasts (spiders, worms, snails, centipedes) are the most numerous and diverse group of animals on Earth — there are more species of beetle than any other animal — and that they play vital roles as pollinators (bees, butterflies), decomposers (woodlice, worms), and food for other animals
topic:mt_R7LEuZjTmx:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} spots a bee in the garden, can they explain why bees are important — and name at least two other jobs that insects and minibeasts do that help the natural world?
topic:mt_R7LEuZjTmx:evidence:0: Knows that insects/minibeasts are the most numerous animal group
topic:mt_R7LEuZjTmx:evidence:1: Names at least 3 roles minibeasts play: pollinators, decomposers, food source
topic:mt_R7LEuZjTmx:evidence:2: Distinguishes insects (6 legs) from spiders (8 legs) from other minibeasts
topic:mt_R7LEuZjTmx:evidence:3: Shows appreciation for the importance of invertebrates
topic:mt_fpPLWFIRVo:name: Animal Intelligence
topic:mt_fpPLWFIRVo:description: Explore animal intelligence and complex behaviour — chimpanzees and crows use tools, dolphins recognise themselves in mirrors, octopuses solve puzzles and escape enclosures, elephants mourn their dead, meerkats teach their young to handle scorpions — understanding that many animals think, learn, and have social lives more complex than once believed
topic:mt_fpPLWFIRVo:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a video of a crow using a stick to get food from a tube, can they explain that this shows animal intelligence and give other examples of animals that use tools, solve problems, or show complex behaviour?
topic:mt_fpPLWFIRVo:evidence:0: Gives at least 4 examples of animal intelligence or complex behaviour
topic:mt_fpPLWFIRVo:evidence:1: Explains what 'tool use' means and names at least 2 tool-using animals
topic:mt_fpPLWFIRVo:evidence:2: Discusses how scientists test animal intelligence (mirror test, puzzle boxes, observation)
topic:mt_fpPLWFIRVo:evidence:3: Shows understanding that intelligence takes different forms in different species
topic:mt_NDZYiLvApW:name: Biodiversity
topic:mt_NDZYiLvApW:description: Understand that biodiversity — the variety of different species in an ecosystem — is essential for healthy ecosystems, and that keystone species (like wolves in Yellowstone, sea otters in kelp forests, or bees as pollinators) have an outsized impact on their ecosystem, so that losing one key species can cause a cascade of changes affecting many others
topic:mt_NDZYiLvApW:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns about how wolves were brought back to Yellowstone and the whole ecosystem changed, can they explain what a 'keystone species' is and why having many different species in an area matters?
topic:mt_NDZYiLvApW:evidence:0: Defines biodiversity as the variety of species in an ecosystem
topic:mt_NDZYiLvApW:evidence:1: Explains why biodiversity matters (stability, resilience, ecosystem services)
topic:mt_NDZYiLvApW:evidence:2: Defines keystone species and gives at least 2 examples
topic:mt_NDZYiLvApW:evidence:3: Describes a trophic cascade or chain reaction from removing/adding a species
topic:mt_5S4byWDX6n:name: Endangered & Extinct Species
topic:mt_5S4byWDX6n:description: Understand why some animal species become endangered or go extinct — habitat destruction, hunting/poaching, pollution, climate change, and invasive species — and know examples like the giant panda, mountain gorilla, Amur leopard, and the now-extinct dodo and thylacine, using the IUCN Red List as the system scientists use to track threatened species
topic:mt_5S4byWDX6n:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a news story about an endangered animal, can they explain what 'endangered' means and describe at least three reasons why some animals are at risk of disappearing forever?
topic:mt_5S4byWDX6n:evidence:0: Defines endangered as a species at risk of extinction
topic:mt_5S4byWDX6n:evidence:1: Names at least 3 causes of species becoming endangered
topic:mt_5S4byWDX6n:evidence:2: Gives at least 3 examples of endangered or extinct animals
topic:mt_5S4byWDX6n:evidence:3: Knows the IUCN Red List exists as a tracking system
