topic:mt_CBxOcjh69x:name: Invasive Species
topic:mt_CBxOcjh69x:description: Understand that invasive species are animals (or plants) that have been introduced to a place where they don't naturally belong — like grey squirrels outcompeting red squirrels in the UK, cane toads poisoning native predators in Australia, or rabbits devastating ecosystems in Australia — and that they can cause serious harm to native wildlife by competing for food, spreading disease, or having no natural predators
topic:mt_CBxOcjh69x:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that grey squirrels were brought to the UK from America, can they explain why introduced animals can be a problem for the animals that were already living there?
topic:mt_CBxOcjh69x:evidence:0: Defines invasive species as non-native animals introduced to a new environment
topic:mt_CBxOcjh69x:evidence:1: Names at least 2 examples of invasive species and their impacts
topic:mt_CBxOcjh69x:evidence:2: Explains at least 2 reasons invasive species are harmful (no predators, outcompete natives, spread disease)
topic:mt_CBxOcjh69x:evidence:3: Understands the difference between a species naturally expanding its range and being introduced by humans
topic:mt_pWwV_8OgXD:name: Protecting Endangered Animals
topic:mt_pWwV_8OgXD:description: Know how people work to protect endangered animals — through national parks and marine reserves, captive breeding programmes (like those that saved the California condor and Arabian oryx), anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors connecting habitats, and laws banning trade in endangered species — and understand that children can contribute through habitat-friendly choices
topic:mt_pWwV_8OgXD:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visits a zoo with a breeding programme, can they explain how zoos help save endangered species and describe at least two other ways people protect wildlife?
topic:mt_pWwV_8OgXD:evidence:0: Describes at least 3 conservation strategies with specific examples
topic:mt_pWwV_8OgXD:evidence:1: Names an animal saved from near-extinction by conservation efforts
topic:mt_pWwV_8OgXD:evidence:2: Suggests at least one action children or families can take to help wildlife
topic:mt_pWwV_8OgXD:evidence:3: Understands that conservation requires both protecting habitats and helping individual species
topic:mt_EaWjCyn8W2:name: Structural Adaptations
topic:mt_EaWjCyn8W2:description: Understand that animals have structural adaptations (body features like the giraffe's long neck, eagle's talons, dolphin's streamlined shape), behavioural adaptations (migration, hibernation, tool use), and physiological adaptations (antifreeze in Arctic fish blood, echolocation in bats) — and that these developed over many generations through natural selection
topic:mt_EaWjCyn8W2:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a woodpecker pecking a tree, can they explain that its strong beak, long tongue, and shock-absorbing skull are all adaptations — and describe what the word 'adaptation' means with other examples?
topic:mt_EaWjCyn8W2:evidence:0: Defines adaptation as a feature or behaviour that helps an animal survive in its environment
topic:mt_EaWjCyn8W2:evidence:1: Gives examples of structural, behavioural, and physiological adaptations
topic:mt_EaWjCyn8W2:evidence:2: Explains that adaptations develop over many generations, not during one animal's lifetime
topic:mt_EaWjCyn8W2:evidence:3: Connects adaptations to the concept of natural selection at a basic level
topic:mt_H8OgKZbgGe:name: Symbiosis
topic:mt_H8OgKZbgGe:description: Understand symbiosis — close relationships between different species — including mutualism (both benefit, like clownfish and anemones), commensalism (one benefits without harming the other, like remora fish riding sharks), and parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense, like ticks on deer) — and recognise these relationships in nature
topic:mt_H8OgKZbgGe:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a nature programme showing a small bird picking insects off a buffalo's back, can they explain that both animals benefit from this relationship and name the type of symbiosis?
topic:mt_H8OgKZbgGe:evidence:0: Defines symbiosis as a close relationship between different species
topic:mt_H8OgKZbgGe:evidence:1: Distinguishes mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism with an example of each
topic:mt_H8OgKZbgGe:evidence:2: Identifies symbiotic relationships when presented with new scenarios
topic:mt_mKNmXqz_Oo:name: The Red Queen Hypothesis
topic:mt_mKNmXqz_Oo:description: Introduce the Red Queen hypothesis — species must keep evolving just to maintain fitness relative to co-evolving partners; describe predator-prey arms races (cheetah speed vs gazelle speed, bat echolocation vs moth hearing jamming) and parasite-host co-evolution (myxomatosis in rabbits); explain Darwin's hawk moth and orchid as a classic example of mutualistic co-evolution predicting an unknown species; understand that co-evolution is a major driver of biological diversification
topic:mt_mKNmXqz_Oo:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the idea of an evolutionary arms race — how a predator and its prey keep evolving better attack and defence strategies in response to each other, never quite getting ahead?
topic:mt_ot9rcUwBtK:name: Deep-Sea Survival
topic:mt_ot9rcUwBtK:description: Explain how deep-sea animals cope with crushing pressure (no gas-filled spaces, flexible proteins, pressure-adapted enzymes); describe thermoregulation extremes — antifreeze glycoproteins in Antarctic fish, supercooling in wood frogs; introduce tardigrades and cryptobiosis (surviving desiccation, extreme temperatures, radiation, vacuum); survey other extremophiles (thermophiles at hydrothermal vents, halophiles in salt flats); consider what these organisms tell us about the limits of life
topic:mt_ot9rcUwBtK:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe an animal that can survive being frozen solid, completely dried out, or exposed to the vacuum of space — and explain roughly how it manages to survive conditions that would kill almost any other living thing?
topic:mt_YNrrNE23dZ:name: Sexual Selection
topic:mt_YNrrNE23dZ:description: Explain sexual selection as a form of natural selection: runaway selection for peacock tails, bird of paradise displays, and frog calls; explain kin selection and altruistic behaviour — why worker bees die to protect the hive, why meerkats stand guard at personal risk (Hamilton's rule, inclusive fitness); introduce game theory in animal behaviour using the hawk-dove model; define cognitive ethology and survey evidence for animal emotions, play, and culture
topic:mt_YNrrNE23dZ:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a worker bee dying to protect the hive actually makes evolutionary sense — even though the bee never has its own offspring? What's the logic that makes this a successful strategy?
topic:mt_44HkROUnzE:name: The Biodiversity Crisis
topic:mt_44HkROUnzE:description: Quantify the current biodiversity crisis: extinction rates 100-1000x the background rate; explain methods for measuring biodiversity loss (species-area relationship, population viability analysis, IUCN Red List categories); evaluate rewilding case studies — Yellowstone wolf reintroduction triggering a trophic cascade that changed river courses; Iberian lynx recovery; describe minimum viable population theory and conservation triage; examine ethical debates in deciding which species to prioritise
topic:mt_44HkROUnzE:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe what happened to Yellowstone National Park after wolves were reintroduced — what unexpected changes rippled through the whole ecosystem, including effects on rivers, as a result of one predator coming back?
topic:mt_fqAkSv3cUE:name: Grouping Species Using DNA
topic:mt_fqAkSv3cUE:description: Explain cladistics: organisms are grouped by shared derived characters, not just similarity; how phylogenetic trees are built using molecular data (DNA sequence alignment) and the molecular clock; explain why birds are technically a group within dinosaurs (crown Avemetatarsalia); distinguish convergent evolution (unrelated species evolving similar traits) from parallel evolution; introduce horizontal gene transfer and why the tree of life is more accurately a web; explain why classification systems keep changing as new data emerge
topic:mt_fqAkSv3cUE:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why biologists now say that birds ARE a type of dinosaur — not just their descendants but literally within the dinosaur family tree? What does that tell us about how scientists classify animals?
topic:mt_u0TeRwRII_:name: Dinosaur Sizes
topic:mt_u0TeRwRII_:description: Compare dinosaur sizes to familiar things — some dinosaurs were as tall as a house, others were as small as a chicken — and understand that dinosaurs came in a huge range of sizes
topic:mt_u0TeRwRII_:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you that some dinosaurs were enormous and others were tiny — maybe using comparisons like 'as tall as a building' or 'as small as a cat'?
topic:mt_u0TeRwRII_:evidence:0: Compare the size of a large dinosaur to a familiar object like a bus or house
topic:mt_u0TeRwRII_:evidence:1: Name a very large dinosaur (e.g. Brachiosaurus) and a small one (e.g. Compsognathus)
topic:mt_u0TeRwRII_:evidence:2: Use words like 'taller than', 'longer than', 'heavier than' when comparing
topic:mt_dpM1l5IOk6:name: Dinosaurs Were Real
topic:mt_dpM1l5IOk6:description: Understand that dinosaurs were real animals that lived on Earth a very long time ago and are now extinct — none are alive today
topic:mt_dpM1l5IOk6:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a dinosaur toy, can they tell you that real dinosaurs lived long ago but aren't alive any more?
topic:mt_dpM1l5IOk6:evidence:0: State that dinosaurs were real animals, not made up
topic:mt_dpM1l5IOk6:evidence:1: Explain that 'extinct' means no living ones are left anywhere
topic:mt_dpM1l5IOk6:evidence:2: Distinguish between 'a long time ago' and recent events like last year
topic:mt_BnabTHkNIp:name: Famous Dinosaur Species
topic:mt_BnabTHkNIp:description: Recognise and name common well-known dinosaur species: Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and Brachiosaurus/Diplodocus, describing a basic feature of each
topic:mt_BnabTHkNIp:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees pictures of different dinosaurs, can they name at least three — like T. rex, Triceratops, and Stegosaurus?
topic:mt_BnabTHkNIp:evidence:0: Name at least four common dinosaur species from pictures or models
topic:mt_BnabTHkNIp:evidence:1: Describe one visible feature of each (e.g. T. rex has tiny arms, Triceratops has three horns)
topic:mt_BnabTHkNIp:evidence:2: Match a dinosaur name to a picture or model without help
topic:mt_bKlnc7dyVK:name: Fossils & Palaeontologists
topic:mt_bKlnc7dyVK:description: Understand that fossils are the remains of ancient living things preserved in rock, and that scientists called palaeontologists study fossils to learn about dinosaurs
topic:mt_bKlnc7dyVK:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a fossil-shaped rock on a beach or at a museum, could they explain what a fossil is and who studies them?
topic:mt_bKlnc7dyVK:evidence:0: Describe a fossil as the remains of a living thing preserved in rock
topic:mt_bKlnc7dyVK:evidence:1: Name the job of a palaeontologist as someone who studies fossils
topic:mt_bKlnc7dyVK:evidence:2: Identify examples of fossils: bones, teeth, footprints in rock
topic:mt_DJh2JPwTf6:name: Plant-Eaters vs Meat-Eaters
topic:mt_DJh2JPwTf6:description: Sort dinosaurs into plant-eaters (herbivores) and meat-eaters (carnivores) by looking at clues like tooth shape — flat teeth for plants, sharp teeth for meat
topic:mt_DJh2JPwTf6:assessmentPrompt: If you showed {{name}} a picture of a dinosaur's teeth, could they guess whether it ate plants or meat?
topic:mt_DJh2JPwTf6:evidence:0: Sort a set of dinosaur pictures or models into herbivore and carnivore groups
topic:mt_DJh2JPwTf6:evidence:1: Explain that sharp pointed teeth are for tearing meat and flat teeth are for grinding plants
topic:mt_DJh2JPwTf6:evidence:2: Give an example of one herbivore and one carnivore dinosaur
topic:mt_JednrdYqpt:name: Real Dinosaurs vs Fiction
topic:mt_JednrdYqpt:description: Distinguish real dinosaurs from fictional or commonly confused creatures — pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) were not dinosaurs, and movie dinosaurs are not always accurate
topic:mt_JednrdYqpt:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a flying reptile in a dinosaur book, can they tell you it's actually not a dinosaur but a different kind of prehistoric animal?
topic:mt_JednrdYqpt:evidence:0: State that pterosaurs could fly but were not dinosaurs
topic:mt_JednrdYqpt:evidence:1: State that plesiosaurs lived in the sea but were not dinosaurs
topic:mt_JednrdYqpt:evidence:2: Identify at least one way a movie or cartoon dinosaur differs from the real animal
topic:mt_oH1XC8aQYn:name: Dinosaurs Around the World
topic:mt_oH1XC8aQYn:description: Understand that different dinosaurs lived on different continents and that fossil discoveries around the world show dinosaurs were a global phenomenon, with some species found only in certain regions
topic:mt_oH1XC8aQYn:assessmentPrompt: If you showed {{name}} a world map, could they tell you that dinosaur fossils have been found on every continent — and maybe name a place where a famous dinosaur was discovered?
topic:mt_oH1XC8aQYn:evidence:0: State that dinosaur fossils have been found on every continent including Antarctica
topic:mt_oH1XC8aQYn:evidence:1: Name at least one dinosaur discovery location (e.g. T. rex in North America, Velociraptor in Mongolia)
topic:mt_oH1XC8aQYn:evidence:2: Suggest a reason why the same type of dinosaur is sometimes found on continents now far apart
topic:mt_1dXhJp6qLJ:name: Fossilised Dinosaur Dung
topic:mt_1dXhJp6qLJ:description: Describe what coprolites are (fossilised dinosaur dung) and how palaeontologists analyse them to discover what dinosaurs ate, including plant fragments, bones, and seeds
topic:mt_1dXhJp6qLJ:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know what a coprolite is? Can they explain — with a giggle — how fossilised poo helps scientists figure out what a dinosaur ate?
topic:mt_1dXhJp6qLJ:evidence:0: Define a coprolite as fossilised dung (animal droppings preserved as rock)
topic:mt_1dXhJp6qLJ:evidence:1: Explain that scientists cut coprolites open to find plant seeds, bone fragments, or fish scales inside
topic:mt_1dXhJp6qLJ:evidence:2: State one example of what coprolite contents reveal about a dinosaur's diet
topic:mt_fKwgN61ttR:name: Fossils Reveal Ancient Environments
topic:mt_fKwgN61ttR:description: Understand that fossils tell us not only about ancient animals but also about ancient environments — for example, marine fossils found on a mountaintop show that area was once underwater
topic:mt_fKwgN61ttR:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that seashell fossils were found on a mountain, could they explain what that tells us about what the area used to be like?
topic:mt_fKwgN61ttR:evidence:0: Give an example of a fossil that reveals a past environment different from today's
topic:mt_fKwgN61ttR:evidence:1: Explain that finding marine fossils inland means that area was once covered by sea
topic:mt_fKwgN61ttR:evidence:2: State that plant fossils can show whether an area was once a forest, desert, or swamp
topic:mt_iycQEai3dK:name: How Fossils Form
topic:mt_iycQEai3dK:description: Explain in simple terms how fossils form: an organism dies and is quickly buried in sediment; over millions of years minerals replace the remains and the sediment turns to rock, preserving the shape
topic:mt_iycQEai3dK:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} made a salt-dough fossil at school, could they explain how real fossils form underground over millions of years?
topic:mt_iycQEai3dK:evidence:0: Describe the basic sequence: organism dies, buried in sediment, minerals replace remains over time
topic:mt_iycQEai3dK:evidence:1: Explain why fossilisation is rare — most organisms decompose before being buried
topic:mt_iycQEai3dK:evidence:2: Use the words 'sediment', 'minerals', and 'rock' correctly when explaining
topic:mt_excSPNHJWZ:name: Mary Anning, Fossil Hunter
topic:mt_excSPNHJWZ:description: Know who Mary Anning was — a pioneering fossil hunter from Lyme Regis, England, who discovered ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons in the early 1800s and contributed to our understanding of prehistoric life
topic:mt_excSPNHJWZ:assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} heard of Mary Anning? Can they tell you who she was and why she was important to the study of fossils?
topic:mt_excSPNHJWZ:evidence:0: State that Mary Anning lived in England in the early 1800s and hunted for fossils along the coast
topic:mt_excSPNHJWZ:evidence:1: Name at least one of her major discoveries (ichthyosaur or plesiosaur)
topic:mt_excSPNHJWZ:evidence:2: Explain why her work was important — she helped scientists understand that extinct creatures once lived on Earth
topic:mt_Wpvuz3mvBq:name: Reading Dinosaur Trackways
topic:mt_Wpvuz3mvBq:description: Use dinosaur trackways (fossilised footprints) to make inferences about a dinosaur's size, speed, and behaviour — widely spaced prints suggest running, closely spaced suggest walking
topic:mt_Wpvuz3mvBq:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a line of dinosaur footprints at a museum, could they figure out whether the dinosaur was walking or running based on how far apart the prints are?
topic:mt_Wpvuz3mvBq:evidence:0: Explain that larger footprints generally mean a larger dinosaur
topic:mt_Wpvuz3mvBq:evidence:1: Compare spacing between prints to infer walking versus running
topic:mt_Wpvuz3mvBq:evidence:2: Suggest what a set of parallel trackways might mean (e.g. dinosaurs travelling in a group)
topic:mt_uQljqc0J5j:name: The Mesozoic Era
topic:mt_uQljqc0J5j:description: Place the three periods of the Mesozoic Era — Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous — in order and understand that different dinosaurs lived in different periods, not all at the same time
topic:mt_uQljqc0J5j:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that T. rex and Stegosaurus didn't actually live at the same time — and can they name the three dinosaur time periods in order?
topic:mt_uQljqc0J5j:evidence:0: List Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous in the correct chronological order
topic:mt_uQljqc0J5j:evidence:1: Assign at least one well-known dinosaur to the correct period
topic:mt_uQljqc0J5j:evidence:2: Explain that millions of years separated these periods and different species lived in each
topic:mt_1VSFoM44JU:name: Types of Fossils
topic:mt_1VSFoM44JU:description: Distinguish body fossils (preserved bones, teeth, shells) from trace fossils (footprints, trackways, eggs, burrows, coprolites) and explain what each type can tell scientists
topic:mt_1VSFoM44JU:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a dinosaur footprint in rock at a museum, could they explain how it's different from a fossil bone and what scientists can learn from it?
topic:mt_1VSFoM44JU:evidence:0: Sort examples into body fossils (bones, teeth, shells) and trace fossils (footprints, eggs, dung)
topic:mt_1VSFoM44JU:evidence:1: Explain that body fossils show what an animal looked like physically
topic:mt_1VSFoM44JU:evidence:2: Explain that trace fossils show how an animal behaved — how it moved, what it ate, where it nested
topic:mt_6Z42wJaKYG:name: Fossils as Evidence
topic:mt_6Z42wJaKYG:description: Analyse and interpret data from fossils to provide evidence of organisms and environments that existed long ago
topic:mt_6Z42wJaKYG:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a fossil of a fish in a rock on a hillside, can they explain that the area must have been underwater millions of years ago?
topic:mt_6Z42wJaKYG:evidence:0: Explain that fossils are preserved remains or traces of organisms that lived long ago
topic:mt_6Z42wJaKYG:evidence:1: Use fossil evidence to make inferences about past organisms and their environments
topic:mt_6Z42wJaKYG:evidence:2: Describe how comparing fossils with living organisms helps us understand how life has changed
topic:mt_T8JGTJ-oNI:name: Birds Evolved from Dinosaurs
topic:mt_T8JGTJ-oNI:description: Understand that modern birds evolved from a group of small feathered theropod dinosaurs, using evidence such as the fossil Archaeopteryx, feathered dinosaur fossils from China, and shared skeletal features
topic:mt_T8JGTJ-oNI:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why scientists say birds are actually living dinosaurs — and point to evidence like feathered dinosaur fossils?
topic:mt_T8JGTJ-oNI:evidence:0: State that birds evolved from small theropod dinosaurs
topic:mt_T8JGTJ-oNI:evidence:1: Name Archaeopteryx or Chinese feathered dinosaurs as key fossil evidence
topic:mt_T8JGTJ-oNI:evidence:2: List at least two features birds share with theropods (e.g. hollow bones, wishbone, three-toed feet)
topic:mt_0T0Zf0YG6k:name: Changing Scientific Knowledge
topic:mt_0T0Zf0YG6k:description: Evaluate competing scientific explanations about dinosaurs by weighing fossil evidence — understanding that scientific knowledge changes as new fossils are discovered and new methods of analysis are developed
topic:mt_0T0Zf0YG6k:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read two different explanations for why dinosaurs went extinct, could they discuss what evidence supports each idea and why scientists sometimes change their minds?
topic:mt_0T0Zf0YG6k:evidence:0: Give an example of a scientific idea about dinosaurs that changed when new evidence was found
topic:mt_0T0Zf0YG6k:evidence:1: Explain that different scientists may interpret the same fossil evidence differently
topic:mt_0T0Zf0YG6k:evidence:2: State that the best scientific explanation is the one supported by the most evidence from multiple sources
topic:mt_yrSdVrXrsF:name: Dinosaur Hip Groups
topic:mt_yrSdVrXrsF:description: Classify dinosaurs into the two major groups based on hip structure: Saurischia (lizard-hipped, including theropods and sauropods) and Ornithischia (bird-hipped, including Triceratops and Stegosaurus)
topic:mt_yrSdVrXrsF:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that scientists divide dinosaurs into two big groups based on their hip bones — and tell you which group includes T. rex?
topic:mt_yrSdVrXrsF:evidence:0: Name the two major dinosaur groups: Saurischia and Ornithischia
topic:mt_yrSdVrXrsF:evidence:1: Explain the difference is based on hip bone structure (lizard-hipped vs bird-hipped)
topic:mt_yrSdVrXrsF:evidence:2: Correctly classify at least two dinosaurs into each group (e.g. T. rex = Saurischia, Triceratops = Ornithischia)
topic:mt_JBWMqZVO7S:name: How Palaeontologists Work
topic:mt_JBWMqZVO7S:description: Describe how palaeontologists work in the field and lab: prospecting for exposed fossils, careful excavation with hand tools, plaster jacketing for transport, preparation in the lab, and scientific description and publication
topic:mt_JBWMqZVO7S:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe the steps a palaeontologist goes through from first spotting a fossil in a cliff to it ending up on display in a museum?
topic:mt_JBWMqZVO7S:evidence:0: List the main stages: prospecting, excavation, jacketing, transport, preparation, study, display
topic:mt_JBWMqZVO7S:evidence:1: Explain why careful excavation with small tools is necessary to avoid damaging the fossil
topic:mt_JBWMqZVO7S:evidence:2: Describe plaster jacketing as wrapping fossils in plaster for safe transport to a lab
topic:mt_M8UQTURODF:name: Palaeoart & Speculation
topic:mt_M8UQTURODF:description: Understand that palaeoart — scientific illustrations and models of dinosaurs — is based on fossil evidence but involves informed speculation about skin colour, feathers, and soft tissues that don't usually fossilise
topic:mt_M8UQTURODF:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that pictures of dinosaurs are educated guesses? Can they explain what parts are based on evidence and what parts scientists have to imagine?
topic:mt_M8UQTURODF:evidence:0: Explain that bones and teeth are known from fossils but skin colour and soft tissues usually are not
topic:mt_M8UQTURODF:evidence:1: State that recent discoveries of preserved skin impressions and feather fossils have improved reconstructions
topic:mt_M8UQTURODF:evidence:2: Give an example of how our picture of a dinosaur has changed over time (e.g. feathered vs scaly Velociraptor)
topic:mt_cSPtyLF3q1:name: Reading Cladograms
topic:mt_cSPtyLF3q1:description: Read and create simple cladograms (branching diagrams) that show how groups of dinosaurs are related based on shared features, understanding that species sharing more features are more closely related
topic:mt_cSPtyLF3q1:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a branching tree diagram showing dinosaur relationships, could they explain which dinosaurs are most closely related by looking at where the branches split?
topic:mt_cSPtyLF3q1:evidence:0: Explain that a cladogram shows evolutionary relationships based on shared features
topic:mt_cSPtyLF3q1:evidence:1: Read a simple cladogram to identify which two dinosaurs share the most recent common ancestor
topic:mt_cSPtyLF3q1:evidence:2: Add a new species to a partially completed cladogram based on its listed features
topic:mt_EGIlsfHxb6:name: Rock Layers & Relative Dating
topic:mt_EGIlsfHxb6:description: Understand that rock layers (strata) form in sequence with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest at the top, and that fossils found in deeper layers are older — this is the principle of relative dating
topic:mt_EGIlsfHxb6:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a cliff with layers of rock, could they explain that the bottom layers are the oldest and that fossils found deeper down lived longer ago?
topic:mt_EGIlsfHxb6:evidence:0: Explain that sedimentary rock forms in layers with the oldest at the bottom
topic:mt_EGIlsfHxb6:evidence:1: Use a diagram of rock strata to determine which fossil is older based on its position
topic:mt_EGIlsfHxb6:evidence:2: Define relative dating as working out the age of something by comparing its position in rock layers
topic:mt_QHKqckBdAk:name: The K-Pg Extinction Event
topic:mt_QHKqckBdAk:description: Describe the Cretaceous–Palaeogene (K-Pg) extinction event approximately 66 million years ago, including the asteroid impact theory and its evidence (iridium layer, Chicxulub crater), and understand that this ended the reign of non-avian dinosaurs
topic:mt_QHKqckBdAk:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what scientists think caused the dinosaurs to go extinct — and describe at least one piece of evidence for the asteroid theory?
topic:mt_QHKqckBdAk:evidence:0: State that the K-Pg extinction happened about 66 million years ago and wiped out non-avian dinosaurs
topic:mt_QHKqckBdAk:evidence:1: Describe the asteroid impact hypothesis and name the Chicxulub crater in Mexico
topic:mt_QHKqckBdAk:evidence:2: Explain one piece of evidence: the iridium-rich layer found worldwide in rocks from that time
topic:mt_gTDqxYkLs9:name: Life Changed Over Time
topic:mt_gTDqxYkLs9:description: Recognise that living things have changed over time and that fossils provide information about organisms that inhabited the Earth millions of years ago
topic:mt_gTDqxYkLs9:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that the animals and plants alive today are different from those that lived millions of years ago, and that we know this from fossils?
topic:mt_gTDqxYkLs9:evidence:0: State that living things have changed (evolved) over millions of years
topic:mt_gTDqxYkLs9:evidence:1: Describe how fossils form and what information they provide about the past
topic:mt_gTDqxYkLs9:evidence:2: Compare a fossil organism with a modern relative, noting similarities and differences
topic:mt_mqQ-DtH5m-:name: Dinosaur-to-Bird Transition
topic:mt_mqQ-DtH5m-:description: Trace the evidence for the dinosaur-to-bird transition in depth: feathered theropods from the Liaoning Formation (China), the mix of dinosaur and bird features in Archaeopteryx, and the competing ground-up versus trees-down hypotheses for the origin of flight
topic:mt_mqQ-DtH5m-:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was told that a sparrow is technically a living dinosaur, could they explain the chain of fossil evidence that supports this — naming at least one key transitional fossil and describing what makes it part dinosaur, part bird?
topic:mt_mqQ-DtH5m-:evidence:0: Describes at least three specific feathered theropod fossils (e.g. Microraptor, Anchiornis, Sinosauropteryx) and what each tells us
topic:mt_mqQ-DtH5m-:evidence:1: Describes Archaeopteryx as showing a mix of bird features (feathers, wishbone) and dinosaur features (teeth, clawed wings, long bony tail)
topic:mt_mqQ-DtH5m-:evidence:2: Outlines the ground-up (running and leaping) and trees-down (gliding from trees) hypotheses for flight origin and the evidence supporting each
topic:mt_bHbpLW1HUg:name: Radiometric Dating
topic:mt_bHbpLW1HUg:description: Explain how radiometric dating works — radioactive isotopes decay at a known rate (half-life), so measuring the ratio of parent to daughter isotope in a rock or fossil gives an absolute age; distinguish between carbon-14 (useful up to ~50,000 years) and uranium-lead (useful for millions to billions of years)
topic:mt_bHbpLW1HUg:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was told a dinosaur bone was dated using uranium-lead radiometric dating, could they explain what that means — what is decaying, why the rate of decay is useful, and roughly why scientists don't use carbon-14 for 70-million-year-old bones?
topic:mt_bHbpLW1HUg:evidence:0: Defines half-life as the time for half the radioactive parent isotope to decay to the daughter isotope
topic:mt_bHbpLW1HUg:evidence:1: Explains that the parent:daughter ratio in a sample gives an estimate of absolute age
topic:mt_bHbpLW1HUg:evidence:2: Distinguishes carbon-14 (for recent organic material) from uranium-lead or potassium-argon (for deep geological time), explaining why carbon-14 cannot be used for dinosaur bones
topic:mt_IP0PTVfTXp:name: Mass Extinctions in Earth History
topic:mt_IP0PTVfTXp:description: Compare the five major mass extinction events in Earth history (End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, K-Pg), describe proposed kill mechanisms for each (glaciation, oceanic anoxia, volcanic mega-eruptions, asteroid impact), and explain why mass extinctions, while catastrophic, also open ecological space for subsequent evolutionary radiations
topic:mt_IP0PTVfTXp:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs was actually the fifth mass extinction in Earth history — and describe what happened in the worst one, which killed over 90% of all species?
topic:mt_IP0PTVfTXp:evidence:0: Names all five major mass extinctions in chronological order with approximate dates
topic:mt_IP0PTVfTXp:evidence:1: Describes the End-Permian extinction as the most severe and links it to the Siberian Traps volcanic eruption and its atmospheric consequences
topic:mt_IP0PTVfTXp:evidence:2: Explains how each mass extinction was followed by an adaptive radiation — e.g. the K-Pg extinction removing non-avian dinosaurs allowed mammals to diversify and eventually produce humans
topic:mt_8_BxtNDrLZ:name: Reconstructing Ancient Ecosystems
topic:mt_8_BxtNDrLZ:description: Reconstruct an ancient ecosystem using multiple independent lines of evidence: isotope analysis of teeth to infer diet and migration, bone histology (growth rings) to estimate age and growth rate, coprolite chemistry for diet, and palaeobotany for habitat — understanding that palaeontology is an evidence-synthesis discipline
topic:mt_8_BxtNDrLZ:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked how scientists know a large dinosaur migrated hundreds of kilometres every year, could they explain what kind of evidence they look for and how they rule out alternative explanations?
topic:mt_8_BxtNDrLZ:evidence:0: Explains how stable oxygen isotope ratios in teeth shift with geographic location, allowing detection of seasonal migration
topic:mt_8_BxtNDrLZ:evidence:1: Explains how annual growth rings in bone cross-sections reveal growth rate and approximate age at death
topic:mt_8_BxtNDrLZ:evidence:2: Describes how combining evidence from teeth isotopes, coprolites, and fossil plant assemblages builds a richer picture of ancient ecology than any single source alone
topic:mt_tGZ2sMzMGz:name: Megafauna Extinction & De-Extinction
topic:mt_tGZ2sMzMGz:description: Evaluate the debate over what drove Pleistocene megafauna to extinction — human overkill, climate change, or a combination — using evidence from fossil records, ancient DNA, and archaeological sites; connect to the present-day sixth mass extinction and consider the ethics and feasibility of de-extinction using ancient DNA
topic:mt_tGZ2sMzMGz:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that scientists are trying to bring back the woolly mammoth using ancient DNA, could they explain what ancient DNA is, what challenges exist, and why some scientists think reviving extinct species might actually help ecosystems?
topic:mt_tGZ2sMzMGz:evidence:0: Summarises the overkill hypothesis (human hunting pressure) and the climate hypothesis (rapid warming) for Pleistocene megafauna extinction, citing specific evidence for each
topic:mt_tGZ2sMzMGz:evidence:1: Explains how ancient DNA sequencing from permafrost-preserved specimens provides information about genetics, diet, and relatedness of extinct species
topic:mt_tGZ2sMzMGz:evidence:2: Evaluates the de-extinction concept — describing what it would take technically and raising at least two substantive scientific or ecological arguments for and against
topic:mt_qixeaiswFP:name: How Organisms Shape Habitats
topic:mt_qixeaiswFP:description: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how plants and animals can change the environment to meet their needs
topic:mt_qixeaiswFP:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a beaver builds a dam that changes a river into a pond, or how tree roots can crack rocks apart?
topic:mt_qixeaiswFP:evidence:0: Give at least three examples of organisms changing their environment (beaver dams, bird nests, plant roots breaking rock)
topic:mt_qixeaiswFP:evidence:1: Explain why organisms change their environment (to meet needs for shelter, food, water)
topic:mt_qixeaiswFP:evidence:2: Construct an argument with evidence showing how a specific organism changes its environment

topic:mt_fkwcCB5px7:evidence:3: Gives an everyday example of thermal expansion causing a problem or being used usefully
topic:mt_2qkn8Lhc8e:name: Electromagnets
topic:mt_2qkn8Lhc8e:description: Describe the magnetic effect of an electric current (a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field), and investigate how the strength of an electromagnet depends on current, number of coil turns, and core material
topic:mt_2qkn8Lhc8e:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} built an electromagnet using a battery, wire, and iron nail, could they describe two ways to make it pick up more paperclips — and explain why it stops working when the circuit is switched off?
topic:mt_2qkn8Lhc8e:evidence:0: Describes that a current-carrying wire produces a circular magnetic field
topic:mt_2qkn8Lhc8e:evidence:1: Lists three factors that affect electromagnet strength: current size, number of coil turns, and core material
topic:mt_2qkn8Lhc8e:evidence:2: Explains why an electromagnet can be switched on and off, unlike a permanent magnet
topic:mt_xkn2sf93WJ:name: Investigating Forces
topic:mt_xkn2sf93WJ:description: Plan and carry out investigations into forces, including measuring force with a newton meter, investigating Hooke's Law, and collecting and interpreting motion data to test Newton's laws
topic:mt_xkn2sf93WJ:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} set up an experiment hanging weights on a spring and measuring how much it stretched, could they describe how they would make it a fair test, record the results, and show what Hooke's Law looks like on a graph?
topic:mt_xkn2sf93WJ:evidence:0: Uses a newton meter correctly to measure forces in newtons

topic:mt_xkn2sf93WJ:evidence:2: Identifies and controls variables in a force investigation
topic:mt_xkn2sf93WJ:evidence:3: Calculates acceleration from force and mass data and compares with experimental results
topic:mt_vuNjYx3qOy:name: Moments, Pressure & Hooke's Law
topic:mt_vuNjYx3qOy:description: Calculate the turning effect (moment = force × perpendicular distance), explain how pressure is transmitted equally in liquids (Pascal's principle) and the concept of atmospheric pressure, and describe Hooke's Law (extension ∝ force up to the elastic limit)
topic:mt_vuNjYx3qOy:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was using a long spanner to loosen a tight bolt, could they explain why a longer spanner makes it easier — and work out what force would be needed with a spanner of a specific length?

topic:mt_vuNjYx3qOy:evidence:2: States Hooke's Law and plots force-extension graphs identifying the elastic limit
topic:mt_vuNjYx3qOy:evidence:3: Calculates spring constant k from a force-extension graph (k = F/x)
topic:mt_tXxxCFl32J:name: Newton's First & Second Laws
topic:mt_tXxxCFl32J:description: State and apply Newton's First Law (an object stays at rest or constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force) and Second Law (force = mass × acceleration), including the relationship between mass, force, and acceleration
topic:mt_tXxxCFl32J:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked why you need a seatbelt in a car but not when sitting still, could they explain what Newton's First Law says about moving objects — and then calculate how much force a 60 kg person experiences in a sudden stop?
topic:mt_tXxxCFl32J:evidence:0: States Newton's First Law and gives a real example (e.g. why a moving spacecraft doesn't need engines in space)

topic:mt_tXxxCFl32J:evidence:2: Explains why a heavier object requires more force to achieve the same acceleration
topic:mt_tXxxCFl32J:evidence:3: Explains why seatbelts are needed in cars using Newton's First Law
topic:mt_fbYbe3YSVj:name: Newton's Third Law
topic:mt_fbYbe3YSVj:description: State and apply Newton's Third Law: every force has an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a different object, distinguishing action-reaction pairs from balanced forces
topic:mt_fbYbe3YSVj:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a video of a rocket launching into space, could they explain what force is pushing the rocket upward and where that force comes from — and which law of motion that demonstrates?
topic:mt_fbYbe3YSVj:evidence:0: States Newton's Third Law correctly, identifying both the action and reaction force and the objects they act on

topic:mt_fbYbe3YSVj:evidence:2: Distinguishes a Newton's Third Law pair from balanced forces on the same object
topic:mt_fbYbe3YSVj:evidence:3: Explains why a gun recoils when fired using Newton's Third Law
topic:mt__7BVYUN180:name: Motors & the Motor Effect
topic:mt__7BVYUN180:description: Explain the motor effect as the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, and describe how this principle is used in electric motors and loudspeakers
topic:mt__7BVYUN180:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked inside an electric motor or the back of a loudspeaker, could they explain why the coil of wire moves — and what would happen to the movement if you reversed the direction of the current?
topic:mt__7BVYUN180:evidence:0: Explains that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (the motor effect)
topic:mt__7BVYUN180:evidence:1: Predicts how reversing the current or reversing the magnetic field affects the direction of the force
topic:mt__7BVYUN180:evidence:2: Describes how the motor effect is applied in an electric motor and in a loudspeaker
topic:mt_LTb0ZReMR2:name: Caring for minibeasts
topic:mt_LTb0ZReMR2:description: Caring for minibeasts: observing minibeasts gently, handling them carefully, putting them back where you found them. Why minibeasts matter — they help gardens grow, break down dead leaves, and feed other animals.
topic:mt_LTb0ZReMR2:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} finds a minibeast, do they handle it gently and put it back — and can they tell you why minibeasts are important for the garden?
topic:mt_LTb0ZReMR2:evidence:0: Demonstrate careful handling of a minibeast such as letting a woodlouse walk onto a hand rather than grabbing it
topic:mt_LTb0ZReMR2:evidence:1: Explain one reason why minibeasts are important, such as bees helping flowers grow or worms helping soil
topic:mt_LTb0ZReMR2:evidence:2: State that minibeasts should be returned to where they were found after observing them
topic:mt_Wr6DDgr_kH:name: Caterpillar to butterfly
topic:mt_Wr6DDgr_kH:description: Caterpillar to butterfly: the life cycle of a butterfly as an observable transformation. Egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly. The idea that one creature can change its whole form. Classroom butterfly kits, The Very Hungry Caterpillar.
topic:mt_Wr6DDgr_kH:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a caterpillar make a chrysalis — or read The Very Hungry Caterpillar — could they tell you what happens next and how it becomes a butterfly?
topic:mt_Wr6DDgr_kH:evidence:0: Describe the four stages of a butterfly's life in order: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly
topic:mt_Wr6DDgr_kH:evidence:1: Explain that the caterpillar and the butterfly are the same creature at different stages of life
topic:mt_Wr6DDgr_kH:evidence:2: Retell or draw the transformation from caterpillar to butterfly after reading a story or watching it happen
topic:mt_yR1moI5kX1:name: Common minibeasts: naming and recognising
topic:mt_yR1moI5kX1:description: Recognising and naming common minibeasts: ladybird, ant, bee, butterfly, spider, snail, worm, woodlouse, caterpillar, beetle. Building positive attitudes toward all minibeasts, not just the 'pretty' ones.
topic:mt_yR1moI5kX1:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} spots a creepy-crawly in the garden or at the park, can they tell you what it is — even the less cute ones like woodlice or worms?
topic:mt_yR1moI5kX1:evidence:0: Name and identify at least six common minibeasts from pictures or real encounters
topic:mt_yR1moI5kX1:evidence:1: Describe one visible feature that helps tell a ladybird from a beetle or a spider from an ant
topic:mt_yR1moI5kX1:evidence:2: Show interest or curiosity toward less popular minibeasts like woodlice, worms, or spiders rather than only butterflies
topic:mt__7hXSTbu9s:name: How minibeasts move
topic:mt__7hXSTbu9s:description: How minibeasts move: crawling (ants, beetles), flying (butterflies, bees), slithering (worms, slugs), jumping (grasshoppers, fleas), burrowing (earthworms). Counting legs as a first step toward grouping creatures.
topic:mt__7hXSTbu9s:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} watch a few minibeasts and describe how each one moves differently — like ants crawling, butterflies flying, and worms wriggling?
topic:mt__7hXSTbu9s:evidence:0: Describe at least three different ways minibeasts move such as crawling, flying, and slithering
topic:mt__7hXSTbu9s:evidence:1: Match a minibeast to its way of moving, for example grasshoppers jump and worms slither
topic:mt__7hXSTbu9s:evidence:2: Count legs on a minibeast and notice that ants have six while spiders have eight
topic:mt_zir5yyAzUB:name: Minibeast Habitats
topic:mt_zir5yyAzUB:description: Where minibeasts live: micro-habitats. Different minibeasts prefer different conditions — under logs (damp, dark), in soil (underground), on leaves (sunny), in pond water (wet). The idea that you find different creatures in different places.
topic:mt_zir5yyAzUB:assessmentPrompt: If you asked {{name}} where to look for woodlice or worms in the garden, could they tell you the kind of spot those creatures prefer — like somewhere damp and dark?
topic:mt_zir5yyAzUB:evidence:0: Name at least two micro-habitats where minibeasts live such as under logs, in soil, or on leaves
topic:mt_zir5yyAzUB:evidence:1: Predict what type of minibeast might be found in a damp dark place versus a sunny leaf
topic:mt_zir5yyAzUB:evidence:2: Explain that different minibeasts prefer different conditions like wet, dry, dark, or light
topic:mt_QH-Fs97twT:name: Minibeasts in the food chain
topic:mt_QH-Fs97twT:description: Minibeasts in the food chain: simple garden food chains. A caterpillar eats a leaf, a bird eats the caterpillar. The idea that minibeasts are food for other animals, and that minibeasts eat things too.
topic:mt_QH-Fs97twT:assessmentPrompt: If you asked {{name}} what a caterpillar eats and what eats the caterpillar, could they describe that chain — leaf, caterpillar, bird?
topic:mt_QH-Fs97twT:evidence:0: Describe a simple food chain such as leaf → caterpillar → bird
topic:mt_QH-Fs97twT:evidence:1: Explain that minibeasts eat plants or other tiny creatures and are eaten by bigger animals
topic:mt_QH-Fs97twT:evidence:2: Give an example of what a specific minibeast eats, such as caterpillars eating leaves or ladybirds eating aphids
topic:mt_BI6oGIO-xM:name: What is a minibeast?
topic:mt_BI6oGIO-xM:description: What is a minibeast? Small creatures without backbones, found in gardens, parks, and woodland. Bug hunts — searching under logs, stones, and leaves using magnifying glasses to observe minibeasts up close.
topic:mt_BI6oGIO-xM:assessmentPrompt: If you went on a bug hunt in the garden with {{name}}, could they find creatures under logs and stones and tell you what makes something a minibeast?
topic:mt_BI6oGIO-xM:evidence:0: Explain that minibeasts are small animals without a backbone found in gardens and parks
topic:mt_BI6oGIO-xM:evidence:1: Find at least three different minibeasts during a garden bug hunt under logs, stones, or leaves
topic:mt_BI6oGIO-xM:evidence:2: Use a magnifying glass to observe and describe one minibeast's appearance in detail
topic:mt_SZJ1mN7Vfk:name: Bees and pollination
topic:mt_SZJ1mN7Vfk:description: Bees and pollination: how flowers and insects depend on each other. Bees visit flowers for nectar, pollen sticks to their bodies and transfers to the next flower. Without pollination many plants cannot make seeds or fruit. Why bees matter for the food we eat.
topic:mt_SZJ1mN7Vfk:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a bee buzzing around flowers in the garden, could they explain how the bee is helping the plant — and why that matters for the food we eat?
topic:mt_SZJ1mN7Vfk:evidence:0: Describe how pollen moves from one flower to another when a bee visits to collect nectar
topic:mt_SZJ1mN7Vfk:evidence:1: Explain that many fruits and vegetables depend on bees or other insects for pollination
topic:mt_SZJ1mN7Vfk:evidence:2: State what would happen to a garden or farm if there were no pollinating insects
topic:mt_07Geg7LITa:name: Camouflage, warning colours, and mimicry
topic:mt_07Geg7LITa:description: Camouflage, warning colours, and mimicry: how insects survive by hiding or sending visual signals. Stick insects look like twigs, leaf insects look like leaves. Wasps have warning stripes; hoverflies mimic wasps but are harmless. The 'can you spot it?' challenge.
topic:mt_07Geg7LITa:assessmentPrompt: If you showed {{name}} pictures of stick insects hiding on branches or hoverflies pretending to be wasps, could they explain why those insects look the way they do?
topic:mt_07Geg7LITa:evidence:0: Give at least two examples of insect camouflage such as stick insects resembling twigs or leaf insects resembling leaves
topic:mt_07Geg7LITa:evidence:1: Explain why bright warning colours like a wasp's yellow and black stripes help the insect survive
topic:mt_07Geg7LITa:evidence:2: Describe mimicry by explaining that a harmless insect like a hoverfly copies a dangerous one like a wasp to trick predators
topic:mt_M7YrfAZk8u:name: Incredible insects: record-breakers
topic:mt_M7YrfAZk8u:description: Incredible insects — record-breakers and superpowers. Dung beetles are the strongest animals relative to body weight. Dragonflies are among the fastest flying insects. Fleas can jump over 150 times their own body length. Bombardier beetles spray boiling chemicals. The 'wow factor' of the insect world.
topic:mt_M7YrfAZk8u:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you about insect record-breakers — like which insect is the world's strongest for its size, or which one can jump the farthest?
topic:mt_M7YrfAZk8u:evidence:0: Name at least three insect record-breakers and their extreme abilities such as dung beetle strength or flea jumping
topic:mt_M7YrfAZk8u:evidence:1: Compare an insect's ability to a human scale, for example a flea's jump would be like a person leaping over a skyscraper
topic:mt_M7YrfAZk8u:evidence:2: Explain why being very small helps insects achieve extreme feats of strength or speed relative to their size
topic:mt_hsN-YvCNQY:name: Insect life cycles: complete metamorphosis
topic:mt_hsN-YvCNQY:description: Insect life cycles — complete metamorphosis in detail. Egg → larva → pupa → adult. The larva (caterpillar, grub, maggot) looks completely different from the adult. Inside the pupa the body is rebuilt. Butterflies, beetles, flies, and ladybirds all undergo complete metamorphosis.
topic:mt_hsN-YvCNQY:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the full life cycle of a beetle or butterfly using the proper words — egg, larva, pupa, adult — and tell you what happens at each stage?
topic:mt_hsN-YvCNQY:evidence:0: Name the four stages of complete metamorphosis using the correct terms: egg, larva, pupa, adult
topic:mt_hsN-YvCNQY:evidence:1: Explain that the larva stage is when the insect eats and grows, and the pupa stage is when its body transforms
topic:mt_hsN-YvCNQY:evidence:2: Give at least two examples of insects that undergo complete metamorphosis such as butterflies and beetles
topic:mt_4vHa3I5bNj:name: Not all minibeasts are insects
topic:mt_4vHa3I5bNj:description: Not all minibeasts are insects: distinguishing insects from other minibeasts. Spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts (arachnids), woodlice have 14 legs (crustaceans), worms have no legs, snails have a shell and one foot. The 'Is it an insect?' sorting game.
topic:mt_4vHa3I5bNj:assessmentPrompt: If you showed {{name}} a spider and asked whether it's an insect, could they explain why not — for example, that spiders have eight legs, not six?
topic:mt_4vHa3I5bNj:evidence:0: Sort a set of minibeasts into 'insect' and 'not insect' groups using the six-legs rule
topic:mt_4vHa3I5bNj:evidence:1: Explain why a spider is not an insect by noting it has eight legs and two body parts
topic:mt_4vHa3I5bNj:evidence:2: Name at least one difference between insects and another minibeast group such as worms having no legs or woodlice having fourteen
topic:mt_guaaD6Dn2M:name: Social insects: ants and bees
topic:mt_guaaD6Dn2M:description: Social insects: how ants and bees live and work together in colonies. Queens, workers, and drones. Division of labour — some gather food, some build, some guard. Ant tunnels and bee hives as organised homes. Parallels to human teamwork.
topic:mt_guaaD6Dn2M:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a nature programme about ants or bees, could they tell you about the different jobs inside the colony — like the queen, the workers, and the guards?
topic:mt_guaaD6Dn2M:evidence:0: Describe at least two different roles within an ant colony or bee hive such as queen, worker, or guard
topic:mt_guaaD6Dn2M:evidence:1: Explain that social insects live together in large groups and divide up the jobs needed to survive
topic:mt_guaaD6Dn2M:evidence:2: Compare an ant colony or bee hive to a human team, describing how different members do different tasks
topic:mt__bhJX2SuFJ:name: Sorting and Identifying Minibeasts
topic:mt__bhJX2SuFJ:description: Using classification keys to identify minibeasts. Branching yes/no questions: 'Does it have legs?' → 'How many legs?' → 'Does it have wings?' Dichotomous keys as a systematic tool for sorting and identifying creatures.
topic:mt__bhJX2SuFJ:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found an unfamiliar minibeast, could they use a set of yes/no questions — like 'Does it have legs? How many?' — to work out what group it belongs to?
topic:mt__bhJX2SuFJ:evidence:0: Follow a simple branching key to correctly identify at least four different minibeasts
topic:mt__bhJX2SuFJ:evidence:1: Create a yes/no question that separates insects from spiders, such as 'Does it have six legs?'
topic:mt__bhJX2SuFJ:evidence:2: Explain why asking questions in a set order helps identify a creature you have never seen before
topic:mt_oNWXXAn3cn:name: The insect body plan
topic:mt_oNWXXAn3cn:description: The insect body plan: all insects share three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs attached to the thorax, and antennae on the head. Most have wings. They have an exoskeleton — a hard outer shell — instead of bones inside.
topic:mt_oNWXXAn3cn:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a picture of a beetle or ant, could they point out the head, thorax, and abdomen, and tell you that all insects have six legs and a hard outer shell?
topic:mt_oNWXXAn3cn:evidence:0: Label the three body parts of an insect — head, thorax, and abdomen — on a diagram or real specimen
topic:mt_oNWXXAn3cn:evidence:1: State that all insects have exactly six legs and that the legs attach to the thorax
topic:mt_oNWXXAn3cn:evidence:2: Explain that insects have an exoskeleton, a hard outer covering, instead of bones inside their body
topic:mt_7_XXh9NCp0:name: Insect Adaptations
topic:mt_7_XXh9NCp0:description: Adaptation and evolution in insects: peppered moths as a famous example of natural selection (dark moths survived better on soot-covered trees during the Industrial Revolution). Stick insects evolved to look like twigs. Ant-mimicking spiders evolved to fool predators. How small changes over many generations lead to remarkable disguises.
topic:mt_7_XXh9NCp0:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why peppered moths changed colour during the Industrial Revolution — and how that's an example of how living things adapt over many generations?
topic:mt_7_XXh9NCp0:evidence:0: Retell the peppered moth story and explain how the environment changed which colour moth survived best
topic:mt_7_XXh9NCp0:evidence:1: Describe how a stick insect's body shape is an adaptation that helps it avoid being eaten
topic:mt_7_XXh9NCp0:evidence:2: Explain that adaptations develop over many generations through natural selection, not during one insect's lifetime
topic:mt_Oz8yNPNtub:name: Insect anatomy in depth
topic:mt_Oz8yNPNtub:description: Insect anatomy in depth: compound eyes made of thousands of tiny lenses, spiracles (breathing holes along the body), diverse mouthparts (chewing mandibles in beetles, sucking proboscis in butterflies, sponging pad in flies), and moulting the exoskeleton to grow. Biomimicry — how engineers copy insect designs.
topic:mt_Oz8yNPNtub:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a close-up photo of an insect's eye or mouth, could they explain how those body parts work and why they look so different from ours?
topic:mt_Oz8yNPNtub:evidence:0: Describe at least two specialised insect structures such as compound eyes or spiracles and explain their function
topic:mt_Oz8yNPNtub:evidence:1: Compare the mouthparts of a beetle (chewing) and a butterfly (sucking) and explain how each is suited to its food
topic:mt_Oz8yNPNtub:evidence:2: Give one example of biomimicry where human technology is inspired by an insect structure or ability
topic:mt_a9VnPBhoYs:name: Insect communication and behaviour
topic:mt_a9VnPBhoYs:description: Insect communication and behaviour: bees perform a waggle dance to tell hive-mates where flowers are. Ants lay pheromone trails for others to follow. Fireflies flash light patterns to find mates. Crickets chirp by rubbing their wings. Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of miles across continents. How insects 'talk' without words.
topic:mt_a9VnPBhoYs:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how bees tell each other where to find flowers, how ants leave invisible trails, or how fireflies use light to send messages?
topic:mt_a9VnPBhoYs:evidence:0: Describe at least three ways insects communicate such as the bee waggle dance, ant pheromone trails, and firefly light signals
topic:mt_a9VnPBhoYs:evidence:1: Explain what information a bee conveys through its waggle dance, including direction and distance to flowers
topic:mt_a9VnPBhoYs:evidence:2: Describe the monarch butterfly migration and explain why it is remarkable in terms of distance and navigation
topic:mt_r6oKXpN0er:name: Insects in ecosystems
topic:mt_r6oKXpN0er:description: Insects in ecosystems: the many roles insects play. Pollinators (bees, butterflies, hoverflies), decomposers (dung beetles, fly larvae), food source for birds, bats, fish, and frogs, and pest controllers (ladybirds eating aphids). The thought experiment: what would happen if all insects disappeared?
topic:mt_r6oKXpN0er:assessmentPrompt: If you asked {{name}} what would happen if all the insects in the world disappeared tomorrow, could they explain the chain of problems that would cause — for plants, animals, and people?
topic:mt_r6oKXpN0er:evidence:0: Name at least three different ecological roles that insects play such as pollinator, decomposer, and food source
topic:mt_r6oKXpN0er:evidence:1: Explain how the removal of one insect group like bees would affect plants, other animals, and humans
topic:mt_r6oKXpN0er:evidence:2: Describe a specific example of insects as pest controllers such as ladybirds controlling aphid populations
topic:mt_5_Zr9xXDNH:name: The most successful animals on Earth
topic:mt_5_Zr9xXDNH:description: The most successful animals on Earth: there are roughly one million described insect species, and scientists estimate 5–10 million may exist. More insect species than all other animal groups combined. Why so many? Small body size means less food needed, fast reproduction with many offspring, flight allows reaching new habitats, and the exoskeleton is incredibly versatile.
topic:mt_5_Zr9xXDNH:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know which group of animals has more species than any other on Earth — and can they explain why insects are so incredibly successful?
topic:mt_5_Zr9xXDNH:evidence:0: State that insects are the most species-rich group of animals with about one million known species
topic:mt_5_Zr9xXDNH:evidence:1: Give at least two reasons why insects are so successful such as small size, fast reproduction, or flight
topic:mt_5_Zr9xXDNH:evidence:2: Compare insect diversity to another animal group, explaining that there are far more insect species than mammals or birds
topic:mt__EL7DHjf5R:name: Threats to insects and conservation
topic:mt__EL7DHjf5R:description: Threats to insects and conservation: insect populations are declining worldwide. Causes include habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution disrupting nocturnal insects, and climate change. Pollinator decline threatens food production. What children can do: plant pollinator-friendly gardens, reduce pesticide use, participate in citizen science like the Big Butterfly Count.
topic:mt__EL7DHjf5R:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you why insect numbers are falling around the world, why that matters for people too, and what your family could do to help?
topic:mt__EL7DHjf5R:evidence:0: Name at least three threats to insect populations such as habitat loss, pesticides, and light pollution
topic:mt__EL7DHjf5R:evidence:1: Explain why declining bee populations are a problem for humans and the food we eat
topic:mt__EL7DHjf5R:evidence:2: Suggest at least two actions that children or families can take to help insects such as planting wildflowers or joining a butterfly count
topic:mt_ShAptVcQR3:name: Types of Metamorphosis
topic:mt_ShAptVcQR3:description: Complete vs incomplete metamorphosis. Complete: egg → larva → pupa → adult (butterflies, beetles, flies). Incomplete: egg → nymph → adult — the nymph looks like a small version of the adult and moults as it grows (grasshoppers, dragonflies, crickets). Why do some insects transform completely while others grow gradually?
topic:mt_ShAptVcQR3:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the difference between a butterfly's life cycle and a grasshopper's — why the caterpillar looks nothing like the butterfly, but a baby grasshopper already looks like a small grasshopper?
topic:mt_ShAptVcQR3:evidence:0: Compare complete and incomplete metamorphosis by describing the stages of each on a diagram
topic:mt_ShAptVcQR3:evidence:1: Classify at least three insects into the correct metamorphosis type such as butterfly (complete) and grasshopper (incomplete)
topic:mt_ShAptVcQR3:evidence:2: Explain that nymphs resemble adults while larvae look completely different from their adult form
topic:mt_auVZZEuXjs:name: Describing Material Properties
topic:mt_auVZZEuXjs:description: Describe simple physical properties of everyday materials such as hard/soft, stretchy/stiff, shiny/dull, rough/smooth, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque
topic:mt_auVZZEuXjs:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} pick up different objects and describe their properties — like 'this is smooth and shiny' or 'this is rough and bendy'?
topic:mt_auVZZEuXjs:evidence:0: Use at least five property words correctly: hard, soft, stretchy, shiny, rough, smooth, transparent, waterproof
topic:mt_auVZZEuXjs:evidence:1: Describe the properties of three different materials using at least two property words each
topic:mt_auVZZEuXjs:evidence:2: Explain why a property matters (e.g. 'waterproof means water doesn't soak through')
topic:mt_SwaNNdm_Ks:name: Grouping Materials
topic:mt_SwaNNdm_Ks:description: Compare and group everyday materials based on their simple physical properties
topic:mt_SwaNNdm_Ks:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} sort a pile of objects into groups based on their properties, like all the waterproof ones together or all the transparent ones?
