topic:mt_kDKo4lxRKi:description: Understand how polar animals are adapted to survive extreme cold — blubber (thick fat layer) insulates seals and whales, hollow fur traps air for warmth in polar bears, counter-current heat exchange in penguin flippers prevents heat loss, Arctic foxes grow thick white winter coats for camouflage and warmth, and some animals migrate to avoid the harshest months
topic:mt_kDKo4lxRKi:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain several ways polar animals survive the freezing cold — like a polar bear's hollow fur trapping warm air, a seal's thick blubber, or an Arctic fox changing colour in winter?
topic:mt_kDKo4lxRKi:evidence:0: Describe at least three cold-weather adaptations: blubber, hollow fur, counter-current heat exchange, white winter coats, or migration
topic:mt_kDKo4lxRKi:evidence:1: Explain the purpose of each adaptation (e.g. blubber insulates against cold water, white fur provides camouflage in snow)
topic:mt_kDKo4lxRKi:evidence:2: Use the word adaptation correctly to mean a feature that helps an animal survive in its environment
topic:mt_z9jn9HogfE:name: Comparing Arctic & Antarctic
topic:mt_z9jn9HogfE:description: Compare the Arctic and Antarctic in detail — the Arctic is an ocean covered by floating sea ice with surrounding land masses (Canada, Russia, Greenland, Scandinavia), while Antarctica is a continent larger than Europe buried under ice up to 4 km thick; polar bears, Arctic foxes, and walruses live only in the Arctic while penguins, leopard seals, and albatrosses are found only in the Antarctic
topic:mt_z9jn9HogfE:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain in detail how the Arctic and Antarctic are different — which animals live where, that one is frozen ocean and the other is a frozen continent, and which countries border the Arctic?
topic:mt_z9jn9HogfE:evidence:0: State that the Arctic is a frozen ocean surrounded by land (name at least two bordering countries), while Antarctica is a continent covered by ice sheet up to 4 km thick
topic:mt_z9jn9HogfE:evidence:1: Correctly assign at least three animals to the Arctic and three to the Antarctic
topic:mt_z9jn9HogfE:evidence:2: Name at least two differences in human presence: indigenous peoples in the Arctic vs research stations only in Antarctica
topic:mt_scbDHJZZHK:name: Ice & States of Matter
topic:mt_scbDHJZZHK:description: Understand ice in different forms and states of matter — sea ice forms when ocean water freezes (it's salty and relatively thin), glacial ice forms from compacted snow over centuries (fresh water, very thick), and icebergs break off from glaciers and float in the sea; know that water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (water vapour), and that salt lowers the freezing point of water
topic:mt_scbDHJZZHK:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the difference between sea ice and glacier ice, and describe how water changes between solid, liquid, and gas — maybe by doing a simple freezing experiment with salt and fresh water?
topic:mt_scbDHJZZHK:evidence:0: Distinguish between sea ice (frozen ocean, salty, thin) and glacial ice (compacted snow, fresh water, thick)
topic:mt_scbDHJZZHK:evidence:1: Explain that icebergs break off from glaciers and float because ice is less dense than liquid water
topic:mt_scbDHJZZHK:evidence:2: Describe the three states of water (solid, liquid, gas) and explain that salt lowers the freezing point
topic:mt_rqalOvjkj3:name: Inuit & Sami Peoples
topic:mt_rqalOvjkj3:description: Know that indigenous peoples have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years — the Inuit across Canada, Alaska, and Greenland, and the Sami in northern Scandinavia — developing remarkable knowledge of the environment, using dog sleds and kayaks for transport, wearing animal-skin clothing for warmth, and building igloos as temporary shelters, with a deep respect for the animals and land they depend on
topic:mt_rqalOvjkj3:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you about the Inuit and Sami peoples who have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years — how they travel by dog sled, wear animal-skin clothing, and know the ice and animals incredibly well?
topic:mt_rqalOvjkj3:evidence:0: Name the Inuit (Canada, Alaska, Greenland) and Sami (northern Scandinavia) as Arctic indigenous peoples
topic:mt_rqalOvjkj3:evidence:1: Describe at least three aspects of traditional Arctic life: dog sleds, kayaks, animal-skin clothing, igloos, or hunting practices
topic:mt_rqalOvjkj3:evidence:2: Explain that indigenous Arctic peoples have deep knowledge of their environment developed over thousands of years
topic:mt_7nduoLvoB1:name: Polar Food Chains
topic:mt_7nduoLvoB1:description: Understand polar food chains — in the Antarctic, phytoplankton are eaten by krill, krill are eaten by fish and penguins, and penguins are eaten by leopard seals and orcas; in the Arctic, algae under ice feeds zooplankton, which feeds fish, which feeds seals, which feeds polar bears — and that tiny organisms like krill and plankton are the foundation of all polar life
topic:mt_7nduoLvoB1:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain a polar food chain — starting from tiny plankton, through krill and fish, up to seals and polar bears or orcas — and explain why the tiny creatures at the bottom are so important?
topic:mt_7nduoLvoB1:evidence:0: Construct an Antarctic food chain: phytoplankton → krill → penguin → leopard seal or orca
topic:mt_7nduoLvoB1:evidence:1: Construct an Arctic food chain: algae → zooplankton → fish → seal → polar bear
topic:mt_7nduoLvoB1:evidence:2: Explain why krill and plankton are critical — without them, the entire food chain collapses
topic:mt_X4CJpPRxae:name: The Arctic Tundra
topic:mt_X4CJpPRxae:description: Know what the Arctic tundra is — a vast, treeless landscape with permafrost (permanently frozen ground) just below the surface, a very short growing season in summer when mosses, lichens, and tough grasses burst into life, and home to caribou/reindeer, musk oxen, lemmings, and snowy owls
topic:mt_X4CJpPRxae:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know what tundra is — the huge flat landscape near the Arctic with no trees, frozen ground underneath, and short summers where everything bursts into life?
topic:mt_X4CJpPRxae:evidence:0: Describe the tundra as a treeless landscape with permafrost (permanently frozen ground) beneath the surface
topic:mt_X4CJpPRxae:evidence:1: Explain that the tundra has a very short summer growing season when mosses, lichens, and grasses grow quickly
topic:mt_X4CJpPRxae:evidence:2: Name at least three tundra animals: caribou/reindeer, musk oxen, lemmings, or snowy owls
topic:mt_islVn_P28Z:name: The Race to the South Pole
topic:mt_islVn_P28Z:description: Know the story of the race to the South Pole in detail — Norwegian Roald Amundsen and British Robert Falcon Scott both set out in 1911, Amundsen arrived first on 14 December using dog sleds and careful planning, Scott arrived 34 days later using man-hauled sledges and tragically died with his team on the return journey; also know about Ernest Shackleton's 1914 Endurance expedition where the ship was trapped and crushed by ice, and Shackleton's extraordinary boat journey to South Georgia to rescue his crew
topic:mt_islVn_P28Z:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you the detailed story of Amundsen and Scott's race to the South Pole — who won and why, what went wrong for Scott, and the incredible survival story of Shackleton's Endurance?
topic:mt_islVn_P28Z:evidence:0: Describe the Scott vs Amundsen race: Amundsen arrived 14 December 1911 using dog sleds; Scott arrived 34 days later and died on the return
topic:mt_islVn_P28Z:evidence:1: Explain at least two reasons Amundsen succeeded: better planning, dog sleds, polar experience, and lighter supplies
topic:mt_islVn_P28Z:evidence:2: Narrate the key events of the Endurance expedition: ship crushed, camps on ice, boat journey to South Georgia, all crew rescued
topic:mt_f9syMry-0S:name: Why Polar Seasons Are Extreme
topic:mt_f9syMry-0S:description: Understand why the poles have extreme seasons — Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°, so as it orbits the Sun, each pole spends half the year tilted toward the Sun (continuous daylight, warmer summer) and half tilted away (continuous darkness, bitter winter); this tilt also drives the annual cycle of sea ice expanding in winter and retreating in summer, and triggers animal behaviours like migration and breeding
topic:mt_f9syMry-0S:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain WHY the poles have months of daylight in summer and months of darkness in winter — that it's because Earth is tilted on its axis as it goes around the Sun?
topic:mt_f9syMry-0S:evidence:0: Explain that Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5° and this tilt causes the extreme polar seasons
topic:mt_f9syMry-0S:evidence:1: Describe how the tilt means each pole faces toward the Sun for half the year (summer/daylight) and away for the other half (winter/darkness)
topic:mt_f9syMry-0S:evidence:2: Connect the seasonal cycle to at least one animal behaviour, such as migration or sea ice retreat affecting hunting
topic:mt_itldWmVItr:name: Antarctic Treaty & Research
topic:mt_itldWmVItr:description: Know that Antarctica is governed by the Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force since 1961) — which sets Antarctica aside for peaceful purposes and scientific research, bans military activity and mining, and is signed by over 50 countries; understand that international research stations study climate, astronomy, biology, and geology, and that Antarctica is the closest thing on Earth to a continent for science rather than politics
topic:mt_itldWmVItr:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know about the Antarctic Treaty — that over 50 countries agreed Antarctica should be used only for science and peace, not war or mining — and that research stations there study everything from ice to stars?
topic:mt_itldWmVItr:evidence:0: State that the Antarctic Treaty (1959) sets Antarctica aside for peace and science, banning military activity and mining
topic:mt_itldWmVItr:evidence:1: Know that over 50 countries have signed the treaty and that many operate research stations
topic:mt_itldWmVItr:evidence:2: Name at least two areas of scientific research conducted in Antarctica: climate, astronomy, biology, or geology
topic:mt_Fqna9qHffr:name: Climate Change at the Poles
topic:mt_Fqna9qHffr:description: Understand how climate change is affecting polar regions — Arctic sea ice is shrinking dramatically (losing about 13% per decade since 1979), the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are losing mass and contributing to sea level rise, permafrost is thawing and releasing methane (a powerful greenhouse gas), and these changes create positive feedback loops where melting leads to more warming which leads to more melting
topic:mt_Fqna9qHffr:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how climate change is melting polar ice — that Arctic sea ice is shrinking, ice sheets are losing mass, and that melting actually makes more melting happen in a vicious cycle?
topic:mt_Fqna9qHffr:evidence:0: State that Arctic sea ice has been declining at roughly 13% per decade since 1979
topic:mt_Fqna9qHffr:evidence:1: Explain the positive feedback loop: warming → ice melts → dark ocean absorbs more heat → more warming → more melting
topic:mt_Fqna9qHffr:evidence:2: Describe at least two consequences of polar ice loss: sea level rise and permafrost thawing releasing methane
topic:mt_cMmG8VLbAp:name: Earth's Frozen Water
topic:mt_cMmG8VLbAp:description: Understand the cryosphere and its role in Earth's water system — the cryosphere is all frozen water on Earth (ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow cover); polar ice sheets hold about 69% of Earth's fresh water; if all polar ice melted, sea levels would rise over 65 metres; and the water cycle connects polar ice to the global system through evaporation, precipitation, and meltwater flowing into oceans
topic:mt_cMmG8VLbAp:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that most of Earth's fresh water is actually locked up as ice at the poles — and that if it all melted, the sea would rise over 65 metres, flooding coastal cities worldwide?
topic:mt_cMmG8VLbAp:evidence:0: Define the cryosphere as all frozen water on Earth and name its components: ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow
topic:mt_cMmG8VLbAp:evidence:1: State that polar ice sheets hold approximately 69% of Earth's fresh water
topic:mt_cMmG8VLbAp:evidence:2: Explain how polar ice connects to the global water cycle and what would happen if it all melted (65m+ sea level rise)
topic:mt_5_kErPeeNu:name: Glaciers & Ice Sheets
topic:mt_5_kErPeeNu:description: Understand how glaciers and ice sheets form and behave — snow accumulates over centuries and compresses into dense ice, glaciers flow slowly downhill under their own weight carving U-shaped valleys and depositing moraines; the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets together hold enough ice to raise sea levels by over 65 metres; and ice cores drilled from these sheets contain trapped air bubbles that reveal Earth's climate history going back 800,000 years
topic:mt_5_kErPeeNu:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how glaciers form from layers of snow pressed into ice, how they slowly carve valleys, and that scientists drill into ice sheets to learn about Earth's climate thousands of years ago?
topic:mt_5_kErPeeNu:evidence:0: Describe how glaciers form: snow accumulates, compresses, and becomes dense ice that flows slowly under its own weight
topic:mt_5_kErPeeNu:evidence:1: Explain that the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets hold enough water to raise sea levels dramatically if melted
topic:mt_5_kErPeeNu:evidence:2: Describe how ice cores reveal climate history through trapped air bubbles from hundreds of thousands of years ago
topic:mt_GbZFuGDFsa:name: Polar Climate Zone
topic:mt_GbZFuGDFsa:description: Understand that polar regions belong to the polar climate zone — one of Earth's five main climate zones (tropical, arid, temperate, continental, polar) — characterised by temperatures rarely above 10°C even in summer, low precipitation (polar deserts receive less rain than the Sahara), and strong winds; know that latitude is the key factor determining climate zones, with polar regions above 60°N/S
topic:mt_GbZFuGDFsa:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain where the polar climate zone fits among Earth's five climate zones, and why the poles are so cold — linking it to their position at high latitudes far from the Equator?
topic:mt_GbZFuGDFsa:evidence:0: Name the five main climate zones and place polar regions correctly within them
topic:mt_GbZFuGDFsa:evidence:1: State that polar regions are above approximately 60° latitude and explain that distance from the Equator is the main reason they are cold
topic:mt_GbZFuGDFsa:evidence:2: Describe polar climate characteristics: rarely above 10°C in summer, very low precipitation, strong winds
topic:mt_7QeiS95TRC:name: Polar Conservation & Future
topic:mt_7QeiS95TRC:description: Understand the conservation challenges facing polar regions — marine protected areas in the Southern Ocean aim to preserve Antarctic ecosystems, Arctic nations dispute sovereignty over northern sea routes and resources as ice retreats, indigenous peoples fight for land rights and voice in environmental decisions, and international cooperation (Paris Agreement, Antarctic Treaty) is essential but difficult to maintain as economic pressures grow
topic:mt_7QeiS95TRC:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} discuss the big challenges facing the poles — like countries arguing over Arctic resources as ice melts, the push for marine protected areas in Antarctica, and why indigenous peoples' voices matter in these decisions?
topic:mt_7QeiS95TRC:evidence:0: Describe at least two conservation measures: marine protected areas in the Southern Ocean and the Antarctic Treaty
topic:mt_7QeiS95TRC:evidence:1: Explain why Arctic sovereignty is contested as ice retreats and shipping routes open
topic:mt_7QeiS95TRC:evidence:2: Describe the role of indigenous peoples in Arctic environmental decisions and why their knowledge matters
topic:mt_kOYw43NPzr:name: Polar Ecosystems Compared
topic:mt_kOYw43NPzr:description: Compare Arctic and Antarctic ecosystems — the Arctic has both terrestrial (tundra) and marine ecosystems supporting large land mammals and indigenous human communities, while the Antarctic is almost entirely marine-based with virtually no land plants or mammals; both regions have short, intense food chains anchored by phytoplankton and krill, and both are disproportionately affected by climate change and human activity
topic:mt_kOYw43NPzr:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} compare the Arctic and Antarctic ecosystems — explaining that the Arctic has land animals and people while Antarctica's life is almost all in the sea, and that both depend on tiny creatures like krill?
topic:mt_kOYw43NPzr:evidence:0: Compare Arctic (terrestrial + marine, land mammals, human communities) with Antarctic (almost entirely marine, no land mammals)
topic:mt_kOYw43NPzr:evidence:1: Explain that both polar food chains depend on phytoplankton and krill at the base
topic:mt_kOYw43NPzr:evidence:2: Describe why polar ecosystems are particularly vulnerable to climate change (short food chains, specialised organisms)
topic:mt_I_c57p0aGN:name: Polar Exploration Then & Now
topic:mt_I_c57p0aGN:description: Compare historical polar exploration with modern polar science — the Heroic Age (1897–1922) relied on ships, dogs, and human endurance with many fatalities, while today's polar scientists use GPS, satellites, icebreaker ships, heated research stations, and aircraft; understand that modern challenges include studying climate change data, and that polar science now includes diverse international teams including women scientists like glaciologist Liz Thomas and marine biologist Sylvia Earle
topic:mt_I_c57p0aGN:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} compare old polar exploration — dog sleds, freezing camps, real danger of death — with modern polar science using satellites, heated research stations, and diverse international teams?
topic:mt_I_c57p0aGN:evidence:0: Compare Heroic Age exploration (dog sleds, man-hauling, many deaths) with modern science (GPS, satellites, icebreakers, heated stations)
topic:mt_I_c57p0aGN:evidence:1: Name at least two technologies that make modern polar science possible
topic:mt_I_c57p0aGN:evidence:2: Name a modern polar scientist and explain that today's polar teams are diverse and international
topic:mt_g1qgxmlJQ2:name: Polar Oceans and World Climate
topic:mt_g1qgxmlJQ2:description: Understand how polar oceans connect to the global climate system — cold, dense polar water sinks and drives thermohaline circulation (a global conveyor belt of ocean currents), sea ice reflects sunlight back to space (the albedo effect) helping regulate Earth's temperature, and the Southern Ocean around Antarctica is one of the most productive marine ecosystems on Earth due to upwelling nutrients
topic:mt_g1qgxmlJQ2:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how cold polar water sinks and drives a global conveyor belt of ocean currents, and how white sea ice reflects sunlight to help keep the planet cool?
topic:mt_g1qgxmlJQ2:evidence:0: Explain that cold, dense polar water sinks and drives global ocean circulation (thermohaline circulation)
topic:mt_g1qgxmlJQ2:evidence:1: Describe the albedo effect: white ice reflects sunlight back to space, while dark ocean absorbs heat
topic:mt_g1qgxmlJQ2:evidence:2: State that the Southern Ocean is extremely productive because upwelling brings nutrients to the surface
topic:mt_s08-QxASd2:name: Everyday Foods from Rainforests
topic:mt_s08-QxASd2:description: Know that many everyday foods come from rainforests — chocolate is made from cacao beans, bananas grow in tropical forests, coffee berries ripen in forest shade, and Brazil nuts fall from giant trees — connecting our daily lives to faraway forests
topic:mt_s08-QxASd2:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is eating a chocolate bar or a banana, can they tell you that those foods originally come from rainforests?
topic:mt_s08-QxASd2:evidence:0: Name at least three foods that come from rainforests, such as chocolate (cacao), bananas, and Brazil nuts
topic:mt_s08-QxASd2:evidence:1: Explain that cacao beans grow on trees in the rainforest and are made into chocolate
topic:mt_s08-QxASd2:evidence:2: Connect their own food choices to rainforest origins by identifying a product they eat that comes from the forest
topic:mt_2zJ1NrGgYm:name: Indigenous Rainforest Peoples
topic:mt_2zJ1NrGgYm:description: Know that indigenous peoples such as the Yanomami have lived in rainforests for thousands of years, building homes from forest materials, finding food by hunting, fishing, and gathering, and knowing the forest and its plants and animals deeply
topic:mt_2zJ1NrGgYm:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that some people have lived in rainforests for thousands of years — building their homes from the trees and knowing which plants are food and which are medicine?
topic:mt_2zJ1NrGgYm:evidence:0: Explain that indigenous peoples like the Yanomami have lived in rainforests for thousands of years
topic:mt_2zJ1NrGgYm:evidence:1: Describe how they use the forest for shelter, food, and medicine
topic:mt_2zJ1NrGgYm:evidence:2: Show respect for indigenous knowledge by explaining that these communities understand the forest very deeply
topic:mt_ntxlccnYzB:name: Inside a Rainforest
topic:mt_ntxlccnYzB:description: Describe what it feels like inside a rainforest — hot and sticky (humid), dark on the ground because the treetops block the light, loud with animal calls and insect buzzing, and dripping with water from rain and condensation
topic:mt_ntxlccnYzB:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a rainforest video clip, can they describe what it would feel, sound, and look like to stand inside — the heat, the noise, the darkness on the ground?
topic:mt_ntxlccnYzB:evidence:0: Describe the air inside a rainforest as hot and sticky (humid)
topic:mt_ntxlccnYzB:evidence:1: Explain that the forest floor is dark because tall trees block most of the sunlight
topic:mt_ntxlccnYzB:evidence:2: Name at least two sounds you would hear in a rainforest, such as bird calls, insect buzzing, or rain dripping
topic:mt_xVW5U41tbp:name: Rainforest Animals
topic:mt_xVW5U41tbp:description: Name and recognise iconic rainforest animals — jaguars, toucans, sloths, poison dart frogs, howler monkeys, macaws, and butterflies — and know which layer of the rainforest each lives in
topic:mt_xVW5U41tbp:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name at least five animals that live in the rainforest and tell you something about each — like a toucan's big colourful beak or a sloth hanging upside down in the trees?
topic:mt_xVW5U41tbp:evidence:0: Name at least five iconic rainforest animals such as jaguars, toucans, sloths, poison dart frogs, and howler monkeys
topic:mt_xVW5U41tbp:evidence:1: Match at least three animals to the rainforest layer where they live (e.g. monkeys in the canopy, jaguars on the forest floor)
topic:mt_xVW5U41tbp:evidence:2: Describe one distinctive feature of each named animal
topic:mt_XL2gqdKJfu:name: Rainforest Insects
topic:mt_XL2gqdKJfu:description: Know that rainforests are home to millions of insects — leaf-cutter ants that farm fungus, giant beetles, jewel-coloured butterflies, enormous spiders, and stick insects — and that insects are the most numerous animals in the rainforest
topic:mt_XL2gqdKJfu:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that rainforests are packed with insects — like leaf-cutter ants that carry bits of leaf in a long line, or butterflies as big as a dinner plate?
topic:mt_XL2gqdKJfu:evidence:0: Name at least three types of insect or minibeast found in the rainforest, such as leaf-cutter ants, morpho butterflies, and giant beetles
topic:mt_XL2gqdKJfu:evidence:1: Explain that insects are the most numerous animals in the rainforest
topic:mt_XL2gqdKJfu:evidence:2: Describe one interesting behaviour, such as leaf-cutter ants carrying leaf pieces back to grow fungus
topic:mt_-0cjwyYhce:name: Rainforest Layers
topic:mt_-0cjwyYhce:description: Know that a rainforest has four layers from ground to sky — the forest floor (dark, damp, full of decomposing leaves), the understory (small trees and shrubs in the shade), the canopy (a thick roof of treetops where most animals live), and the emergent layer (the tallest trees poking above the canopy into bright sunlight)
topic:mt_-0cjwyYhce:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a rainforest, can they show the four layers — the dark forest floor, the shady understory, the leafy canopy, and the tallest emergent trees poking into the sky?
topic:mt_-0cjwyYhce:evidence:0: Name the four rainforest layers in order from ground to sky: forest floor, understory, canopy, emergent
topic:mt_-0cjwyYhce:evidence:1: Describe one key feature of each layer, such as the canopy being a thick roof of leaves or the forest floor being dark and damp
topic:mt_-0cjwyYhce:evidence:2: Explain that most rainforest animals live in the canopy because that is where there is food and light
topic:mt_x5ZrQMAZ5v:name: Rainforest Plants
topic:mt_x5ZrQMAZ5v:description: Know that rainforests contain an enormous variety of plants — towering kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing vines called lianas, colourful orchids that grow on tree branches, giant water lilies, and huge leaves that funnel rainwater
topic:mt_x5ZrQMAZ5v:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name some plants that grow in the rainforest — like giant trees, climbing vines, or orchids that grow on branches — and explain why they grow so big and tall?
topic:mt_x5ZrQMAZ5v:evidence:0: Name at least three types of rainforest plant, such as kapok trees, lianas (climbing vines), and orchids
topic:mt_x5ZrQMAZ5v:evidence:1: Explain that rainforest plants grow very tall because they compete for sunlight
topic:mt_x5ZrQMAZ5v:evidence:2: Describe one unusual feature, such as orchids growing on tree branches or lianas climbing up trunks
topic:mt_FZ_ixwU1p1:name: What Is a Rainforest?
topic:mt_FZ_ixwU1p1:description: Know that a rainforest is a thick, tall forest found in hot, wet places near the Equator where it rains almost every day, creating a warm, damp environment where plants and animals thrive
topic:mt_FZ_ixwU1p1:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a picture of a thick, green jungle with huge trees and dangling vines, can they tell you it's a rainforest and explain that it's hot and rainy there almost every day?
topic:mt_FZ_ixwU1p1:evidence:0: Describe a rainforest as a forest that is hot and wet, located near the Equator
topic:mt_FZ_ixwU1p1:evidence:1: Explain that it rains very often in a rainforest, which is why the plants grow so tall and thick
topic:mt_FZ_ixwU1p1:evidence:2: Point to the Equator on a globe and say that rainforests are found in the hot belt near it
topic:mt_0u3QNroZ34:name: Where Rainforests Are
topic:mt_0u3QNroZ34:description: Know that rainforests are found in a belt around the middle of the Earth — in South America (the Amazon), Central Africa (the Congo), and Southeast Asia — and that they appear on every continent except Antarctica and Europe
topic:mt_0u3QNroZ34:assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a world map, can they point to where rainforests grow — near the middle of the Earth in places like South America, Africa, and Asia?
topic:mt_0u3QNroZ34:evidence:0: Point to the Amazon, Congo, and Southeast Asian rainforest regions on a world map
topic:mt_0u3QNroZ34:evidence:1: Explain that rainforests grow near the Equator where it is hot and wet all year
topic:mt_0u3QNroZ34:evidence:2: Name at least two continents that have large rainforests
topic:mt_OtShuvs3x8:name: Classifying Rainforest Organisms
topic:mt_OtShuvs3x8:description: Classify rainforest organisms into major groups — mammals (jaguars, monkeys, bats), birds (toucans, macaws, hummingbirds), reptiles (snakes, lizards, caimans), amphibians (tree frogs, poison dart frogs), insects (butterflies, ants, beetles), and plants (trees, epiphytes, ferns) — using observable features to sort them
topic:mt_OtShuvs3x8:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at pictures of different rainforest creatures, can they sort them into groups like mammals, birds, reptiles, and insects, and explain why each one belongs in its group?
topic:mt_OtShuvs3x8:evidence:0: Sort at least eight rainforest organisms into correct groups: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, or plants
topic:mt_OtShuvs3x8:evidence:1: State the key feature that defines each group (e.g. mammals have fur and feed milk to their young)
topic:mt_OtShuvs3x8:evidence:2: Explain why classification helps scientists understand and study the huge variety of life in rainforests
topic:mt_m43jiOAOCt:name: Indigenous Ecological Knowledge
topic:mt_m43jiOAOCt:description: Understand that indigenous peoples of the rainforest have developed deep ecological knowledge over thousands of years — using plants for medicine, food, and building materials, practising sustainable farming methods like shifting cultivation, and understanding animal behaviour and forest ecology in ways that modern science is only beginning to appreciate
topic:mt_m43jiOAOCt:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that indigenous rainforest peoples know an enormous amount about forest plants and animals — like which plants cure illnesses — and that scientists are learning from this knowledge?
topic:mt_m43jiOAOCt:evidence:0: Give at least two examples of indigenous knowledge, such as using specific plants as medicine or practising sustainable farming
topic:mt_m43jiOAOCt:evidence:1: Explain what shifting cultivation is and why it is less harmful to the forest than permanent clearing
topic:mt_m43jiOAOCt:evidence:2: Describe how indigenous knowledge and modern science can work together to protect rainforests
topic:mt_XxgU_91AXg:name: Rainforest Animal Survival Tricks
topic:mt_XxgU_91AXg:description: Know how rainforest animals are adapted to their environment — camouflage helps leaf insects and tree frogs hide, bright warning colours (aposematism) signal that poison dart frogs are toxic, prehensile tails let monkeys grip branches, toucans' large beaks help reach distant fruit, and many animals are nocturnal to avoid daytime heat
topic:mt_XxgU_91AXg:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a poison dart frog is so brightly coloured — that it's warning predators it's dangerous — or why a sloth moves so slowly that algae grows on its fur, helping it blend in?
topic:mt_XxgU_91AXg:evidence:0: Describe at least three animal adaptations such as camouflage, warning colours, and prehensile tails
topic:mt_XxgU_91AXg:evidence:1: Explain how each adaptation helps the animal survive (e.g. camouflage hides prey from predators)
topic:mt_XxgU_91AXg:evidence:2: Give a specific example for each adaptation, linking the animal to its rainforest layer
topic:mt_1LFVPjdGg-:name: Rainforest Food Webs
topic:mt_1LFVPjdGg-:description: Understand how energy and nutrients flow through a rainforest food web — from plants (producers) to herbivores (primary consumers) to predators (secondary consumers) — and that decomposers like fungi and insects break down dead material on the forest floor, recycling nutrients back into the soil for plants to use again
topic:mt_1LFVPjdGg-:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain a rainforest food chain — like how a fruit tree feeds a monkey, the monkey might be hunted by a jaguar, and when things die, tiny organisms break them down to feed the trees again?
topic:mt_1LFVPjdGg-:evidence:0: Construct a simple rainforest food chain with at least three levels: producer → herbivore → predator
topic:mt_1LFVPjdGg-:evidence:1: Explain the role of decomposers in breaking down dead material and returning nutrients to the soil
topic:mt_1LFVPjdGg-:evidence:2: Use the terms producer, consumer, and decomposer correctly
topic:mt_Wx5m6mwkpj:name: Rainforest Plant Adaptations
topic:mt_Wx5m6mwkpj:description: Know how rainforest plants are adapted to their environment — drip-tip leaves channel water off quickly to prevent rot, buttress roots spread wide to support tall trees in thin soil, epiphytes (like orchids and bromeliads) grow on tree branches to reach sunlight without needing soil, and lianas climb trunks to reach the canopy
topic:mt_Wx5m6mwkpj:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why some rainforest trees have huge roots spreading out like wings, or why leaves have pointy tips that water drips off — that these are clever adaptations to life in a hot, wet forest?
topic:mt_Wx5m6mwkpj:evidence:0: Describe at least three plant adaptations: drip-tip leaves, buttress roots, and epiphytes
topic:mt_Wx5m6mwkpj:evidence:1: Explain the purpose of each adaptation (e.g. drip-tips shed water to prevent rot)
topic:mt_Wx5m6mwkpj:evidence:2: Use the word adaptation to mean a feature that helps an organism survive in its environment
topic:mt_ZWTk6eP1qF:name: Rainforest Water Cycle
topic:mt_ZWTk6eP1qF:description: Understand how the water cycle works in a rainforest — trees absorb water through their roots and release it through their leaves (transpiration), this moisture forms clouds above the canopy, and the clouds produce rain that falls back into the forest — creating a self-sustaining cycle that generates much of the rainforest's own rainfall
topic:mt_ZWTk6eP1qF:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how rainforest trees help make their own rain — by releasing water from their leaves, which forms clouds, which rain back down on the forest?
topic:mt_ZWTk6eP1qF:evidence:0: Describe the sequence: trees absorb water → release it through leaves (transpiration) → moisture rises → clouds form → rain falls
topic:mt_ZWTk6eP1qF:evidence:1: Explain that rainforests generate much of their own rainfall through this cycle
topic:mt_ZWTk6eP1qF:evidence:2: Use the word transpiration correctly when describing how water leaves a plant through its leaves
topic:mt_38d-k-dJPa:name: The Amazon Rainforest
topic:mt_38d-k-dJPa:description: Know that the Amazon is Earth's greatest rainforest — spanning nine countries across South America, containing the world's largest river by water volume, and home to an estimated 10% of all species on Earth including 40,000 plant species, 1,300 bird species, and 3,000 types of fish
topic:mt_38d-k-dJPa:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you about the Amazon — that it's the biggest rainforest in the world, spread across nine countries, with more types of animals and plants than almost anywhere else on Earth?
topic:mt_38d-k-dJPa:evidence:0: Locate the Amazon rainforest on a map of South America and name at least two countries it spans
topic:mt_38d-k-dJPa:evidence:1: State that the Amazon contains the world's largest river by volume and is home to roughly 10% of all species on Earth
topic:mt_38d-k-dJPa:evidence:2: Give at least two specific numbers showing the Amazon's biodiversity, such as 40,000 plant species or 1,300 bird species
topic:mt_v6CBCMuvz1:name: Tropical Rainforest Climate
topic:mt_v6CBCMuvz1:description: Understand that rainforests have a tropical climate — consistently hot (25–30°C) with over 2000 mm of rainfall per year — and that this combination of heat and moisture creates ideal conditions for rapid plant growth and extraordinary biodiversity
topic:mt_v6CBCMuvz1:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why rainforests grow so well — that it's the combination of being really hot and really rainy all year round that makes everything grow so fast?
topic:mt_v6CBCMuvz1:evidence:0: State that tropical rainforests are hot (25–30°C) and wet (over 2000 mm rain per year) all year round
topic:mt_v6CBCMuvz1:evidence:1: Explain that the constant heat and moisture create ideal growing conditions for plants
topic:mt_v6CBCMuvz1:evidence:2: Compare tropical rainforest climate to the UK or local climate, noting key differences in temperature and rainfall
topic:mt_2OSTHTWDpa:name: Deforestation Causes & Scale
topic:mt_2OSTHTWDpa:description: Understand the causes and scale of rainforest deforestation — cattle ranching (largest driver in the Amazon), soy and palm oil plantations, logging for timber, and mining — and know that approximately 10 million hectares of forest are lost globally each year, with devastating consequences for biodiversity, climate, and indigenous communities
topic:mt_2OSTHTWDpa:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why rainforests are being cut down — naming causes like cattle farming, palm oil, and logging — and say roughly how fast it's happening?
topic:mt_2OSTHTWDpa:evidence:0: Name at least three major causes of deforestation: cattle ranching, palm oil, soy, logging, and mining
topic:mt_2OSTHTWDpa:evidence:1: State that approximately 10 million hectares of forest are lost globally each year
topic:mt_2OSTHTWDpa:evidence:2: Explain the impact of deforestation on at least two of: biodiversity, climate, and indigenous peoples
topic:mt_JcfP1hWKa_:name: Nutrient Cycling in Thin Soil
topic:mt_JcfP1hWKa_:description: Understand the paradox of nutrient cycling in rainforests — despite lush growth, rainforest soil is typically thin and nutrient-poor because most nutrients are locked in living organisms, not the soil; decomposition is rapid in the warm, wet conditions, and nutrients released from dead material are immediately absorbed by plant roots and fungi, creating a fast, closed-loop recycling system
topic:mt_JcfP1hWKa_:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the surprising fact that rainforest soil is actually poor and thin — that the nutrients aren't in the ground but locked inside the living plants and animals, constantly being recycled?
topic:mt_JcfP1hWKa_:evidence:0: Explain that rainforest soil is thin and nutrient-poor despite the lush growth above
topic:mt_JcfP1hWKa_:evidence:1: Describe the rapid decomposition cycle: dead material → decomposers → nutrients released → immediately absorbed by roots
topic:mt_JcfP1hWKa_:evidence:2: Explain why clearing rainforest for farming fails after a few years — once the trees are gone, the nutrients are lost
topic:mt_pPGaf8bR8r:name: Rainforest Biodiversity
topic:mt_pPGaf8bR8r:description: Understand that rainforests are biodiversity hotspots — covering just 6% of Earth's land surface but containing over 50% of all known plant and animal species — and that this extraordinary richness makes them irreplaceable for global biodiversity and a priority for conservation
topic:mt_pPGaf8bR8r:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the mind-boggling fact that rainforests cover only a tiny fraction of Earth but are home to more than half of all species — and why that makes protecting them so important?
topic:mt_pPGaf8bR8r:evidence:0: State that rainforests cover about 6% of Earth's land but hold over 50% of all species
topic:mt_pPGaf8bR8r:evidence:1: Explain why this concentration of species makes rainforests a conservation priority
topic:mt_pPGaf8bR8r:evidence:2: Give specific examples of rainforest biodiversity, such as one hectare containing more tree species than all of northern Europe
topic:mt_kON8bYEHYl:name: Rainforest Conservation
topic:mt_kON8bYEHYl:description: Know the main approaches to rainforest conservation — protected areas and national parks, reforestation and rewilding programmes, sustainable certification schemes (Rainforest Alliance, FSC), recognition of indigenous land rights as the most effective form of forest protection, and international agreements like REDD+ that pay countries to keep forests standing
topic:mt_kON8bYEHYl:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe what people are doing to save the rainforests — like creating nature reserves, planting new trees, supporting indigenous land rights, and buying certified sustainable products?
topic:mt_kON8bYEHYl:evidence:0: Name at least three conservation approaches: protected areas, reforestation, sustainable certification, and indigenous land rights
topic:mt_kON8bYEHYl:evidence:1: Explain why protecting indigenous territories is one of the most effective ways to prevent deforestation
topic:mt_kON8bYEHYl:evidence:2: Describe what certification labels like Rainforest Alliance or FSC mean and how they help
topic:mt_ZM7u9m-gS4:name: Rainforest Futures & Trade-Offs
topic:mt_ZM7u9m-gS4:description: Understand that the future of rainforests depends on balancing competing needs — economic development for local communities, indigenous peoples' rights to their ancestral lands, global biodiversity conservation, and climate stability — and that there are no simple answers, requiring cooperation between governments, businesses, scientists, indigenous leaders, and consumers worldwide
topic:mt_ZM7u9m-gS4:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} discuss the tricky problem of rainforest protection — that farmers need land, companies want resources, indigenous people have rights, and the whole planet needs the forests for climate — and there's no easy answer?
topic:mt_ZM7u9m-gS4:evidence:0: Name at least three competing interests: economic development, indigenous rights, biodiversity, and climate stability
topic:mt_ZM7u9m-gS4:evidence:1: Explain why there is no single simple solution to rainforest protection
topic:mt_ZM7u9m-gS4:evidence:2: Suggest how different groups (governments, businesses, consumers, scientists) can each contribute to a better outcome
topic:mt_xE_b3JiDZU:name: Rainforest Products in Daily Life
topic:mt_xE_b3JiDZU:description: Understand how rainforest products connect to everyday life through global supply chains — palm oil is in snacks, soap, and cosmetics; soy feeds livestock worldwide; cocoa becomes chocolate; rubber is in tyres and gloves; timber becomes furniture; and many medicines originate from rainforest plants — and that consumer choices can drive either destruction or sustainable practices
topic:mt_xE_b3JiDZU:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} check ingredient labels at the supermarket and spot products linked to rainforests — like palm oil in biscuits or cocoa in chocolate — and explain why choosing sustainable versions helps protect forests?
topic:mt_xE_b3JiDZU:evidence:0: Name at least four products linked to rainforests: palm oil, soy, cocoa, rubber, timber, and medicines
topic:mt_xE_b3JiDZU:evidence:1: Explain how a product like palm oil travels from a rainforest region to a supermarket shelf
topic:mt_xE_b3JiDZU:evidence:2: Describe how consumer choices (e.g. buying Rainforest Alliance certified products) can reduce deforestation pressure
topic:mt_HJd-8EEC6N:name: Rainforests & Global Climate
topic:mt_HJd-8EEC6N:description: Understand the connection between rainforests and global climate — rainforests absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen through photosynthesis, store enormous amounts of carbon in their biomass, and generate rainfall through transpiration; when forests are burned or cleared, stored carbon is released as CO₂, accelerating climate change and disrupting regional rainfall patterns
topic:mt_HJd-8EEC6N:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how rainforests help fight climate change by absorbing carbon dioxide — and how cutting them down makes climate change worse by releasing all that stored carbon?
topic:mt_HJd-8EEC6N:evidence:0: Explain that rainforests absorb CO₂ and store carbon in their trees, acting as a carbon sink
topic:mt_HJd-8EEC6N:evidence:1: Describe how deforestation releases stored carbon back into the atmosphere, accelerating climate change
topic:mt_HJd-8EEC6N:evidence:2: Explain that transpiration from rainforest trees generates rainfall, and losing trees disrupts rain patterns
topic:mt_hbDflQfW-U:name: Temperate Rainforests
topic:mt_hbDflQfW-U:description: Know that not all rainforests are tropical — temperate rainforests exist in cooler, wet regions like the Pacific Northwest of North America, western Scotland and Wales, southern Chile, and New Zealand — with similar features (high rainfall, moss-draped trees, dense canopy) but different species, including ancient oaks, giant redwoods, and tree ferns
topic:mt_hbDflQfW-U:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that rainforests aren't only in hot places — that there are cool, misty rainforests in places like Wales, Scotland, and the Pacific Northwest, with mossy trees and ferns instead of monkeys and parrots?
topic:mt_hbDflQfW-U:evidence:0: Name at least two locations of temperate rainforests, such as the Pacific Northwest, western Scotland, or southern Chile
topic:mt_hbDflQfW-U:evidence:1: Compare temperate and tropical rainforests: both have high rainfall and dense canopy, but differ in temperature and species
topic:mt_hbDflQfW-U:evidence:2: Name species found in temperate rainforests, such as ancient oaks, giant redwoods, or tree ferns
topic:mt_XirhnAB6Ye:name: Asking scientific questions
topic:mt_XirhnAB6Ye:description: Ask simple scientific questions and recognise that they can be answered in different ways including observation, testing, and research
topic:mt_XirhnAB6Ye:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} wonders about something — like 'why do leaves change colour?' — can they suggest how to find the answer, whether by looking closely, doing a test, or looking it up?
topic:mt_XirhnAB6Ye:evidence:0: Ask at least three 'how' or 'why' questions about the natural world
topic:mt_XirhnAB6Ye:evidence:1: Suggest different ways to answer a question: observing, testing, asking an expert, reading a book
topic:mt_XirhnAB6Ye:evidence:2: Choose an appropriate method to investigate a specific question
topic:mt_nNYo5A-7Bl:name: Comparing Design Solutions
topic:mt_nNYo5A-7Bl:description: Analyse data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of each design
topic:mt_nNYo5A-7Bl:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} tests two different paper aeroplane designs, can they compare the results and explain which one flew better and why?
topic:mt_nNYo5A-7Bl:evidence:0: Test two designs that address the same problem and collect data on their performance
topic:mt_nNYo5A-7Bl:evidence:1: Compare the results, identifying strengths and weaknesses of each design
topic:mt_nNYo5A-7Bl:evidence:2: Use data as evidence to recommend which design works better and suggest improvements
topic:mt_hi8cVycbwn:name: Modelling with Sketches
topic:mt_hi8cVycbwn:description: Develop a simple sketch, drawing, or physical model to illustrate how the shape of an object helps it function as needed to solve a given problem
topic:mt_hi8cVycbwn:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw or build a model to show how they'd design something — like a boat shape that floats well — and explain why the shape matters?
topic:mt_hi8cVycbwn:evidence:0: Create a sketch, drawing, or physical model of a design solution
topic:mt_hi8cVycbwn:evidence:1: Explain how the shape or structure of the design helps solve the problem
topic:mt_hi8cVycbwn:evidence:2: Relate the model to the real-world problem it addresses
topic:mt_vJO5Bxk4z-:name: Observing with simple equipment
topic:mt_vJO5Bxk4z-:description: Observe closely using simple equipment such as hand lenses, and use observations to describe, compare, and identify things
topic:mt_vJO5Bxk4z-:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a magnifying glass to look carefully at something like a leaf or an insect and describe in detail what they see?
topic:mt_vJO5Bxk4z-:evidence:0: Use a hand lens or other simple equipment to make detailed observations
topic:mt_vJO5Bxk4z-:evidence:1: Describe observations using specific vocabulary (colour, shape, size, texture, pattern)
topic:mt_vJO5Bxk4z-:evidence:2: Compare two objects based on careful observation, noting similarities and differences
topic:mt_ZFwPZaDJ0_:name: Recording Data
topic:mt_ZFwPZaDJ0_:description: Gather and record data using simple methods such as tables, tally charts, and drawings to help answer questions
topic:mt_ZFwPZaDJ0_:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} collect information during an experiment — like counting, measuring, or drawing — and put it into a simple table or chart?

topic:mt_Wa44s-f8Ws:name: Simple tests and experiments
topic:mt_Wa44s-f8Ws:description: Perform simple tests and use observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions
topic:mt_Wa44s-f8Ws:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} do a simple experiment — like testing which paper towel absorbs the most water — and use what they find out to answer the question?
topic:mt_Wa44s-f8Ws:evidence:0: Carry out a simple test with one thing changing at a time

topic:mt_obF-6VYRya:name: Changing Your Mind with Evidence
topic:mt_obF-6VYRya:description: Be willing to change your mind when evidence doesn't support your prediction — a result that surprises you is more valuable than one that confirms what you already thought
topic:mt_obF-6VYRya:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} predicts what will happen in an experiment and gets a different result, do they accept the evidence rather than deciding the experiment must have gone wrong?
topic:mt_obF-6VYRya:evidence:1: hypothesis testing and argumentation from evidence in young children
topic:mt_Hw70LI5xza:name: Observation vs Interpretation
topic:mt_Hw70LI5xza:description: Notice the difference between what you observed and what you think it means — 'the ice melted' is an observation; 'the ice melted because of the heat' is an interpretation
topic:mt_Hw70LI5xza:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} does a science activity, can they tell the difference between what they actually saw or measured — and what they think caused it or what it means?
topic:mt_Hw70LI5xza:evidence:0: observation vs interpretation in primary science
topic:mt_Hw70LI5xza:evidence:1: BERA: children's observation skills in nature

topic:mt_7IFpDVNsmt:assessmentPrompt: After doing an experiment, can {{name}} put their results into a neat table, draw a bar chart, and add labels to a diagram to show what they found?

topic:mt_QrVF5n7vci:name: Could there be another explanation?
topic:mt_QrVF5n7vci:description: For any result, ask: is there another explanation? — the first explanation that fits isn't always the right one, and good scientists actively look for alternatives

topic:mt_7VrR1GzhrN:assessmentPrompt: After finishing an experiment, can {{name}} explain what they found out, what it means, what they'd predict for next time, and how they could improve the test?

topic:mt_nyPMkeHlVJ:name: Drawing conclusions from evidence (age 9+)
topic:mt_nyPMkeHlVJ:description: Report and present findings including conclusions, causal relationships, explanations, and a degree of trust in results using oral and written forms
topic:mt_nyPMkeHlVJ:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write up or present their experiment results, explain what caused what, and discuss how confident they are in their findings?
topic:mt_nyPMkeHlVJ:evidence:0: Present findings clearly in written and oral form with appropriate scientific vocabulary
topic:mt_nyPMkeHlVJ:evidence:1: Identify causal relationships (X caused Y because...) supported by evidence
topic:mt_nyPMkeHlVJ:evidence:2: Discuss the degree of trust in results, considering sample size, repeat readings, and possible errors
topic:mt_AstzvYDU2m:name: Evidence Supporting Ideas
topic:mt_AstzvYDU2m:description: Identify scientific evidence that has been used to support or refute ideas or arguments, evaluating the strength of evidence
topic:mt_AstzvYDU2m:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a science claim — like 'plants grow faster with music' — can they evaluate whether the evidence actually supports it or if the test wasn't fair?
topic:mt_AstzvYDU2m:evidence:0: Distinguish between a claim and the evidence supporting it
topic:mt_AstzvYDU2m:evidence:1: Evaluate whether evidence is strong (fair test, multiple trials) or weak (single observation, no controls)
topic:mt_AstzvYDU2m:evidence:2: Identify when evidence supports or refutes a scientific idea and explain why
topic:mt_5PgQB0QkWi:name: Fair testing (age 9+)
topic:mt_5PgQB0QkWi:description: Use test results to make predictions and set up further comparative and fair tests to investigate new questions
topic:mt_5PgQB0QkWi:assessmentPrompt: After getting results from one experiment, can {{name}} use the pattern to predict what would happen in a new situation and then design a follow-up test to check?
topic:mt_5PgQB0QkWi:evidence:0: Use results from an investigation to make a specific, testable prediction
topic:mt_5PgQB0QkWi:evidence:1: Design a follow-up test to verify the prediction
topic:mt_5PgQB0QkWi:evidence:2: Explain the reasoning linking the original results to the new prediction
topic:mt_1GVAmcwAiO:name: Science Can Be Revised
topic:mt_1GVAmcwAiO:description: Scientific knowledge is provisional — it is the best current explanation based on available evidence, and it can and should be revised when better evidence arrives
topic:mt_1GVAmcwAiO:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that scientific facts can be revised as new discoveries are made — and that this is science working properly, not a sign that scientists were wrong?
topic:mt_1GVAmcwAiO:evidence:0: Give an example of a scientific idea that changed when new evidence was found — e.g. people once thought the Sun orbited the Earth
topic:mt_1GVAmcwAiO:evidence:1: Explain that scientists update their ideas when experiments give unexpected results, and that this is a strength not a weakness
topic:mt_1GVAmcwAiO:evidence:2: Describe why it is important to keep testing ideas rather than just accepting them because an expert said so
topic:mt_Ae56umVlTT:name: Controlling variables (age 11+)
topic:mt_Ae56umVlTT:description: Form a testable scientific hypothesis linking an independent variable to a predicted outcome, plan a full investigation identifying independent, dependent, and control variables, sample size, and risk assessment
topic:mt_Ae56umVlTT:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to investigate whether temperature affects how quickly sugar dissolves, could they write a clear prediction, state exactly what they would change and measure, list three things to keep the same, and identify any safety steps?
topic:mt_Ae56umVlTT:evidence:0: Writes a hypothesis in the form 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because...' supported by scientific reasoning
topic:mt_Ae56umVlTT:evidence:1: Identifies and labels the independent variable, dependent variable, and at least three control variables
topic:mt_Ae56umVlTT:evidence:2: Plans repeat readings and an appropriate sample size, and identifies relevant hazards with control measures
topic:mt_auJqTemMpI:name: Repeated tests for reliability
topic:mt_auJqTemMpI:description: Distinguish between precision (consistency of repeated readings) and accuracy (closeness to true value), use significant figures and standard form correctly, and choose and use appropriate measuring instruments to minimise uncertainty
topic:mt_auJqTemMpI:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} weighed the same stone five times and got very similar answers but they were all slightly too high, could they explain the difference between being precise and being accurate — and why having lots of repeats doesn’t always fix the problem?
topic:mt_auJqTemMpI:evidence:0: Explains the distinction between precision and accuracy with examples
topic:mt_auJqTemMpI:evidence:1: Rounds measurements to an appropriate number of significant figures
topic:mt_auJqTemMpI:evidence:2: Selects a measuring instrument with appropriate resolution for the context (e.g. choosing a 10 ml measuring cylinder rather than a 1-litre measuring jug for a 5 ml measurement)
topic:mt_3jmBpEepYX:name: Drawing conclusions from evidence (age 12+)
topic:mt_3jmBpEepYX:description: Identify patterns and trends in data, draw conclusions that directly address the hypothesis with quantitative reference to evidence, and evaluate the investigation by distinguishing between systematic and random errors and proposing targeted improvements
topic:mt_3jmBpEepYX:assessmentPrompt: After finishing an experiment, can {{name}} describe the trend in the results, write a conclusion that says whether their prediction was right (with figures), and suggest one specific improvement that would make the results more reliable — rather than just saying 'do more repeats'?
topic:mt_3jmBpEepYX:evidence:0: Identifies the pattern or trend in a graph or data table using specific values
topic:mt_3jmBpEepYX:evidence:1: Writes a conclusion that references the hypothesis, states whether the prediction was supported, and quotes numerical evidence
topic:mt_3jmBpEepYX:evidence:2: Distinguishes between a systematic error (affects all readings in the same direction) and a random error, and proposes a specific procedural improvement to address each
topic:mt_YHsUhi4Prc:name: Tables, charts, and graphs
topic:mt_YHsUhi4Prc:description: Construct data tables with correct headings and SI units, plot appropriate graph types (bar chart, line graph, scatter graph), draw a line of best fit, and calculate the gradient of a straight-line graph
topic:mt_YHsUhi4Prc:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} collected data on how spring length changes with the weight added, could they put it in a correct table, plot it as a line graph with axes labelled in the right units, draw a line of best fit, and calculate the gradient?
topic:mt_YHsUhi4Prc:evidence:0: Constructs a table with column headings that include quantity and unit (e.g. Mass / g)
topic:mt_YHsUhi4Prc:evidence:1: Selects the appropriate graph type for the data and plots it accurately with labelled axes and scales
topic:mt_YHsUhi4Prc:evidence:2: Draws a line of best fit for linear data and correctly calculates its gradient using two points
topic:mt_ThTbUuNb3p:name: Writing Science Reports
topic:mt_ThTbUuNb3p:description: Communicate scientific findings in a structured report using appropriate scientific vocabulary, SI units, and standard notation; describe how peer review and replication contribute to the reliability of scientific knowledge
topic:mt_ThTbUuNb3p:assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} write up an experiment with all the right sections and scientific language, and explain why a scientific discovery isn’t accepted straight away — describing what peer review means and why other scientists need to repeat the experiment?
topic:mt_ThTbUuNb3p:evidence:0: Writes a structured scientific report including aim, hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, and evaluation using appropriate scientific vocabulary
topic:mt_ThTbUuNb3p:evidence:1: Uses SI units and standard form consistently throughout a report
topic:mt_ThTbUuNb3p:evidence:2: Explains what peer review is and why replication by independent researchers is essential for scientific claims to be accepted
topic:mt_ByXgbTld6R:name: Moon Phases
topic:mt_ByXgbTld6R:description: Observe and describe the Moon's changing shape over about a month, recognising that it goes through a repeating cycle of phases from new moon (invisible) to full moon (complete circle) and back again
topic:mt_ByXgbTld6R:assessmentPrompt: If you asked {{name}} to look at the Moon several nights in a row, could they notice that it changes shape and describe the pattern?
topic:mt_ByXgbTld6R:evidence:0: Describe that the Moon appears to change shape over about a month
topic:mt_ByXgbTld6R:evidence:1: Name or draw at least three phases: new moon (dark), half moon, and full moon
topic:mt_ByXgbTld6R:evidence:2: State that the pattern repeats — the Moon goes through the same shapes again and again
topic:mt_XlyF294bPR:name: Our Solar System
topic:mt_XlyF294bPR:description: Know that there are other planets besides Earth and that our group of planets orbiting the Sun is called the solar system — and that space is the vast area beyond Earth's sky
topic:mt_XlyF294bPR:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that Earth is one of several planets that go around the Sun, and that this group is called the solar system?
topic:mt_XlyF294bPR:evidence:0: State that Earth is a planet and there are other planets too
topic:mt_XlyF294bPR:evidence:1: Use the term 'solar system' to describe the Sun and the planets that orbit it
topic:mt_XlyF294bPR:evidence:2: Explain that space is the area beyond the Earth's sky, where the planets and stars are
topic:mt_BVpB5wyijZ:name: Spotting Constellations
topic:mt_BVpB5wyijZ:description: Recognise a few star patterns (constellations) in the night sky, starting with the Big Dipper (the Plough), and understand that the North Star (Polaris) can be found using the Big Dipper
topic:mt_BVpB5wyijZ:assessmentPrompt: On a clear night, could {{name}} find the Big Dipper in the sky — or draw its shape from memory?
topic:mt_BVpB5wyijZ:evidence:0: Identify or draw the Big Dipper (the Plough) as a pattern of seven stars
topic:mt_BVpB5wyijZ:evidence:1: Explain that the two end stars of the Big Dipper's bowl point towards the North Star
topic:mt_BVpB5wyijZ:evidence:2: State that constellations are patterns of stars that people have named
topic:mt_PiWZA8Z0ZJ:name: Sun, Moon & Stars
topic:mt_PiWZA8Z0ZJ:description: Identify the Sun, Moon, and stars as objects in the sky and describe basic differences: the Sun gives light and heat during the day, stars are tiny points of light at night, and the Moon can appear in both the day and night sky
topic:mt_PiWZA8Z0ZJ:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} point out the Sun, Moon, and stars and tell you something simple about each one — like that the Sun gives us light and heat?
topic:mt_PiWZA8Z0ZJ:evidence:0: Name the Sun, Moon, and stars as objects in the sky
topic:mt_PiWZA8Z0ZJ:evidence:1: State that the Sun appears during the day and gives us light and heat
topic:mt_PiWZA8Z0ZJ:evidence:2: State that stars appear at night and the Moon can sometimes be seen during the day too
topic:mt_oiqsIP97V3:name: What Astronauts Do
topic:mt_oiqsIP97V3:description: Know that astronauts are people who travel to space in rockets, that humans have walked on the Moon (Apollo missions), and that astronauts today live and work on the International Space Station
topic:mt_oiqsIP97V3:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you what an astronaut is, and that people have actually walked on the Moon and live on a space station?
topic:mt_oiqsIP97V3:evidence:0: Define an astronaut as a person who travels to space
topic:mt_oiqsIP97V3:evidence:1: State that humans landed on the Moon during the Apollo missions
topic:mt_oiqsIP97V3:evidence:2: Describe the International Space Station as a place where astronauts live and work in orbit around Earth
topic:mt_uoTBeyMhGm:name: Asteroids, Comets & Dwarf Planets
topic:mt_uoTBeyMhGm:description: Identify other objects in the solar system beyond planets: asteroids (rocky bodies mostly between Mars and Jupiter), comets (icy bodies with tails when near the Sun), and meteoroids/meteors/meteorites (space rocks that enter Earth’s atmosphere)
topic:mt_uoTBeyMhGm:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a shooting star, could they explain that it’s actually a tiny space rock burning up in our atmosphere — and tell you the difference between that and a comet?
topic:mt_uoTBeyMhGm:evidence:0: Describe asteroids as rocky bodies mostly found in the belt between Mars and Jupiter
topic:mt_uoTBeyMhGm:evidence:1: Describe comets as icy bodies that develop a glowing tail when they approach the Sun
topic:mt_uoTBeyMhGm:evidence:2: Explain the difference between a meteoroid (in space), meteor (streak of light in atmosphere), and meteorite (lands on Earth)
topic:mt_w2xiMNkyyX:name: Earth's Spin & Orbit
topic:mt_w2xiMNkyyX:description: Understand that Earth moves in two ways: it rotates (spins) on its axis once every 24 hours causing day and night, and it orbits (travels around) the Sun once every 365 days, which is one year
topic:mt_w2xiMNkyyX:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that we have day and night because the Earth spins, and that a year is the time it takes Earth to go all the way around the Sun?
topic:mt_w2xiMNkyyX:evidence:0: Demonstrate with a globe or ball that Earth's rotation causes day on the Sun-facing side and night on the opposite side
topic:mt_w2xiMNkyyX:evidence:1: State that one full rotation takes about 24 hours (one day)
topic:mt_w2xiMNkyyX:evidence:2: State that one full orbit around the Sun takes about 365 days (one year)
topic:mt_-SZU6cVB_-:name: How Telescopes Work
topic:mt_-SZU6cVB_-:description: Know that telescopes are instruments that help us see distant objects in space, and that space telescopes like Hubble and James Webb orbit above Earth’s atmosphere to get clearer views of the universe
topic:mt_-SZU6cVB_-:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know what a telescope does and why some telescopes are sent into space — like the Hubble or James Webb telescopes?
topic:mt_-SZU6cVB_-:evidence:0: Explain that a telescope magnifies distant objects so we can see them in more detail
topic:mt_-SZU6cVB_-:evidence:1: State that Earth's atmosphere blurs the view, so space telescopes get clearer pictures
topic:mt_-SZU6cVB_-:evidence:2: Name at least one space telescope (Hubble or James Webb) and describe what it does
topic:mt_W8Eq3CqWJf:name: Planet Features
topic:mt_W8Eq3CqWJf:description: Describe a key feature of each planet: Mercury is smallest and closest, Venus is the hottest, Mars is red with rust, Jupiter is the largest with a Great Red Spot, Saturn has rings, Uranus tilts on its side, Neptune is the farthest and very cold
topic:mt_W8Eq3CqWJf:assessmentPrompt: If you named a planet, could {{name}} tell you one interesting fact about it — like Saturn's rings or Jupiter's Great Red Spot?
topic:mt_W8Eq3CqWJf:evidence:0: State one distinctive feature for at least six of the eight planets
topic:mt_W8Eq3CqWJf:evidence:1: Compare at least two planets (e.g. Jupiter is much bigger than Earth, Venus is hotter than Mercury)
topic:mt_W8Eq3CqWJf:evidence:2: Explain why Mars appears red (iron oxide/rust in its rocks)
topic:mt_7GwWplh-48:name: Space Robots & Rovers
topic:mt_7GwWplh-48:description: Describe how robots and rovers have explored places humans cannot easily go — Mars rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance drive across Mars taking photos, collecting rock samples, and searching for signs of past water
topic:mt_7GwWplh-48:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know about the Mars rovers? Can they tell you what Curiosity or Perseverance does on Mars?
topic:mt_7GwWplh-48:evidence:0: Name at least one Mars rover (Curiosity or Perseverance) and state it drives on Mars's surface
topic:mt_7GwWplh-48:evidence:1: Explain that rovers take photos, analyse rocks, and look for evidence of water
topic:mt_7GwWplh-48:evidence:2: State why we send robots instead of people: Mars is very far away and has no breathable air
topic:mt_AVk2EmSULC:name: The Eight Planets
topic:mt_AVk2EmSULC:description: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), know that Pluto is a dwarf planet, and distinguish rocky inner planets from gas giant outer planets
topic:mt_AVk2EmSULC:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} list all eight planets in order from the Sun — maybe using a memory trick like 'My Very Eager Mother Just Served Us Nachos'?
topic:mt_AVk2EmSULC:evidence:0: List all eight planets in order from the Sun
topic:mt_AVk2EmSULC:evidence:1: State that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006
topic:mt_AVk2EmSULC:evidence:2: Explain that the four inner planets are small and rocky while the four outer planets are large gas giants
topic:mt_15FduGRf5c:name: The Moon's Orbit
topic:mt_15FduGRf5c:description: Know that the Moon orbits Earth approximately once a month, that it does not make its own light but reflects sunlight, and that its changing appearance (phases) is caused by how much of the sunlit side we can see from Earth
topic:mt_15FduGRf5c:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why the Moon seems to change shape — that it’s always round but we only see the part lit up by the Sun?
topic:mt_15FduGRf5c:evidence:0: State that the Moon orbits Earth roughly once every 28-30 days
topic:mt_15FduGRf5c:evidence:1: Explain that the Moon reflects sunlight rather than producing its own light
topic:mt_15FduGRf5c:evidence:2: Describe how Moon phases happen: we see different amounts of the lit-up side as the Moon orbits Earth
topic:mt_u3Y3Tb-G_n:name: The Sun is a star
topic:mt_u3Y3Tb-G_n:description: Know that the Sun is a star — the closest star to Earth — and that it is at the centre of our solar system, with all eight planets orbiting around it
topic:mt_u3Y3Tb-G_n:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that the Sun is actually a star — just a very close one — and that the planets go around it?
topic:mt_u3Y3Tb-G_n:evidence:0: State that the Sun is a star, not a unique type of object
topic:mt_u3Y3Tb-G_n:evidence:1: Explain that the Sun appears bigger and brighter than other stars because it is much closer
topic:mt_u3Y3Tb-G_n:evidence:2: Describe the solar system as the Sun at the centre with planets orbiting around it
topic:mt_KiRn5lnRgj:name: Changing Ideas About Space
topic:mt_KiRn5lnRgj:description: Understand that ideas about the solar system changed over time: ancient people believed Earth was at the centre (geocentric model, Ptolemy), until Copernicus proposed the Sun was at the centre (heliocentric model), later confirmed by Galileo’s telescope observations
topic:mt_KiRn5lnRgj:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you that people used to think the Sun went around the Earth, and explain how scientists like Copernicus and Galileo changed our understanding?
topic:mt_KiRn5lnRgj:evidence:0: Describe the geocentric model (Earth at the centre) and name Ptolemy as its main proponent
topic:mt_KiRn5lnRgj:evidence:1: Describe the heliocentric model (Sun at the centre) and name Copernicus as the person who proposed it
topic:mt_KiRn5lnRgj:evidence:2: Explain that Galileo used a telescope to find evidence supporting the heliocentric model (e.g. moons orbiting Jupiter)
topic:mt_Y2WcY2lOTK:name: Gravity Pulls Things Down
topic:mt_Y2WcY2lOTK:description: Understand gravity as a force that pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth, that 'down' means towards Earth’s centre regardless of where you stand on the sphere, and that gravity keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and planets orbiting the Sun
topic:mt_Y2WcY2lOTK:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why things fall 'down' and that gravity is the same force keeping the Moon going around the Earth?
topic:mt_Y2WcY2lOTK:evidence:0: Define gravity as a pulling force that attracts objects towards the centre of the Earth
topic:mt_Y2WcY2lOTK:evidence:1: Explain that 'down' points towards Earth's centre, so people on opposite sides of the globe both feel pulled 'down'
topic:mt_Y2WcY2lOTK:evidence:2: State that gravity keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and planets orbiting the Sun
topic:mt_iTjrKEdAOj:name: Life Cycle of Stars
topic:mt_iTjrKEdAOj:description: Understand the basics of a star’s life cycle: stars are born in clouds of gas and dust (nebulae), shine for millions or billions of years by fusing hydrogen, and eventually die — massive stars explode as supernovae while smaller stars fade into white dwarfs
topic:mt_iTjrKEdAOj:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that stars are born, live for a very long time, and eventually die — and that really big stars can explode at the end?
topic:mt_iTjrKEdAOj:evidence:0: Describe that stars form from clouds of gas and dust called nebulae
topic:mt_iTjrKEdAOj:evidence:1: State that stars produce energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores
topic:mt_iTjrKEdAOj:evidence:2: Explain that massive stars end in a supernova explosion while smaller stars shrink to become white dwarfs
topic:mt_TlGhXAqC4p:name: Scale of the Solar System
topic:mt_TlGhXAqC4p:description: Use scale models, diagrams, or calculations to represent the relative sizes and distances of objects in the solar system, understanding that the distances between planets are enormously larger than the planets themselves
topic:mt_TlGhXAqC4p:assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} ever built or looked at a scale model of the solar system? Can they explain why the planets would need to be spread across a whole playing field to be the right distance apart?
topic:mt_TlGhXAqC4p:evidence:0: Explain that if the Sun were the size of a beach ball, Earth would be a pea about 26 metres away
topic:mt_TlGhXAqC4p:evidence:1: State that the distances between planets are much greater than the sizes of the planets themselves
topic:mt_TlGhXAqC4p:evidence:2: Create or interpret a scale model showing both relative sizes and distances
topic:mt_9VZem2vUqk:name: Seasonal Constellations
topic:mt_9VZem2vUqk:description: Recognise named constellations visible in different seasons and understand why we see different constellations at different times of year — because Earth’s orbit around the Sun changes which part of the sky we face at night
topic:mt_9VZem2vUqk:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that you can see different constellations in winter than in summer, and can they explain why?
topic:mt_9VZem2vUqk:evidence:0: Name at least three constellations (e.g. Orion, Ursa Major/Big Dipper, Leo, Cassiopeia)
topic:mt_9VZem2vUqk:evidence:1: State that different constellations are visible in different seasons
topic:mt_9VZem2vUqk:evidence:2: Explain that this happens because Earth's orbit means we face different directions in space at different times of year
topic:mt_H9RAGGiHBL:name: Space Exploration Milestones
topic:mt_H9RAGGiHBL:description: Describe key milestones in human space exploration: the Space Race (Sputnik, Yuri Gagarin, Apollo 11 Moon landing), the Space Shuttle era, the International Space Station, and current missions (Artemis programme, Mars exploration plans, commercial spaceflight)
topic:mt_H9RAGGiHBL:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you about the history of space exploration — from the first satellite to the Moon landing to what’s happening now?
topic:mt_H9RAGGiHBL:evidence:0: Name Sputnik as the first satellite (1957) and Yuri Gagarin as the first person in space (1961)
topic:mt_H9RAGGiHBL:evidence:1: Describe the Apollo 11 Moon landing (1969) with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin
topic:mt_H9RAGGiHBL:evidence:2: Name at least one current space programme (Artemis, SpaceX, ISS) and describe its goal
topic:mt_aulwq39aj8:name: The Vast Scale of Space
topic:mt_aulwq39aj8:description: Describe the scale of the universe in nested layers: Earth is one planet in our solar system, the Sun is one star among billions in the Milky Way galaxy, and the Milky Way is one galaxy among billions in the universe
topic:mt_aulwq39aj8:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe how our place in the universe works — that we’re on a planet in a solar system in a galaxy among billions of galaxies?
topic:mt_aulwq39aj8:evidence:0: State that the Milky Way is our galaxy and it contains billions of stars
topic:mt_aulwq39aj8:evidence:1: Explain the hierarchy: planet → solar system → galaxy → universe
topic:mt_aulwq39aj8:evidence:2: Use a comparison to convey cosmic scale (e.g. if the Sun were a football, Earth would be a peppercorn 26 metres away)
topic:mt_ae-cHHFR76:name: Why the Sun Looks Brightest
topic:mt_ae-cHHFR76:description: Explain why the Sun appears much brighter than other stars: it is the nearest star to Earth, not the biggest or brightest star in the universe — understanding the difference between apparent brightness (how bright something looks) and actual brightness
topic:mt_ae-cHHFR76:assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that the Sun looks so bright because it’s close, not because it’s the biggest star — and that some faraway stars are actually much larger?
topic:mt_ae-cHHFR76:evidence:0: State that the Sun is a medium-sized star that appears brightest because it is the closest star to Earth
topic:mt_ae-cHHFR76:evidence:1: Explain the difference between apparent brightness (how bright it looks) and actual brightness (how much light it gives off)
topic:mt_ae-cHHFR76:evidence:2: Give an example: a torch held close looks brighter than a distant floodlight, even though the floodlight is more powerful
topic:mt_UjuriPLVgT:name: Finding Exoplanets
topic:mt_UjuriPLVgT:description: Describe how astronomers detect planets around other stars using transit photometry (dip in starlight as a planet crosses) and radial velocity (Doppler wobble of the star), explain the habitable zone concept, and discuss what atmospheric biosignatures — such as oxygen, methane, and water vapour detected together — would suggest about a planet
topic:mt_UjuriPLVgT:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a planet the size of Earth had been found in the habitable zone of a nearby star, could they explain how astronomers detected it, what the habitable zone means, and what they'd look for in its atmosphere to decide if life might exist there?
topic:mt_UjuriPLVgT:evidence:0: Explains transit photometry: the small, periodic dip in a star's brightness when a planet passes in front of it
topic:mt_UjuriPLVgT:evidence:1: Explains the habitable zone as the range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface
topic:mt_UjuriPLVgT:evidence:2: Describes two or more atmospheric biosignatures and explains why their co-presence is significant (e.g. oxygen + methane together suggests active life replenishing both)
topic:mt_rbY77m8_s1:name: Observing with Light Waves
topic:mt_rbY77m8_s1:description: Explain how the electromagnetic spectrum is the primary tool of modern astronomy — different wavelengths (radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray) reveal different phenomena, why some telescopes must be in space, and what specific discoveries each wavelength range has enabled (e.g. CMB in microwave, black hole jets in X-ray, cold gas clouds in radio)
topic:mt_rbY77m8_s1:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was told that we can't see most of the universe with our eyes, could they explain why — and describe two types of telescope that detect something other than visible light, naming what they've helped us discover?
topic:mt_rbY77m8_s1:evidence:0: Lists at least four regions of the EM spectrum and gives a specific astronomical object or phenomenon observed in each
topic:mt_rbY77m8_s1:evidence:1: Explains why some telescopes must be placed in space (Earth's atmosphere blocks X-ray, gamma-ray, and much infrared radiation)
topic:mt_rbY77m8_s1:evidence:2: Describes the James Webb Space Telescope or Hubble and explains which part of the spectrum each primarily observes and why that was chosen
topic:mt_1nl396BaVa:name: Orbital Mechanics
topic:mt_1nl396BaVa:description: Apply Newton's laws to explain orbital motion: why orbit is continuously falling sideways rather than floating; how a gravity assist (slingshot manoeuvre) transfers momentum from a planet to a spacecraft; and why rockets need to reach a specific speed to enter orbit — with a conceptual (not algebraic) treatment of the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation
topic:mt_1nl396BaVa:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked why astronauts in the ISS float even though they're still close to Earth and gravity hasn't disappeared, could they explain that they're actually in freefall and describe what 'being in orbit' really means physically?
topic:mt_1nl396BaVa:evidence:0: Explains that orbit is a state of continuous freefall — the spacecraft is falling towards Earth but moving so fast horizontally that it keeps missing
topic:mt_1nl396BaVa:evidence:1: Describes how a gravity assist works: a spacecraft flying past a planet gains speed by 'borrowing' from the planet's orbital momentum
