topic:mt_KYx0m4OyZv:name: Where Elements Come From
topic:mt_KYx0m4OyZv:description: Explain stellar nucleosynthesis: the Big Bang produced mainly hydrogen and helium; main-sequence fusion builds elements up to iron; and supernovae produce elements heavier than iron and scatter them into space — meaning the atoms in our bodies were forged in ancient stars
topic:mt_KYx0m4OyZv:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was told that the calcium in their bones and the iron in their blood were made inside ancient stars that exploded billions of years ago, could they explain the chain of events from the Big Bang to the formation of those atoms to how they ended up on Earth?
topic:mt_KYx0m4OyZv:evidence:0: States that the Big Bang produced primarily hydrogen and helium, and that all heavier elements were made later in stars
topic:mt_KYx0m4OyZv:evidence:1: Explains that nuclear fusion in main-sequence stars converts hydrogen to helium and can continue building heavier elements up to iron
topic:mt_KYx0m4OyZv:evidence:2: Explains why elements heavier than iron require supernova explosions to form, and describes how supernovae distribute these elements into interstellar space where they become the raw material for new stars, planets, and life
topic:mt_EIbltgXRWR:name: Journey to Mars

topic:mt_EIbltgXRWR:evidence:0: Identifies and explains at least three major challenges of a Mars mission: radiation (no magnetosphere), bone/muscle loss from low gravity, psychological isolation, and delayed communications

topic:mt_EIbltgXRWR:evidence:2: States the Fermi Paradox ('Where is everybody?') and discusses two contrasting proposed resolutions
topic:mt_EHuU1ZeUFA:name: Naming the Planets

topic:mt_EHuU1ZeUFA:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name the planets in order from the Sun — and explain the difference between a star, a planet, and a moon?

topic:mt_EHuU1ZeUFA:evidence:2: Distinguish between a planet, a moon, a star, and an asteroid using the correct vocabulary
topic:mt_K0mZxY2AM8:name: Why seasons change

topic:mt_K0mZxY2AM8:evidence:0: Describe the pattern: more daylight hours in summer, fewer in winter

topic:mt_fk33IEGP-T:name: Sun, Moon, and stars
topic:mt_fk33IEGP-T:description: Use observations of the sun, moon, and stars to describe predictable patterns such as the sun rising and setting, the moon changing shape, and stars appearing at night

topic:mt_ZJu8s-Q1xa:name: Rapid earth changes

topic:mt_LQt4vnKeB4:name: Earth & Space Vocabulary
topic:mt_LQt4vnKeB4:description: Use technical vocabulary for Earth's motion and the wider universe — rotation, revolution, axis, tilt, orbit, light year, gravitational force, atmosphere, lunar phases, waxing, waning, solstice, equinox, eclipse — and apply these when explaining day and night, the seasons, and the Moon's phases

topic:mt_LQt4vnKeB4:evidence:2: Apply 'solstice' and 'equinox' correctly when explaining why seasons exist and why day length varies
topic:mt_q15w--Fb5H:name: Earth's rotation and day/night

topic:mt_GheLsWvrJ4:name: How fossils form
topic:mt_GheLsWvrJ4:description: Identify evidence from patterns in rock formations and fossils in rock layers to support an explanation for changes in a landscape over time

topic:mt_5l7iGkf1Tp:name: The solar system
topic:mt_5l7iGkf1Tp:description: Describe the sun, Earth, and moon as approximately spherical bodies, and describe the movement of the Earth and other planets orbiting the sun in the solar system

topic:mt_tMLsTPQHwF:name: Shadows

topic:mt_ZhKuYCbXz1:name: Star Brightness & Distance

topic:mt_4V-vYhFUcm:name: Phases of the Moon
topic:mt_4V-vYhFUcm:description: Explain the phases of the Moon as the changing angle of sunlight on the lunar surface as seen from Earth, and describe how solar and lunar eclipses occur

topic:mt_4V-vYhFUcm:evidence:0: Explains that the phases of the Moon arise from the changing geometry of Sun, Earth, and Moon, not Earth's shadow
topic:mt_4V-vYhFUcm:evidence:1: Describes the sequence of Moon phases over approximately 28 days

topic:mt_33RrpbceZE:name: The solar system (age 11+)
topic:mt_33RrpbceZE:description: Describe the detailed structure of the solar system, including moons, asteroids, and comets, compare orbital periods and distances of the planets, and distinguish between planets, dwarf planets, and other bodies
topic:mt_33RrpbceZE:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was making a model of the solar system, could they describe the difference between a planet, a moon, an asteroid, and a comet — and explain why planets closest to the Sun take less time to complete an orbit?
topic:mt_33RrpbceZE:evidence:0: Names the eight planets in order and gives one distinguishing fact about each
topic:mt_33RrpbceZE:evidence:1: Describes the difference between a planet, a dwarf planet, an asteroid, and a comet
topic:mt_33RrpbceZE:evidence:2: Explains the relationship between distance from the Sun and orbital period (planets further out take longer)
topic:mt_lFiDFPkVmH:name: Why We Have Seasons
topic:mt_lFiDFPkVmH:description: Explain that the seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis during its orbit around the Sun, distinguishing this from the common misconception that seasons are caused by changing distance from the Sun
topic:mt_lFiDFPkVmH:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked why the UK is hot in summer but Australia is cold at the same time, could they explain that it's not about being closer to the Sun but about which half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun?
topic:mt_lFiDFPkVmH:evidence:0: Explains that Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5° relative to its orbit
topic:mt_lFiDFPkVmH:evidence:1: Describes how the tilted axis causes one hemisphere to receive more direct sunlight in summer and less in winter
topic:mt_lFiDFPkVmH:evidence:2: Refutes the misconception that distance from the Sun causes seasons by noting Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun in January
topic:mt_v9uYnIY5-B:name: Galaxies and the universe
topic:mt_v9uYnIY5-B:description: Describe the scale of the universe, including the structure of galaxies, the position of the Sun in the Milky Way, and the use of light years as a unit of distance, and appreciate why space exploration requires enormous timescales
topic:mt_v9uYnIY5-B:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a star is 400 light years away, could they explain what a light year means, roughly how far that is, and why we will never be able to visit it with current spacecraft?
topic:mt_v9uYnIY5-B:evidence:0: Defines a light year as the distance light travels in one year
topic:mt_v9uYnIY5-B:evidence:1: Describes the structure of a galaxy and states that the Sun is a star in the Milky Way galaxy
topic:mt_v9uYnIY5-B:evidence:2: Compares the distances within the solar system with the distances between stars and between galaxies, expressing them in appropriate units
topic:mt_oLjz18CxDg:name: Universal Gravitation
topic:mt_oLjz18CxDg:description: Describe gravity as a universal attractive force between all masses, explain that orbital motion arises because gravity provides the centripetal force keeping objects in orbit, and compare gravitational field strengths on different planets
topic:mt_oLjz18CxDg:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked why the Moon doesn't fly off into space but also doesn't crash into Earth, could they explain that gravity is constantly pulling it into a curved path — like swinging a ball on a string?
topic:mt_oLjz18CxDg:evidence:0: States that gravity is a universal attractive force acting between all objects with mass
topic:mt_oLjz18CxDg:evidence:1: Explains that orbital motion occurs because gravity continuously deflects the path of the orbiting object
topic:mt_oLjz18CxDg:evidence:2: Compares gravitational field strength on different planets and explains how this affects weight
topic:mt_lHasFmgvnT:name: Life Cycle of a Star
topic:mt_lHasFmgvnT:description: Describe the life cycle of a star from nebula through main sequence to its end state (white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole depending on mass), and relate the life cycle to the origin of elements heavier than hydrogen
topic:mt_lHasFmgvnT:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was told that the iron in their blood was forged inside a star that exploded billions of years ago, could they explain the life cycle of a star and how elements are made inside stars?
topic:mt_lHasFmgvnT:evidence:0: Describes the main stages in the life cycle of a star similar to the Sun: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
topic:mt_lHasFmgvnT:evidence:1: Explains that more massive stars end as a supernova followed by a neutron star or black hole
topic:mt_lHasFmgvnT:evidence:2: States that nuclear fusion inside stars produces heavier elements from hydrogen and helium
topic:mt_cxJRc15osy:name: Basic Body Needs
topic:mt_cxJRc15osy:description: Know that the body needs food for energy, water to stay hydrated, sleep to rest and grow, and exercise to keep muscles and the heart strong — and that these are basic needs every human body has
topic:mt_cxJRc15osy:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why their body needs food, water, sleep, and exercise — and what happens if they miss any of them?
topic:mt_cxJRc15osy:evidence:0: List the four basic needs: food (energy), water (hydration), sleep (rest and growth), exercise (strength)
topic:mt_cxJRc15osy:evidence:1: Explain that food gives the body energy to move, think, and grow
topic:mt_cxJRc15osy:evidence:2: Describe what happens if one need isn't met (e.g. feeling tired without sleep, thirsty without water)
topic:mt_SdIWVjzopp:name: Bones & Muscles

topic:mt_SdIWVjzopp:evidence:2: Explain that muscles pull on bones to make the body move
topic:mt_tiPyEkm4cU:name: How Breathing Works
topic:mt_tiPyEkm4cU:description: Know that we breathe air into our lungs through the nose and mouth, that our lungs take in oxygen from the air which our body needs to stay alive, and that we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste
topic:mt_tiPyEkm4cU:assessmentPrompt: After running around, can {{name}} notice their faster breathing and explain that their lungs are taking in air that the body needs?
topic:mt_tiPyEkm4cU:evidence:0: Trace the path of air: nose/mouth → windpipe → lungs
topic:mt_tiPyEkm4cU:evidence:1: State that lungs take oxygen from the air, which the body needs
topic:mt_tiPyEkm4cU:evidence:2: State that we breathe out carbon dioxide, which the body doesn't need
topic:mt_pJ5zsocdNx:name: The Brain Controls the Body
topic:mt_pJ5zsocdNx:description: Understand that the brain is the body’s control centre: it receives messages from the senses, thinks and makes decisions, and sends messages through nerves to tell muscles what to do
topic:mt_pJ5zsocdNx:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what the brain does — that it’s in charge of thinking, feeling, and telling the body what to do?
topic:mt_pJ5zsocdNx:evidence:0: State that the brain is inside the skull and controls the whole body

topic:mt_pJ5zsocdNx:evidence:2: Give an example (e.g. eyes see a ball coming, brain decides to catch it, nerves tell hands to move)
topic:mt_nwSWPTENmv:name: The Five Senses
topic:mt_nwSWPTENmv:description: Explore the five senses in detail: sight uses eyes to detect light, hearing uses ears to detect sound, touch uses skin to feel pressure and temperature, taste uses the tongue to detect flavours, and smell uses the nose to detect odours

topic:mt_lp1eTsQen7:name: The Heart & Blood
topic:mt_lp1eTsQen7:description: Understand that the heart is a muscle that pumps blood around the body through tubes called blood vessels, and that we can feel our heartbeat by placing a hand on our chest or fingers on our wrist
topic:mt_lp1eTsQen7:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find their own pulse on their wrist or neck, and explain that it’s their heart pumping blood?
topic:mt_lp1eTsQen7:evidence:0: Locate their own heartbeat by touch (chest or pulse point)
topic:mt_lp1eTsQen7:evidence:1: State that the heart pumps blood through the body continuously
topic:mt_lp1eTsQen7:evidence:2: Describe blood vessels as tubes that carry blood to every part of the body
topic:mt_QhLAeAlHI0:name: Balanced Diet & Food Groups
topic:mt_QhLAeAlHI0:description: Know the main food groups (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water) and understand that a balanced diet includes the right amounts from each group to keep the body healthy and provide energy, growth materials, and protection from illness
topic:mt_QhLAeAlHI0:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at their dinner plate, could they identify which foods give energy, which help muscles grow, and which keep them healthy?
topic:mt_QhLAeAlHI0:evidence:0: Name at least five food groups and give an example food for each (e.g. carbohydrates = bread, protein = chicken)
topic:mt_QhLAeAlHI0:evidence:1: Explain what carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), and fats (energy and warmth) do for the body
topic:mt_QhLAeAlHI0:evidence:2: State that vitamins and minerals protect against illness and help the body work properly
topic:mt_C7FNeIDGc6:name: Cells, Tissues & Organs
topic:mt_C7FNeIDGc6:description: Understand that the body is organised in a hierarchy: tiny cells are the building blocks, groups of similar cells form tissues, tissues combine into organs (like the heart or stomach), and organs work together in organ systems (like the circulatory system)
topic:mt_C7FNeIDGc6:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that the body is made of tiny cells, and that cells group together to make tissues, which make organs, which make whole systems?
topic:mt_C7FNeIDGc6:evidence:0: State that cells are the smallest building blocks of the body, too small to see without a microscope
topic:mt_C7FNeIDGc6:evidence:1: Describe the hierarchy: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems
topic:mt_C7FNeIDGc6:evidence:2: Give an example: muscle cells form muscle tissue, which forms the heart organ, which is part of the circulatory system
topic:mt_6N-4TqCleR:name: How Muscles Move Bones
topic:mt_6N-4TqCleR:description: Understand that muscles work in pairs to move bones: when one muscle contracts (gets shorter and pulls), the opposite muscle relaxes, and that some muscles are voluntary (we choose to use them) while others like the heart are involuntary (they work automatically)

topic:mt_6N-4TqCleR:evidence:0: Demonstrate or describe how biceps and triceps work as a pair to bend and straighten the arm
topic:mt_6N-4TqCleR:evidence:1: Explain the difference between voluntary muscles (we control them) and involuntary muscles (they work automatically)
topic:mt_6N-4TqCleR:evidence:2: Name the heart and muscles of the digestive system as examples of involuntary muscles
topic:mt_-gkJdxJUQT:name: How the Eye Works
topic:mt_-gkJdxJUQT:description: Describe how the eye works: light enters through the pupil, the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back of the eye, and the retina sends signals along the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image
topic:mt_-gkJdxJUQT:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what happens inside their eye when they look at something — how light comes in through the pupil and the brain turns it into a picture?
topic:mt_-gkJdxJUQT:evidence:0: Name the main parts: pupil (lets light in), lens (focuses light), retina (detects light), optic nerve (sends signals to brain)
topic:mt_-gkJdxJUQT:evidence:1: Describe the sequence: light enters → lens focuses → retina detects → nerve signals brain → brain interprets image
topic:mt_-gkJdxJUQT:evidence:2: Explain that the pupil gets bigger in dim light and smaller in bright light to control how much light enters
topic:mt_OMmiuv9ZLH:name: Naming Major Bones
topic:mt_OMmiuv9ZLH:description: Identify major bones of the human skeleton by name (skull, spine/vertebrae, ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus) and explain the skeleton’s three jobs: supporting the body’s shape, protecting organs, and enabling movement with muscles
topic:mt_OMmiuv9ZLH:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} point to different parts of their body and name the bones underneath — like the femur in the thigh or the vertebrae in the spine?
topic:mt_OMmiuv9ZLH:evidence:0: Name and locate at least six major bones or bone groups on a diagram or their own body
topic:mt_OMmiuv9ZLH:evidence:1: Explain the three functions: support (holds us upright), protection (skull protects brain, ribs protect heart/lungs), movement (bones work with muscles)
topic:mt_OMmiuv9ZLH:evidence:2: State that not all animals have internal skeletons — some have shells or exoskeletons
topic:mt_JpQUM1129q:name: The Digestive Journey
topic:mt_JpQUM1129q:description: Trace the journey of food through the digestive system: food enters the mouth where teeth break it down and saliva begins digestion, travels down the oesophagus to the stomach, passes through the small intestine where nutrients are absorbed, and waste moves through the large intestine
topic:mt_JpQUM1129q:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} ate a sandwich, could they describe the journey it takes through their body — from mouth to stomach to intestines?
topic:mt_JpQUM1129q:evidence:0: List the organs in order: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
topic:mt_JpQUM1129q:evidence:1: Describe what happens at each stage (teeth chew, stomach churns with acid, small intestine absorbs nutrients)
topic:mt_JpQUM1129q:evidence:2: State that the small intestine is where most nutrients pass into the blood, and the large intestine removes water from waste
topic:mt_I047mKeeaq:name: Types of Teeth
topic:mt_I047mKeeaq:description: Identify the four types of human teeth (incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding) and understand that tooth shape is linked to function, just as in other animals — herbivores have flat teeth, carnivores have sharp teeth
topic:mt_I047mKeeaq:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look in a mirror, point out their different types of teeth, and explain what each type is for?
topic:mt_I047mKeeaq:evidence:0: Name the four tooth types and describe each one's job: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars/molars grind
topic:mt_I047mKeeaq:evidence:1: Compare human teeth to herbivore teeth (flat, for grinding plants) and carnivore teeth (sharp, for tearing meat)
topic:mt_I047mKeeaq:evidence:2: Explain that humans have all types because we are omnivores — we eat both plants and meat
topic:mt_QK-ZZb7UUN:name: Circulation & Breathing Together
topic:mt_QK-ZZb7UUN:description: Understand how the circulatory and respiratory systems work together: the lungs oxygenate the blood, the heart pumps it around the body, cells use the oxygen and produce carbon dioxide waste, and the blood carries the waste back to the lungs to be breathed out
topic:mt_QK-ZZb7UUN:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why their heart beats faster when they run — and how their heart and lungs are working together to deliver more oxygen to their muscles?
topic:mt_QK-ZZb7UUN:evidence:0: Describe the cycle: lungs add oxygen to blood → heart pumps oxygenated blood to body → cells use oxygen → blood returns CO₂ to lungs
topic:mt_QK-ZZb7UUN:evidence:1: Explain why heart rate and breathing rate increase during exercise (muscles need more oxygen)
topic:mt_QK-ZZb7UUN:evidence:2: Measure their own resting and post-exercise heart rate and explain the difference
topic:mt_pu2mmK27UA:name: Growing Up & Puberty
topic:mt_pu2mmK27UA:description: Describe the stages of human development from birth to old age: baby, toddler, child, adolescent (puberty), young adult, middle-aged adult, elderly — understanding the physical changes that happen at each stage, especially during puberty
topic:mt_pu2mmK27UA:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe how a person’s body changes as they grow from a baby to an adult to an elderly person — and explain what happens during puberty?
topic:mt_pu2mmK27UA:evidence:0: Name and order at least six life stages from birth to old age
topic:mt_pu2mmK27UA:evidence:1: Describe key physical changes during puberty (growth spurts, body shape changes, development of adult features)
topic:mt_pu2mmK27UA:evidence:2: Explain that puberty is triggered by hormones — chemical messengers released by glands
topic:mt_4k3HGahK2k:name: Healthy Lifestyle Choices
topic:mt_4k3HGahK2k:description: Understand how lifestyle choices affect the body’s health: a balanced diet, regular exercise, adequate sleep, and avoiding harmful substances (tobacco, alcohol, drugs) help body systems function well, while poor choices increase the risk of disease
topic:mt_4k3HGahK2k:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how what they eat, how much they exercise, and how much they sleep affects how their body works — and why smoking or drugs are harmful?
topic:mt_4k3HGahK2k:evidence:0: Explain how regular exercise strengthens the heart, lungs, and muscles
topic:mt_4k3HGahK2k:evidence:1: Describe how a poor diet high in sugar and fat can lead to obesity, tooth decay, and heart problems
topic:mt_4k3HGahK2k:evidence:2: State at least two harmful effects of smoking (damages lungs, increases heart disease risk) or alcohol (damages liver, affects brain)
topic:mt_g_M4Vh_pK7:name: Heart & Blood Circulation
topic:mt_g_M4Vh_pK7:description: Describe the circulatory system in detail: the heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) that pump blood in a double loop — one to the lungs for oxygen and one to the rest of the body to deliver it — through arteries, veins, and tiny capillaries
topic:mt_g_M4Vh_pK7:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} trace the path blood takes through the heart and body — explaining that it goes to the lungs first for oxygen, then out to the rest of the body?
topic:mt_g_M4Vh_pK7:evidence:0: Name the four heart chambers and describe the double-loop pathway (heart → lungs → heart → body)
topic:mt_g_M4Vh_pK7:evidence:1: Distinguish arteries (carry blood away from heart), veins (carry blood back to heart), and capillaries (tiny vessels where exchange happens)
topic:mt_g_M4Vh_pK7:evidence:2: Name the components of blood: red blood cells (carry oxygen), white blood cells (fight infection), platelets (help clotting), plasma (liquid)
topic:mt_zPDDJLAl-J:name: How the Lungs Work
topic:mt_zPDDJLAl-J:description: Explain how the respiratory system works in detail: air travels through the nose/mouth, down the trachea, into bronchi and bronchioles, reaching tiny air sacs (alveoli) in the lungs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out
topic:mt_zPDDJLAl-J:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe what happens to the air they breathe in — how it travels deeper and deeper into the lungs until oxygen swaps into the blood?
topic:mt_zPDDJLAl-J:evidence:0: Trace the air pathway: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
topic:mt_zPDDJLAl-J:evidence:1: Explain gas exchange in the alveoli: oxygen passes into blood capillaries, carbon dioxide passes out
topic:mt_zPDDJLAl-J:evidence:2: Describe the mechanical process: the diaphragm contracts to pull air in and relaxes to push air out
topic:mt_4JpMXUIxeD:name: The Immune System
topic:mt_4JpMXUIxeD:description: Know that the body has an immune system that protects against illness: the skin acts as a barrier, white blood cells identify and destroy germs (bacteria and viruses), and vaccines train the immune system to recognise specific diseases before they cause illness
topic:mt_4JpMXUIxeD:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how their body fights off germs — and why getting a vaccine helps protect them from getting sick?
topic:mt_4JpMXUIxeD:evidence:0: Describe the skin as the body's first line of defence against germs
topic:mt_4JpMXUIxeD:evidence:1: Explain that white blood cells detect and fight bacteria and viruses inside the body
topic:mt_4JpMXUIxeD:evidence:2: Describe how vaccines work: they contain weakened or inactive germs that train the immune system to recognise the real disease
topic:mt_qzbgwaUQOA:name: The Nervous System
topic:mt_qzbgwaUQOA:description: Understand that the nervous system has two parts — the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and nerves that branch throughout the body — and that nerve signals travel at high speed to coordinate senses, thought, and movement
topic:mt_qzbgwaUQOA:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a message travels from their finger to their brain when they touch something hot, and then back to their hand to pull it away?
topic:mt_qzbgwaUQOA:evidence:0: Name the two parts of the nervous system: central (brain + spinal cord) and peripheral (nerves throughout the body)
topic:mt_qzbgwaUQOA:evidence:1: Describe the reflex arc: stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord/brain → motor nerve → muscle response
topic:mt_qzbgwaUQOA:evidence:2: State that nerve signals travel extremely fast, which is why reflexes happen almost instantly
topic:mt_LkOMijDvL7:name: Immunity & Vaccines
topic:mt_LkOMijDvL7:description: Distinguish innate (non-specific, immediate) from adaptive (specific, memory-forming) immunity; explain how B cells produce antibodies that recognise specific antigens, how T cells destroy infected cells, and why immunological memory makes vaccines work; and describe the gut microbiome as a community of trillions of microbes that significantly influences immune function
topic:mt_LkOMijDvL7:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked why they don't get chickenpox twice, could they explain the difference between just fighting off a germ and actually 'remembering' it — and describe how a vaccine trains the immune system without causing the disease?
topic:mt_LkOMijDvL7:evidence:0: Distinguishes innate immunity (rapid, non-specific barriers and inflammation) from adaptive immunity (slow, specific, memory-forming)
topic:mt_LkOMijDvL7:evidence:1: Explains how B cells produce antibodies that bind to specific antigens on pathogens, targeting them for destruction
topic:mt_LkOMijDvL7:evidence:2: Explains immunological memory: after first exposure, memory B and T cells remain, making subsequent response faster and stronger — the basis of vaccine protection
topic:mt_okUMpHsV-P:name: Neurons & Brain Structure
topic:mt_okUMpHsV-P:description: Explain how neurons transmit signals as electrochemical impulses across synapses, describe how the brain is organised (lobes and functions, limbic system for emotion), and explain neuroplasticity — why learning and practice physically change brain structure — connecting to optical illusions as evidence that the brain constructs reality rather than passively recording it
topic:mt_okUMpHsV-P:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked why practising a skill like piano or football makes you better over time, could they explain what's actually happening physically in the brain — and describe what it means to say the brain 'rewires itself'?
topic:mt_okUMpHsV-P:evidence:0: Describes the neuron-to-neuron signal pathway: electrical impulse travels along axon, neurotransmitter crosses the synapse, new impulse begins in the next neuron
topic:mt_okUMpHsV-P:evidence:1: Names the four lobes of the cerebral cortex (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital) and gives one function for each
topic:mt_okUMpHsV-P:evidence:2: Explains neuroplasticity: repeated neural pathways become stronger and faster — this is the biological mechanism of learning and skill development
topic:mt_0sELh0MYWb:name: DNA & Genes
topic:mt_0sELh0MYWb:description: Describe the double helix structure of DNA (base pairs, complementarity), explain how genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins, introduce the central dogma (DNA → mRNA → protein) conceptually, and discuss the ethical implications of CRISPR gene editing — including potential benefits (genetic disease treatment) and concerns (germline editing, 'designer babies')
topic:mt_0sELh0MYWb:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that scientists have edited a human gene to prevent a hereditary disease, could they explain what DNA actually is, how genes work, and why some people think editing human DNA raises serious ethical questions?
topic:mt_0sELh0MYWb:evidence:0: Describes DNA as a double helix with four bases (A, T, C, G) where A pairs with T and C pairs with G
topic:mt_0sELh0MYWb:evidence:1: Explains that a gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein, and that proteins carry out most of the body's functions
topic:mt_0sELh0MYWb:evidence:2: Describes CRISPR as a molecular tool that can cut and edit DNA sequences, and raises at least two distinct ethical considerations about its use in humans
topic:mt_J40cOn7VWn:name: How the Body Stays in Balance
topic:mt_J40cOn7VWn:description: Explain homeostasis as the process of maintaining a stable internal environment; describe the main feedback loop systems (negative feedback) using blood glucose regulation (insulin/glucagon) and body temperature as concrete examples; and connect the endocrine system (hormone-secreting glands) to the nervous system as two complementary communication systems with different speeds and durations
topic:mt_J40cOn7VWn:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} ate a large meal of sugary food and was asked what their body does to keep blood sugar from getting dangerously high, could they explain the role of insulin and describe how the feedback system brings levels back to normal?
topic:mt_J40cOn7VWn:evidence:0: Defines homeostasis and explains why maintaining a stable internal environment is essential for survival
topic:mt_J40cOn7VWn:evidence:1: Describes the blood glucose negative feedback loop: glucose rises → pancreas releases insulin → cells take up glucose → glucose falls → insulin release stops
topic:mt_J40cOn7VWn:evidence:2: Compares the nervous system (fast, electrical, short-duration signals) with the endocrine system (slower, chemical, longer-duration signals) and gives an example where each is more appropriate
topic:mt_roinupb_7L:name: Cancer & Stem Cells
topic:mt_roinupb_7L:description: Explain that cancer occurs when mutations in DNA disable normal cell-cycle controls, causing uncontrolled cell division and tumour formation; describe how stem cells differ from specialised cells and their potential for regenerative medicine; and evaluate the ethical debates around embryonic stem cell research and genetic testing
topic:mt_roinupb_7L:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was asked to explain what cancer actually is at a cellular level, could they describe what goes wrong with cell division — and explain why some people object to using stem cells from embryos for medical research, even if it could save lives?
topic:mt_roinupb_7L:evidence:0: Explains cancer as the result of DNA mutations that disable tumour suppressor genes or activate oncogenes, causing unchecked mitosis
topic:mt_roinupb_7L:evidence:1: Distinguishes stem cells (unspecialised, can differentiate) from specialised cells (fixed function) and explains why stem cells are medically valuable
topic:mt_roinupb_7L:evidence:2: Presents the embryonic stem cell debate with at least two specific scientific arguments in favour and two ethical objections against, without simply asserting one side is correct
topic:mt_uUa6cgv8zV:name: Earth Is Made of Rock
topic:mt_uUa6cgv8zV:description: Understand that Earth is made of rock and other solid materials
topic:mt_uUa6cgv8zV:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} picks up a stone in the garden, can they tell you that the whole Earth is made of rock and other materials like that stone?
topic:mt_uUa6cgv8zV:evidence:0: State that the ground beneath us is made of rock
topic:mt_uUa6cgv8zV:evidence:1: Identify rocks and stones as pieces of the Earth
topic:mt_uUa6cgv8zV:evidence:2: Explain that Earth is solid and made of natural materials
topic:mt__pMF-Xb0TE:name: Earthquake Safety
topic:mt__pMF-Xb0TE:description: Know basic earthquake safety: drop, cover, and hold on; move away from windows; tell a trusted adult
topic:mt__pMF-Xb0TE:assessmentPrompt: If you asked {{name}} what to do if the ground started shaking, could they show you 'drop, cover, and hold on' and say they'd move away from windows?
topic:mt__pMF-Xb0TE:evidence:0: Demonstrate the drop, cover, and hold on procedure
topic:mt__pMF-Xb0TE:evidence:1: Explain why to move away from windows and shelves during shaking
topic:mt__pMF-Xb0TE:evidence:2: Name a trusted adult to tell if they feel an earthquake
topic:mt_adpdEaKEBC:name: Fast & Slow Earth Changes
topic:mt_adpdEaKEBC:description: Understand that Earth's surface changes: some changes are quick (eruptions, earthquakes) and some are slow (wind, water wearing away rock)
topic:mt_adpdEaKEBC:assessmentPrompt: If you point out a cliff being worn away by waves, can {{name}} explain that this happens slowly, while a volcanic eruption or earthquake changes the land quickly?
topic:mt_adpdEaKEBC:evidence:0: Give an example of a quick change to Earth's surface like a volcanic eruption
topic:mt_adpdEaKEBC:evidence:1: Give an example of a slow change to Earth's surface like erosion by wind or water
topic:mt_adpdEaKEBC:evidence:2: Compare quick and slow changes and explain the difference
topic:mt_BLQ2_OXPod:name: Power of Eruptions
topic:mt_BLQ2_OXPod:description: Appreciate that volcanic eruptions are powerful events that can change the landscape
topic:mt_BLQ2_OXPod:assessmentPrompt: After watching a video of a volcano erupting, does {{name}} show excitement and talk about how powerful it is and how it changes the land around it?
topic:mt_BLQ2_OXPod:evidence:0: Describe an eruption as a powerful, dramatic event
topic:mt_BLQ2_OXPod:evidence:1: Give examples of how an eruption changes the area around a volcano
topic:mt_BLQ2_OXPod:evidence:2: Compare the landscape before and after an eruption using pictures
topic:mt_e29VrLfmYt:name: What Is an Earthquake
topic:mt_e29VrLfmYt:description: Know what an earthquake is: a sudden shaking of the ground that can be strong or weak
topic:mt_e29VrLfmYt:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that an earthquake is when the ground suddenly shakes, and that some earthquakes shake harder than others?
topic:mt_e29VrLfmYt:evidence:0: Describe an earthquake as the ground shaking suddenly
topic:mt_e29VrLfmYt:evidence:1: Explain that earthquakes vary in strength from barely noticeable to very strong
topic:mt_e29VrLfmYt:evidence:2: Describe what it might feel like during an earthquake
topic:mt_S9SKah-yi_:name: What Is a Volcano
topic:mt_S9SKah-yi_:description: Know what a volcano is: an opening in Earth's surface where hot melted rock (lava) comes out
topic:mt_S9SKah-yi_:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a picture of a volcano erupting, can they explain that it's an opening in the ground where very hot melted rock comes out?
topic:mt_S9SKah-yi_:evidence:0: Describe a volcano as a place where hot material comes out of the Earth
topic:mt_S9SKah-yi_:evidence:1: Explain that lava is rock so hot it has melted
topic:mt_S9SKah-yi_:evidence:2: Point to a volcano in a picture and describe what is happening
topic:mt_dSeFrAWE4v:name: Active, Dormant & Extinct
topic:mt_dSeFrAWE4v:description: Classify volcanoes as active (could erupt any time), dormant (sleeping but could wake up), or extinct (will not erupt again)
topic:mt_dSeFrAWE4v:assessmentPrompt: If you told {{name}} about a volcano that last erupted 500 years ago, could they explain whether it's active, dormant, or extinct, and why a dormant volcano might still be dangerous?
topic:mt_dSeFrAWE4v:evidence:0: Define active, dormant, and extinct volcanoes
topic:mt_dSeFrAWE4v:evidence:1: Explain that a dormant volcano is not safe just because it has not erupted recently
topic:mt_dSeFrAWE4v:evidence:2: Classify a given volcano based on its eruption history
topic:mt_jwElFY7Syd:name: Earth's Layers
topic:mt_jwElFY7Syd:description: Know that Earth has layers — a thin outer crust, a thick hot mantle, and a core at the centre — and that the inside of the Earth is extremely hot
topic:mt_jwElFY7Syd:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} cracks open a hard-boiled egg, can they compare it to Earth and name the three layers — crust on the outside, mantle in the middle, and core at the centre?
topic:mt_jwElFY7Syd:evidence:0: Name Earth's three main layers: crust, mantle, and core
topic:mt_jwElFY7Syd:evidence:1: Explain that the crust is thin compared to the other layers
topic:mt_jwElFY7Syd:evidence:2: State that Earth's interior is extremely hot — hot enough to melt rock
topic:mt_QtIAWOcoQT:name: Inside a Volcano
topic:mt_QtIAWOcoQT:description: Understand the inside of a volcano: magma is hot melted rock underground, lava is the same material after it reaches the surface, and volcanoes have a magma chamber, vent, and crater
topic:mt_QtIAWOcoQT:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a cross-section diagram of a volcano, can they point to the magma chamber, vent, and crater, and explain the difference between magma underground and lava on the surface?
topic:mt_QtIAWOcoQT:evidence:0: Explain that magma is melted rock underground and lava is the same material above ground
topic:mt_QtIAWOcoQT:evidence:1: Label a magma chamber, vent, and crater on a volcano cross-section
topic:mt_QtIAWOcoQT:evidence:2: Describe the path magma takes from underground to the surface during an eruption
topic:mt_XG4RqUIXm8:name: Pompeii & Vesuvius
topic:mt_XG4RqUIXm8:description: Know the story of Pompeii: a Roman city buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD, preserved under volcanic ash, and rediscovered by archaeologists centuries later
topic:mt_XG4RqUIXm8:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a picture of the ruins of Pompeii, can they tell the story of how a Roman city was buried by a volcanic eruption and then found again hundreds of years later?
topic:mt_XG4RqUIXm8:evidence:0: Retell the key events: Vesuvius erupted, Pompeii was buried under ash
topic:mt_XG4RqUIXm8:evidence:1: Explain that the ash preserved the city, its buildings, and even people's shapes
topic:mt_XG4RqUIXm8:evidence:2: Describe how archaeologists uncovered the city and what we can learn from it
topic:mt_bhwf_rDXQL:name: Ring of Fire
topic:mt_bhwf_rDXQL:description: Recognise that volcanoes and earthquakes tend to happen in certain places — especially around the edges of the Pacific Ocean (Ring of Fire) — not randomly across the Earth
topic:mt_bhwf_rDXQL:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a world map showing where earthquakes and volcanoes happen, could they spot the pattern — that they cluster in certain lines and bands rather than being scattered everywhere?
topic:mt_bhwf_rDXQL:evidence:0: Describe the pattern that volcanoes and earthquakes cluster in certain zones
topic:mt_bhwf_rDXQL:evidence:1: Locate the Ring of Fire on a world map
topic:mt_bhwf_rDXQL:evidence:2: Explain that the locations of earthquakes and volcanoes are not random
topic:mt_Wu-ftkzoiE:name: Tsunamis
topic:mt_Wu-ftkzoiE:description: Know what a tsunami is: a very large, fast ocean wave caused by an earthquake or volcanic eruption under the sea, which can cause great damage when it reaches land
topic:mt_Wu-ftkzoiE:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears the word 'tsunami' on the news, can they explain that it's a huge wave caused by an earthquake or eruption under the ocean, and that it can travel very fast across the sea?
topic:mt_Wu-ftkzoiE:evidence:0: Explain that a tsunami is caused by an earthquake or eruption under the sea
topic:mt_Wu-ftkzoiE:evidence:1: State that tsunamis travel very fast across the ocean
topic:mt_Wu-ftkzoiE:evidence:2: Describe the damage a tsunami can cause when it reaches the coast
topic:mt_NYA50DFcOO:name: Types of Rock
topic:mt_NYA50DFcOO:description: Know the three main types of rock — igneous (formed when lava or magma cools), sedimentary (formed from layers pressed together), and metamorphic — and that fossils are found in sedimentary rock
topic:mt_NYA50DFcOO:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} finds different rocks on a beach walk, can they sort them and explain that some formed from cooled lava, some from layers pressed together over time, and that fossils are found in the layered ones?
topic:mt_NYA50DFcOO:evidence:0: Name the three main rock types: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic
topic:mt_NYA50DFcOO:evidence:1: Explain that igneous rock forms when lava or magma cools and hardens
topic:mt_NYA50DFcOO:evidence:2: State that fossils are preserved in sedimentary rock because it forms in layers
topic:mt_NVr4AhsvIq:name: Why Earthquakes Happen
topic:mt_NVr4AhsvIq:description: Understand that earthquakes happen when rocks underground suddenly move or break, releasing energy that shakes the ground
topic:mt_NVr4AhsvIq:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} felt a small tremor or saw footage of an earthquake, could they explain that it happens because rocks deep underground suddenly shift or crack?
topic:mt_NVr4AhsvIq:evidence:0: Explain that earthquakes are caused by rocks underground suddenly moving
topic:mt_NVr4AhsvIq:evidence:1: Describe how this movement sends shaking through the surrounding ground
topic:mt_NVr4AhsvIq:evidence:2: Distinguish between the underground cause and the surface effects of an earthquake
topic:mt_yDZbQODIwp:name: Earthquake-Resistant Design
topic:mt_yDZbQODIwp:description: Know that buildings can be designed to resist earthquakes, tsunami warning systems alert coastal communities, and communities prepare through evacuation plans and drills
topic:mt_yDZbQODIwp:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a documentary about earthquake-proof buildings in Japan, could they explain how engineers design buildings to withstand shaking and how tsunami warnings give people time to evacuate?
topic:mt_yDZbQODIwp:evidence:0: Describe at least one feature that makes buildings more earthquake-resistant
topic:mt_yDZbQODIwp:evidence:1: Explain how tsunami warning systems detect danger and alert communities
topic:mt_yDZbQODIwp:evidence:2: Describe how communities prepare for earthquakes and eruptions through drills and evacuation plans
topic:mt_W4j7T_PnGH:name: Eruption Types & Volcano Shape
topic:mt_W4j7T_PnGH:description: Understand that not all volcanic eruptions are the same: some flow gently (effusive) and some explode violently (explosive), depending on the properties of the magma, and that volcano shape is related to eruption type
topic:mt_W4j7T_PnGH:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared pictures of a gently oozing Hawaiian volcano and a violently erupting one like Mount St Helens, could they explain why eruptions look so different and how that relates to the volcano's shape?
topic:mt_W4j7T_PnGH:evidence:0: Contrast effusive eruptions (gentle lava flows) with explosive eruptions (violent blasts of ash and rock)
topic:mt_W4j7T_PnGH:evidence:1: Explain that eruption type depends on properties of the magma such as thickness and gas content
topic:mt_W4j7T_PnGH:evidence:2: Connect volcano shape to eruption style: shield volcanoes from runny lava, steep cones from thick explosive magma
topic:mt_rML9unnd9x:name: Famous Eruptions & Pangaea
topic:mt_rML9unnd9x:description: Know about famous eruptions and their global effects: Mount St Helens (1980), Eyjafjallajökull (2010), and how large eruptions can affect weather and climate worldwide; understand that continents were once joined (Pangaea) and have slowly drifted apart
topic:mt_rML9unnd9x:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you about a famous volcanic eruption like Mount St Helens and explain how a really big eruption can send so much ash into the sky that it affects weather around the whole world?
topic:mt_rML9unnd9x:evidence:0: Describe at least one famous volcanic eruption and its key effects
topic:mt_rML9unnd9x:evidence:1: Explain how volcanic ash and gases in the atmosphere can cool global temperatures
topic:mt_rML9unnd9x:evidence:2: State that continents were once joined in a supercontinent and have slowly moved apart over millions of years
topic:mt_mdZ3nBWChW:name: Measuring Earthquake Strength
topic:mt_mdZ3nBWChW:description: Know that scientists measure earthquakes using seismometers, that earthquakes release energy that travels as waves through the ground, and that a magnitude scale describes their strength
topic:mt_mdZ3nBWChW:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a news report about a magnitude 6 earthquake, could they explain what a seismometer is, that earthquakes send waves through the ground, and that higher numbers mean stronger quakes?
topic:mt_mdZ3nBWChW:evidence:0: Explain that a seismometer is an instrument that detects and records ground shaking
topic:mt_mdZ3nBWChW:evidence:1: Describe earthquake energy as waves that travel outward from where rocks broke
topic:mt_mdZ3nBWChW:evidence:2: Interpret a magnitude number as a measure of an earthquake's strength
topic:mt_ZRoQVXf_aD:name: Monitoring Volcanoes
topic:mt_ZRoQVXf_aD:description: Understand how volcanologists monitor volcanoes by looking for warning signs — gas emissions, ground swelling, small earthquakes — and that prediction involves evidence and uncertainty, not certainty
topic:mt_ZRoQVXf_aD:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how scientists watch for signs that a volcano might erupt — like gas, ground bulging, or tiny earthquakes — and why they can warn people but can't predict the exact moment?
topic:mt_ZRoQVXf_aD:evidence:0: Name at least two warning signs scientists look for before an eruption
topic:mt_ZRoQVXf_aD:evidence:1: Explain that volcanologists combine multiple types of evidence to assess risk
topic:mt_ZRoQVXf_aD:evidence:2: Discuss why volcanic prediction involves uncertainty and cannot guarantee exact timing
topic:mt_cpDpjJaE5u:name: Natural Disaster Solutions
topic:mt_cpDpjJaE5u:description: Generate and compare multiple solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans, such as earthquakes, floods, or volcanic eruptions
topic:mt_cpDpjJaE5u:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} come up with different ideas for keeping people safe from earthquakes or floods, and compare which ones would work best?
topic:mt_cpDpjJaE5u:evidence:0: Identify at least two natural hazards and their impacts on human life and property
topic:mt_cpDpjJaE5u:evidence:1: Generate multiple solutions for reducing impacts (e.g. earthquake-resistant buildings, flood barriers, early warning systems)
topic:mt_cpDpjJaE5u:evidence:2: Compare solutions based on criteria like effectiveness, cost, and feasibility
topic:mt_-JnOhdei6F:name: Plate Boundaries
topic:mt_-JnOhdei6F:description: Explain how plate boundaries cause earthquakes and volcanoes: plates pushing together, pulling apart, or sliding past each other create the forces that trigger these events, and mountains form where plates collide
topic:mt_-JnOhdei6F:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why most volcanoes and earthquakes happen at the edges of tectonic plates — where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other?
topic:mt_-JnOhdei6F:evidence:0: Describe three types of plate boundary movement: convergent, divergent, and transform
topic:mt_-JnOhdei6F:evidence:1: Explain that earthquakes occur when plates grind or collide at boundaries
topic:mt_-JnOhdei6F:evidence:2: Explain that volcanoes form where plates pull apart or one slides under another, allowing magma to rise
topic:mt_XrvPx5kUfO:name: Tectonic Plates
topic:mt_XrvPx5kUfO:description: Understand that Earth's crust is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates that float on hotter, softer rock beneath and move very slowly — a few centimetres per year
topic:mt_XrvPx5kUfO:assessmentPrompt: If you showed {{name}} a map of the tectonic plates, could they explain that Earth's surface is cracked into huge pieces that move very slowly — about as fast as their fingernails grow?
topic:mt_XrvPx5kUfO:evidence:0: Describe Earth's crust as broken into large plates
topic:mt_XrvPx5kUfO:evidence:1: Explain that the plates float on hotter, partially melted rock underneath
topic:mt_XrvPx5kUfO:evidence:2: State that plates move very slowly, typically a few centimetres per year
topic:mt_z7AJZapsJj:name: The Rock Cycle
topic:mt_z7AJZapsJj:description: Understand the rock cycle: rocks slowly change from one type to another over millions of years — igneous rock weathers into sediment, sediment becomes sedimentary rock, heat and pressure create metamorphic rock, and melting starts the cycle again
topic:mt_z7AJZapsJj:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw igneous rock, sandstone, and marble side by side, could they explain how each type forms and how rocks slowly transform from one type to another in a never-ending cycle?
topic:mt_z7AJZapsJj:evidence:0: Describe the rock cycle as a continuous process with no beginning or end
topic:mt_z7AJZapsJj:evidence:1: Trace at least one complete path through the cycle from igneous to sedimentary to metamorphic and back

topic:mt_gv_uoHkdjR:name: How Tectonic Plates Move
topic:mt_gv_uoHkdjR:description: Understand that convection currents in the molten mantle drive the movement of rigid tectonic plates; distinguish between convergent (collision/subduction), divergent (spreading ridges), and transform (sliding) plate boundaries; explain why volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain chains cluster at boundaries; introduce the Wilson cycle of supercontinent assembly and breakup
topic:mt_gv_uoHkdjR:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a world map showing where volcanoes and earthquakes happen, can they explain why these events follow specific ring-shaped patterns rather than occurring randomly around the globe?
topic:mt__kFxuAgs6d:name: Seismic Waves & Earth's Interior
topic:mt__kFxuAgs6d:description: Distinguish between P-waves (compression, travel through solids and liquids) and S-waves (shear, cannot pass through liquids); explain why a seismic shadow zone exists on the far side of an earthquake; describe how seismologists use wave refraction and reflection to infer that Earth has a solid inner core, liquid outer core, mantle, and crust
topic:mt__kFxuAgs6d:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how scientists know Earth has a liquid outer core if nobody has ever drilled that deep — what clues do earthquake waves give us about Earth's hidden interior?
topic:mt_edaoZRkK6M:name: Hazard Assessment & Evacuation
topic:mt_edaoZRkK6M:description: Explain probabilistic hazard assessment using eruption recurrence intervals and fault slip rates; describe how volcano observatories monitor ground deformation, gas emissions, and seismicity to issue alert levels; explore why communities remain near active hazards (fertile volcanic soil, poverty, cultural ties); discuss the ethics and politics of evacuation decisions and the social justice dimensions of disaster risk

topic:mt_Am_iTzHjoe:name: Supervolcanoes & Volcanic Winter
topic:mt_Am_iTzHjoe:description: Describe calderas such as Yellowstone and Toba as supervolcanoes capable of erupting thousands of cubic kilometres of ash; explain how sulphur dioxide aerosols in the stratosphere scatter sunlight and cause volcanic winter; discuss the Toba catastrophe theory and how giant eruptions have interacted with ice ages; contrast supervolcano eruptions with ordinary eruptions in scale and climate impact
topic:mt_Am_iTzHjoe:assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} heard of a supervolcano? Can they describe how a single enormous eruption could cool the entire planet for years — what gets into the atmosphere and why does it block warmth?
topic:mt_QwWo6an9N1:name: Volcanoes & Mass Extinctions
topic:mt_QwWo6an9N1:description: Explain how large igneous provinces (LIPs) — massive outpourings of lava over millions of years — caused global warming and ocean acidification that drove mass extinctions; connect the Siberian Traps to the end-Permian extinction and the Deccan Traps to the end-Cretaceous event; explore how hydrothermal vents on the early Earth may have been the cradle of life; understand volcanoes as both destroyers and creators in the history of life

topic:mt_jc9k_HJQGd:name: Types of Weather
topic:mt_jc9k_HJQGd:description: Identify and describe different types of weather — sunny, rainy, windy, snowy, cloudy, foggy, stormy — and describe what the weather is like today using simple vocabulary
topic:mt_jc9k_HJQGd:assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} looks out the window in the morning, can they describe the weather using words like sunny, cloudy, rainy, or windy, and say whether it's a nice day or a wet day?
topic:mt_jc9k_HJQGd:evidence:0: Name at least five types of weather
topic:mt_jc9k_HJQGd:evidence:1: Describe today's weather accurately using appropriate vocabulary
topic:mt_jc9k_HJQGd:evidence:2: Match weather types to simple pictures or symbols
topic:mt_URezjbU-6f:name: Weather Forecasting & Safety
topic:mt_URezjbU-6f:description: Ask questions to obtain information about the purpose of weather forecasting and how people prepare for and respond to severe weather
topic:mt_URezjbU-6f:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why we check the weather forecast and what people do to get ready for a big storm or very hot weather?
topic:mt_URezjbU-6f:evidence:0: Explain that weather forecasts help people plan and stay safe
topic:mt_URezjbU-6f:evidence:1: Describe how people prepare for at least two types of severe weather (storm, flood, heat wave, blizzard)
topic:mt_URezjbU-6f:evidence:2: Ask relevant questions about weather hazards and find answers from appropriate sources
topic:mt_j7cj9eWN7w:name: What Is Wind?
topic:mt_j7cj9eWN7w:description: Know that wind is moving air, that it can be gentle (a breeze) or very strong (a gale), and that wind can move things like leaves, kites, flags, and even push people
topic:mt_j7cj9eWN7w:assessmentPrompt: On a windy day, can {{name}} explain that wind is air moving, point out things being blown around, and describe whether it's a gentle breeze or a strong gust?
topic:mt_j7cj9eWN7w:evidence:0: Define wind as air that is moving
topic:mt_j7cj9eWN7w:evidence:1: Describe the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong wind
topic:mt_j7cj9eWN7w:evidence:2: Give examples of things that wind can move or affect
topic:mt_IhWzO4sQPg:name: Cloud Types
topic:mt_IhWzO4sQPg:description: Identify the three main cloud types — cumulus (fluffy, fair weather), stratus (flat layers, overcast or drizzle), and cirrus (thin wisps, high up) — and understand that clouds form when water vapour in the air cools and condenses into tiny droplets
topic:mt_IhWzO4sQPg:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked up at the sky, could they identify whether the clouds are fluffy cumulus, flat stratus, or wispy cirrus, and explain that clouds are made of tiny water droplets?
topic:mt_IhWzO4sQPg:evidence:0: Name and describe the three main cloud types: cumulus, stratus, cirrus
topic:mt_IhWzO4sQPg:evidence:1: Explain that clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses
topic:mt_IhWzO4sQPg:evidence:2: Use cloud type to make a simple prediction about the weather
topic:mt_hjJkBWruO6:name: Geography & Local Weather
topic:mt_hjJkBWruO6:description: Know that different places around the world have very different typical weather — tropical places are hot and wet all year, deserts are very dry, polar regions are freezing cold — and that geography (distance from the equator, altitude, nearness to the sea) affects local weather
topic:mt_hjJkBWruO6:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared weather in a tropical rainforest, a desert, and the Arctic, could they describe how different each is and explain why — like distance from the equator?
topic:mt_hjJkBWruO6:evidence:0: Describe typical weather in at least three different climate types
topic:mt_hjJkBWruO6:evidence:1: Explain that places near the equator tend to be hotter
topic:mt_hjJkBWruO6:evidence:2: Name at least one factor that affects a place's weather besides latitude
topic:mt_fhqVdj4BYr:name: The Water Cycle
topic:mt_fhqVdj4BYr:description: Understand the water cycle: the Sun heats water in oceans and lakes causing it to evaporate into water vapour, the vapour rises and cools to form clouds (condensation), and water falls back to Earth as rain, snow, or hail (precipitation) — then the cycle repeats
topic:mt_fhqVdj4BYr:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} trace the journey of a raindrop — from the ocean being heated by the Sun, rising as invisible vapour, forming a cloud, and falling back down as rain — and explain it keeps going round and round?
topic:mt_fhqVdj4BYr:evidence:0: Name the three main stages: evaporation, condensation, precipitation
topic:mt_fhqVdj4BYr:evidence:1: Explain the Sun's role in driving the water cycle
topic:mt_fhqVdj4BYr:evidence:2: Describe the water cycle as a continuous loop with no beginning or end
topic:mt_BO_AHGLCk0:name: Thunder & Lightning
topic:mt_BO_AHGLCk0:description: Know that thunder and lightning happen during thunderstorms: lightning is a giant spark of electricity that forms in clouds, thunder is the sound the lightning makes, and we see lightning before hearing thunder because light travels faster than sound
topic:mt_BO_AHGLCk0:assessmentPrompt: During a thunderstorm, can {{name}} explain that lightning is electricity in the clouds, thunder is its sound, and that we see the flash before the boom because light is faster than sound?
topic:mt_BO_AHGLCk0:evidence:0: Describe lightning as a large electrical discharge in clouds
topic:mt_BO_AHGLCk0:evidence:1: Explain that thunder is the sound caused by lightning
topic:mt_BO_AHGLCk0:evidence:2: State that we see lightning before hearing thunder because light travels faster than sound
topic:mt_sA0RvWXSYY:name: Using Weather Instruments
topic:mt_sA0RvWXSYY:description: Use weather instruments to measure and record weather data: thermometers for temperature in °C, rain gauges for rainfall, wind vanes for direction, and anemometers for wind speed — and keep a weather diary over time
topic:mt_sA0RvWXSYY:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had a thermometer, rain gauge, and wind vane at school, could they take daily readings, record them in a table, and spot patterns over a week or month?
topic:mt_sA0RvWXSYY:evidence:0: Name at least three weather instruments and explain what each measures
topic:mt_sA0RvWXSYY:evidence:1: Read a thermometer and record the temperature in degrees Celsius
topic:mt_sA0RvWXSYY:evidence:2: Record weather data in a table or diary over several days
topic:mt_AghN5YcCHX:name: Weather Forecasting
topic:mt_AghN5YcCHX:description: Know that meteorologists are scientists who study and forecast the weather using satellites, radar, weather balloons, and computer models, and that weather forecasts help people plan their activities and prepare for dangerous weather
topic:mt_AghN5YcCHX:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what a meteorologist does, name some tools they use like satellites and radar, and describe why weather forecasts are important for keeping people safe?
topic:mt_AghN5YcCHX:evidence:0: Define a meteorologist as a scientist who studies and predicts weather
topic:mt_AghN5YcCHX:evidence:1: Name at least three tools meteorologists use
topic:mt_AghN5YcCHX:evidence:2: Explain why weather forecasting is useful for safety and daily planning
topic:mt_AB-TEMXSGJ:name: Weather vs Climate
topic:mt_AB-TEMXSGJ:description: Distinguish between weather and climate: weather is what the atmosphere is doing right now or today (it can change hour to hour), while climate is the typical pattern of weather in a place over many years
topic:mt_AB-TEMXSGJ:assessmentPrompt: If someone said 'It's raining today so climate change isn't real,' could {{name}} explain the difference between weather (today's conditions) and climate (patterns over many years)?
topic:mt_AB-TEMXSGJ:evidence:0: Define weather as short-term atmospheric conditions
topic:mt_AB-TEMXSGJ:evidence:1: Define climate as the long-term pattern of weather in a place
topic:mt_AB-TEMXSGJ:evidence:2: Give an example showing the difference: a cold day doesn't change the overall climate
topic:mt_-UAxilUtUt:name: What Causes Wind
topic:mt_-UAxilUtUt:description: Understand what causes wind: the Sun heats the Earth's surface unevenly, warm air rises because it is lighter, and cooler air rushes in to take its place — this movement of air is wind
topic:mt_-UAxilUtUt:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why wind blows — that the Sun warms some areas more than others, warm air floats upward, and cooler air rushes in to fill the gap?
topic:mt_-UAxilUtUt:evidence:0: Explain that the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly
topic:mt_-UAxilUtUt:evidence:1: State that warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it
topic:mt_-UAxilUtUt:evidence:2: Define this air movement as wind
topic:mt_JmMtZCifJB:name: Designing for Weather Hazards
topic:mt_JmMtZCifJB:description: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impacts of a weather-related hazard such as flooding, wind damage, or extreme temperatures
topic:mt_JmMtZCifJB:assessmentPrompt: If there's a risk of flooding in a town, can {{name}} evaluate different solutions like building levees, planting trees, or improving drainage and argue which works best?
topic:mt_JmMtZCifJB:evidence:0: Identify a specific weather-related hazard and its impacts on people
topic:mt_JmMtZCifJB:evidence:1: Describe at least two design solutions intended to reduce those impacts
topic:mt_JmMtZCifJB:evidence:2: Make a claim supported by evidence about which solution is most effective and why
topic:mt_DbI1kNg_0R:name: Climate Change Basics
topic:mt_DbI1kNg_0R:description: Understand the basics of climate change: Earth’s atmosphere traps some of the Sun's heat (the greenhouse effect), burning fossil fuels adds extra greenhouse gases (especially CO₂), this is making Earth gradually warmer, and this warming changes weather patterns, melts ice, and raises sea levels
topic:mt_DbI1kNg_0R:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the greenhouse effect in simple terms and describe how burning oil, gas, and coal adds extra CO₂ to the air, making Earth warmer and changing weather patterns?
topic:mt_DbI1kNg_0R:evidence:0: Describe the greenhouse effect: the atmosphere traps heat from the Sun
topic:mt_DbI1kNg_0R:evidence:1: Explain that burning fossil fuels increases CO₂ in the atmosphere
topic:mt_DbI1kNg_0R:evidence:2: Name at least two consequences of global warming: changing weather patterns, melting ice, rising seas
topic:mt_TMOzMCE17H:name: Climate Zones
topic:mt_TMOzMCE17H:description: Understand that Earth has distinct climate zones — tropical (hot and wet near the equator), temperate (moderate, with four seasons), polar (freezing cold), arid/desert (very dry), and mountain (cold at high altitude) — and that each zone supports different ecosystems and ways of life
topic:mt_TMOzMCE17H:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a world map showing climate zones, could they explain why the Amazon rainforest, the Sahara desert, and the Arctic all have such different weather, plants, and animals?
topic:mt_TMOzMCE17H:evidence:0: Name and describe at least four climate zones
topic:mt_TMOzMCE17H:evidence:1: Explain what determines which zone a place belongs to (mainly latitude and geography)
topic:mt_TMOzMCE17H:evidence:2: Give an example of how a climate zone affects the plants, animals, or people living there
topic:mt_6EfevRyeFW:name: Extreme Weather Events
topic:mt_6EfevRyeFW:description: Know about extreme weather events — hurricanes (spinning storms over warm ocean), tornadoes (violent rotating columns of air), floods, droughts, and blizzards — how they form, where they typically occur, and their effects on people and the environment
topic:mt_6EfevRyeFW:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw news about a hurricane, could they explain how it forms over warm ocean water, why it spins, and what makes it so destructive when it reaches land?
topic:mt_6EfevRyeFW:evidence:0: Describe how at least two types of extreme weather form
topic:mt_6EfevRyeFW:evidence:1: Explain where hurricanes and tornadoes typically occur and why
topic:mt_6EfevRyeFW:evidence:2: Describe the effects of extreme weather on communities and landscapes
topic:mt_VI5kdtf28e:name: Natural resources
topic:mt_VI5kdtf28e:description: Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels are derived from natural resources and that their uses affect the environment
topic:mt_VI5kdtf28e:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain where petrol, electricity, and gas come from — that they come from natural resources like oil, coal, wind, or sunlight — and how using them affects the environment?
topic:mt_VI5kdtf28e:evidence:0: Name natural resources used for energy and fuels (coal, oil, gas, wind, sun, water)
topic:mt_VI5kdtf28e:evidence:1: Describe how extracting and using these resources affects the environment (pollution, habitat loss, climate change)
topic:mt_VI5kdtf28e:evidence:2: Distinguish between renewable (wind, solar) and non-renewable (fossil fuels) energy sources
topic:mt_3pgTpuetKi:name: Reading Weather Maps
topic:mt_3pgTpuetKi:description: Read and interpret weather maps, data tables, and graphs — identifying symbols for sun, rain, wind, and temperature; spotting trends and patterns in weather data over weeks, months, or seasons; and using data to make simple predictions
topic:mt_3pgTpuetKi:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a weather map with symbols on the news, could they read it and explain what weather is coming — and if shown a graph of monthly rainfall, could they spot the wettest and driest months?
topic:mt_3pgTpuetKi:evidence:0: Interpret common weather map symbols for temperature, precipitation, and wind
topic:mt_3pgTpuetKi:evidence:1: Read a data table or graph of weather data and identify patterns
topic:mt_3pgTpuetKi:evidence:2: Use weather data to make a simple prediction about upcoming conditions
topic:mt_-YYnLLIZh5:name: Sun-Driven Weather Systems
topic:mt_-YYnLLIZh5:description: Understand how the Sun drives weather: the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly (land heats faster than water, equator gets more heat than poles), creating differences in air pressure that cause wind patterns, ocean currents, and large-scale weather systems
topic:mt_-YYnLLIZh5:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why coastal areas often have sea breezes and why the equator is hotter than the poles, connecting it all back to the Sun heating Earth unevenly?
topic:mt_-YYnLLIZh5:evidence:0: Explain that the Sun heats land and water at different rates
topic:mt_-YYnLLIZh5:evidence:1: Describe how temperature differences create air pressure differences that drive wind
topic:mt_-YYnLLIZh5:evidence:2: Connect uneven heating to large-scale weather patterns
topic:mt_fkcxpeYP85:name: The Atmosphere
topic:mt_fkcxpeYP85:description: Know that Earth is surrounded by a layer of air called the atmosphere, that air has weight and exerts pressure, that the atmosphere protects us from harmful radiation and keeps the planet warm enough for life, and that weather happens in the lowest layer (troposphere)
topic:mt_fkcxpeYP85:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that we're surrounded by a blanket of air called the atmosphere, that this air actually has weight and pushes on everything, and that all our weather happens in the lowest layer?
topic:mt_fkcxpeYP85:evidence:0: Define the atmosphere as the layer of air surrounding Earth
topic:mt_fkcxpeYP85:evidence:1: State that air has weight and exerts pressure
topic:mt_fkcxpeYP85:evidence:2: Explain that weather occurs in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere
topic:mt_iiUdDUEEGY:name: Weather-Resistant Engineering
topic:mt_iiUdDUEEGY:description: Understand that engineers design buildings, flood defences, and warning systems to protect communities from extreme weather — hurricane-resistant roofs, flood barriers, tornado shelters, and early-warning alert systems — and evaluate the merits of these solutions
topic:mt_iiUdDUEEGY:assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw pictures of houses on stilts in a flood zone and a tornado shelter, could they explain how each design protects people and discuss whether one solution works better than another?
topic:mt_iiUdDUEEGY:evidence:0: Describe at least two engineering solutions designed to protect against extreme weather
topic:mt_iiUdDUEEGY:evidence:1: Explain how a specific design feature reduces damage from a weather hazard
topic:mt_iiUdDUEEGY:evidence:2: Evaluate the advantages and limitations of a weather protection solution
topic:mt_iYOcfzFqMw:name: Global Wind Patterns
topic:mt_iYOcfzFqMw:description: Explain that unequal solar heating drives large-scale atmospheric circulation: Hadley cells (0-30°), Ferrel cells (30-60°), and polar cells (60-90°) produce the trade winds, westerlies, and polar easterlies; describe how the Coriolis effect from Earth's rotation deflects winds rightward in the Northern Hemisphere; explain the jet stream as a fast high-altitude wind that steers weather systems; connect jet stream waviness and Arctic amplification to prolonged extreme weather
topic:mt_iYOcfzFqMw:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why the UK tends to get wet weather arriving from the west — what global pattern of winds is steering weather systems, and how does Earth's rotation contribute to this?
topic:mt_EQQWKz03P8:name: Greenhouse Gas Science
topic:mt_EQQWKz03P8:description: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum and distinguish between short-wave solar radiation and long-wave infrared radiation emitted by Earth; explain how greenhouse gas molecules (CO2, CH4, N2O, H2O) absorb and re-emit infrared through molecular vibration while O2 and N2 do not; distinguish the natural greenhouse effect (which makes Earth habitable) from the enhanced greenhouse effect driven by human emissions; evaluate the relative potency of different greenhouse gases
topic:mt_EQQWKz03P8:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain, in terms of light and energy, why CO2 in the atmosphere traps heat but nitrogen and oxygen — which make up most of the air — don't? What's physically different about CO2 molecules?
topic:mt__wWHVvqMWb:name: Hurricanes, Tornadoes & Monsoons
topic:mt__wWHVvqMWb:description: Explain how hurricanes form and intensify over warm ocean water (latent heat release, low-pressure spiral); describe tornado formation within supercell thunderstorms; explain monsoon mechanics driven by temperature differences between land and sea; introduce attribution science — how scientists use climate models to calculate whether and by how much climate change increased the probability or intensity of a specific extreme weather event
topic:mt__wWHVvqMWb:assessmentPrompt: When scientists say that climate change made a recent hurricane stronger, can {{name}} explain what they actually mean and how scientists figure that out — what kind of calculation lets them link a specific storm to climate change?
topic:mt_olFzbawexJ:name: Reading Ancient Climate Records
topic:mt_olFzbawexJ:description: Explain how ice cores preserve ancient air bubbles, isotope ratios, and volcanic markers allowing reconstruction of temperature and CO2 going back 800,000 years; describe tree rings, ocean sediment cores, coral skeletons, and pollen records as additional climate proxies; explain how climate models are built and validated against the palaeoclimate record; describe the IPCC process of synthesising scientific evidence across thousands of studies to produce consensus assessments
topic:mt_olFzbawexJ:assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how scientists know what the climate was like 500,000 years ago — what kind of 'time capsules' exist in nature that preserve ancient air and temperature records, and how do scientists read them?
topic:mt_Wzj1RETm9A:name: Net Zero & Energy Transition
topic:mt_Wzj1RETm9A:description: Evaluate the energy transition required to reach net zero: renewable energy scaling, electrification of transport and heat, green hydrogen; describe carbon capture and storage (CCS) and direct air capture (DAC); introduce proposed solar radiation management techniques (stratospheric aerosol injection, marine cloud brightening) and their potential risks and governance challenges; critically evaluate the role of individual behaviour change versus systemic policy in reducing emissions
topic:mt_Wzj1RETm9A:assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} heard of geoengineering? Can they describe one proposal for deliberately cooling the Earth and explain one potential risk of attempting it — and say whether they think individuals or governments bear more responsibility for tackling climate change?
